title: City releases Bearspaw South Feeder Main Third Party Independent Review Panel and Advisory Group Costs
summary: In response to a motion approved at the Regular Council Meeting on October 27, 2026, The City has made public the amounts invoiced and paid to the Chair and Panel Members of the Bearspaw South Feeder Main Independent Review Panel, as well as information provided to Council during the Q4 2024 Regular Update with Chief Administrative Officer related to the third-party panel. The total cost reflects the work required to complete a comprehensive, independent and evidence-based assessment from uniquely qualified industry experts, including: The length and breadth of the review, which took nine months and considered all aspects of the water utility; The need for independent engineering, technical, and advisory expertise; and Additional effort required as the scope became fully defined over the course of the work, coupled with support while The City responded to the second feeder main break. More details of the response can be found here : Bearspaw Feeder Main Independent review

title: Police use intelligence to target drug trafficking through Operation Guardian
summary: We have seized more than $350,000 worth of drugs as part of an ongoing operation that is targeting drug and firearms activity throughout Calgary. In September 2026, our Organized Crime Enforcement Unit (OCEU) and Strategic Data Integration and Intelligence Analytical Unit (SDIIAU) worked together to develop Operation Guardian. Operation Guardian uses geospatial analysis and crime data to detect areas where drug and firearms activity is increasing relative to historical patterns, resulting in early criminal hot spot detection. Officers within OCEU use this analysis to deploy to these areas to disrupt criminal activity, collect intelligence and conduct investigations and enforcement. Since the operation launched on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026, these intelligence-led insights have resulted in 67 traffic stops, four separate drug trafficking investigations, five arrests and 17 charges. In total, we have seized: 3.18 kilograms of fentanyl 175.5 grams of powder cocaine 66.2 grams of crack cocaine 701 fentanyl pills More than $12,000 in cash Photos of some of the seized items are available at The City of Calgary Newsroom. As part of our investigations, five people have been charged: Trevor BREAU, 34, of Calgary, was charged with two counts each of possession of a controlled substance for the purpose of trafficking and resisting or obstructing a peace officer. He was also charged under the Radiocommunications Act with one count each of unlawful operation of a radio apparatus and unlawful possession of equipment/device. He is scheduled to appear in court on Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. Jaden SUAREZ-BALLEZA, 26, of Calgary, was charged with one count each of possession of a controlled substance for the purpose of trafficking and possession of proceeds of crime under $5,000. He is scheduled to appear in court on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. Georgiy PAK, 22, of Calgary, was charged with two counts of possession of a controlled substance for the purpose of trafficking and one count of possession of proceeds of crime under $5,000. He is scheduled to appear in court on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. Prinderjit Singh BINNING, 32, of Calgary, was charged with two counts of possession of a controlled substance for the purpose of trafficking and one count of possession of proceeds of crime over $5,000. He is scheduled to appear in court on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. A 15-year-old girl, of Calgary, who cannot be named under the provisions of the Youth Criminal Justice Act , was charged with two counts of possession of a controlled substance for the purpose of trafficking and one count of possession of proceeds of crime under $5,000. She is scheduled to appear in court on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. This work was enabled by a recent realignment of resources in our Organized Crime & Offender Management Section, which allowed for greater co-ordination between investigative resources. Proactive investigation and enforcement efforts related to Operation Guardian are ongoing. If you have information about drug, firearms or organized crime activity in Calgary, contact police by calling 403-266-1234. title: Calgary volunteers plant more than 8,500 trees to help grow our urban forest
summary: More than 1,200 volunteers supported The City's Urban Forestry team this spring and summer to plant 8,570 trees, helping create a greener, healthier Calgary for generations to come. From June through September, community associations, local businesses, organizations and individual Calgarians dug in to help grow Calgary's urban forest through The City's Volunteer Tree Planting Program. Together, volunteers took part in 35 planting events at 21 locations across 19 communities, with 28 different volunteer groups contributing to this year's success. In total, 8,570 trees were planted, including 1,500 whips (small saplings), which, as they grow, will create a greener city that will benefit Calgarians for decades to come. “We are incredibly grateful to the volunteers and partner groups who contributed their time and energy to help grow Calgary's urban forest," said Randi Kelley, Urban Forestry Field Coordinator, City of Calgary, Parks and Open Spaces. "Their enthusiasm and commitment have made a difference in our communities. The trees they planted will provide shade, beauty and environmental benefits for generations of Calgarians to come. We couldn't do this work without them.” One of this year's planting highlights took place at Ted Harrison School in Taradale, where volunteers planted over 2,000 trees over five planting events. The trees were planted in multiple beds arranged in creative configurations, transforming an area of the school grounds into what students are already calling their very own “maze." While the trees are still young, students are excited to watch their mini forest grow and change over the coming years. As the trees mature, they'll help create a greener, more inviting schoolyard, providing shade, opportunities to connect with nature and lasting benefits for students, families and the surrounding community. The success of the Volunteer Tree Planting Program is made possible through partnerships with community groups, local businesses and organizations, including Trees for Life, one of The City's planting partners. "We at Trees for Life applaud the City of Calgary's efforts to double their urban tree canopy," said Mike Hurley, Development Director, Trees for Life. “We are proud to offer any support we can to help advance the progress toward this ambitious goal and to help engage the local community in the process. Trees are not only vital to the overall health of a vibrant urban community, but they are a phenomenal way to thank and engage local groups and individuals who also contribute to the overall wellbeing of the community.” These community planting efforts also support The City's long-term goal of increasing Calgary's urban tree canopy coverage to 16 per cent by 2060. Calgary's most recent tree canopy measurement was 9.62 per cent in 2024, and every new tree planted helps move us toward that target as it grows and matures. Anyone interested in helping grow Calgary's urban forest can visit calgary.ca/volunteertreeplanting ⁠ to learn more about the Volunteer Tree Planting Program and check back in spring 2027 for next season's planting opportunities. For more information on caring for Calgary's trees, please visit calgary.ca/trees .

title: City of Calgary reminds residents: Celebrate Diwali and Bandi Chhor Divas safely
summary: As Diwali and Bandi Chhor Divas approach, The City of Calgary, Calgary Fire Department (CFD), Emergency Management & Community Safety (EMCS) and Calgary Police Service (CPS) are wishing everyone a happy, safe and joyful festival season. These celebrations hold deep cultural significance for many Calgarians and are celebrated in homes, places of worship and communities across our city. As families and communities prepare to celebrate, it's important to understand Calgary's rules around fireworks and how to celebrate safely. Personal fireworks are not permitted in Calgary. This includes fireworks purchased outside Calgary or ordered online. Fireworks can quickly cause fires, injuries and property damage. "Happy Diwali and Bandi Chhor Divas to everyone celebrating across Calgary," says Glenn Baxter, Fire Marshal with CFD. "Fireworks can quickly ignite grass, vehicles and homes. We've seen first-hand how one firework can lead to significant property damage and put lives at risk. We ask residents to celebrate responsibly and be mindful of those around them." During Diwali 2025, CPS received 167 fireworks-related calls, and The City received 44, 311 reports. CFD crews responded to several fires caused by fireworks, including grass fires, a vehicle fire and a structure fire. In one incident, hundreds of individuals discharged thousands of fireworks over several hours, requiring a significant police response. Updated fines now in effect To improve public safety, The City recently strengthened fireworks enforcement. Effective Sept. 22, 2026, fines increased and a new offence was introduced for carrying or setting up fireworks in public places before they are discharged. Current penalties include: Selling or offering fireworks for sale without authorization: $3,000 Possessing fireworks in a public place: $1,000 Discharging fireworks without a permit: $1,000 "These changes close an important gap in our enforcement tools," says Damian Cole, Deputy Chief of Community Safety. "Officers can now intervene when fireworks are being prepared for use in public spaces, helping prevent dangerous situations before they occur." "We want everyone to enjoy these celebrations safely and respectfully," says Geoff Gawlinski, Staff Sergeant with CPS. "Last year, officers responded to numerous fireworks-related complaints, including reports that were initially believed to be gunshots. Unauthorized fireworks can create safety concerns and place significant demands on emergency services.” Illegal fireworks sales remain prohibited The City is also reminding businesses that selling fireworks without a permit is illegal in Calgary. "Selling fireworks without authorization is against the law and carries significant penalties,” says Michael Briegel, Deputy Chief of Business Safety. “Businesses must understand the regulations and ensure they are operating in compliance with Calgary's bylaws.” Celebrate safely The City recognizes that fireworks are an important part of Diwali celebrations for many people and there is no perfect substitute. However, Calgary's restrictions are in place to protect families, neighbours and communities. Residents are encouraged to light diyas safely, use LED candles, decorate with festive lights, attend community celebrations, and gather with family and friends. Small birthday cake sparklers are exempt from the bylaw, but must be used safely and responsibly. "Safety is a shared responsibility," says Glenn Baxter. "By understanding the rules and making informed choices, we can help ensure everyone enjoys a safe and memorable celebration." Please report illegal fireworks concerns to 311, using the category “Disturbance and Public Behaviour Concerns” and including details about the location. Call 9-1-1 to report a fire or emergency. For more information, visit www.calgary.ca/fireworks . For information on safer Diwali practices, visit www.calgary.ca/Diwali .

title: Man charged in bank investigator fraud scam that impersonated police and financial institutions
summary: The Calgary Police Service Financial Crime Investigation Unit's Fraud Team has charged one man in relation to a bank investigator fraud scam in which offenders allegedly impersonated financial institutions and Calgary police officers using caller ID spoofing technology. Between Saturday, June 7, 2025, and Monday, July 14, 2025, the Calgary Police Service received several reports of bank investigator fraud scams. In these scams, offenders use caller ID spoofing technology to display legitimate financial institution customer service telephone numbers on victims' caller ID. The calls appear to originate from the victims' financial institution. Offenders then falsely claim unauthorized transactions have compromised the victims' accounts and linked them to criminal activity. Victims are then directed to speak with individuals posing as Calgary police officers and instructed to place their bank cards in envelopes for courier pickup from their homes. The cards and associated banking information are then used to conduct unauthorized ATM withdrawals and point-of-sale purchases. Through CCTV footage, investigators identified a suspect allegedly purchasing and redeeming gift cards. The suspect was arrested on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026. As a result, Imani Lionel CROSS, 26, of Calgary, is charged with one count of fraud over $5,000, two counts of possession of property obtained by crime and one count of laundering the proceeds of crime. CROSS was also arrested on an outstanding warrant. CROSS is scheduled to appear in court on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. By the numbers: Bank and police impersonation scams continue to be an emerging trend across Canada and are not isolated to Calgary or the Calgary Police Service. We have also seen offenders pose as RCMP officers and direct victims to transfer cryptocurrency or deposit money into Bitcoin ATMs. Police services across the country continue to investigate these scams and work to identify and hold those responsible accountable. In 2025, we received 24 reports involving both bank and police impersonation, compared with seven reports so far in 2026. For police impersonation scams specifically, we received 171 reports in 2025, compared with 27 reports so far in 2026. The 2026 statistics are current as of Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026. We continue to encourage Calgarians to remain vigilant when contacted by anyone claiming to represent a financial institution, police service or another trusted organization. Police will never ask you to send money, transfer cryptocurrency or deposit funds into a Bitcoin ATM as part of an investigation. Fraud prevention tips: The Calgary Police Service reminds citizens that: · Financial institutions and police will never ask you to mail bank cards, provide banking credentials, send money or make purchases as part of an investigation. · Be cautious of unexpected calls, emails or text messages claiming to be from your bank, police or another trusted organization. Fraudsters can spoof phone numbers and create convincing messages that appear legitimate. · When in doubt, delete suspicious messages or hang up, then contact the organization directly using an official phone number or website to verify the request. · Never share personal information, banking information, passwords or verification codes with an unsolicited caller or sender. · If you feel pressured to act immediately or something does not seem right, stop the conversation and speak with a trusted friend, family member or co-worker before taking any action. Anyone with information about this incident is asked to contact police by calling 403-266-1234. Tips can also be submitted anonymously to Crime Stoppers through any of the following methods: TALK: 1-800-222-8477 TYPE: www.calgarycrimestoppers.org APP: P3 Tips Case #: CA25337952

title: Boil Water Advisory has been rescinded for Eagle Ridge
summary: CALGARY – Effective immediately, Alberta Health Services has rescinded the Boil Water Advisory for the community of Eagle Ridge. The Boil Water Advisory remains for Heritage Park. Heritage Park is a working directly with Alberta Health Services to ensure testing requirement are met for their site. The City of Calgary labs, in collaboration with Alberta Health Services (AHS) and Alberta Environment and Protected Areas) have tested and confirmed that the water in Eagle Ridge meet water-quality guidelines and standards and is safe for consuming. If you have used your household or business water in the past 24 hours, it can now be safely consumed without boiling. If you have not used your household or business water in the past 24 hours, you should flush your system. To flush your household or business water system: ➡️ Turn the bathtub tap on cold for ten minutes. Then turn all other faucets on cold for five minutes. ➡️ For businesses without a bathtub or shower, turn on all your faucets on cold for ten minutes. The City of Calgary thanks affected residents and businesses for their patience and cooperation during this time. For more information visit calgary.ca/boilwater or contact 311.

title: City awards two sites to affordable housing providers under non-market land sale program
summary: Calgary, AB — The City of Calgary has awarded two sites approved for disposition under the fifth Non-Market Housing Land Sale (NMLS) Program to affordable housing providers Liberty Housing Organization and Siksika Off-Reserve Affordable Housing (SORAH). The awarded sites are: 155 Cirrus Cl N.E.: Liberty Housing Organization with an envisioned 105 homes for Calgarians 3010 36 St S.E.: SORAH with an envisioned 95 homes for Indigenous Calgarians The NMLS program uses surplus City-owned land to reduce project costs, provide equity and help non-profit providers secure financing and government funding. Each dollar of City land value has leveraged nearly $4.50 from provincial and federal partners. $3.9 million in the form of a land value contribution is being invested in these two projects in total. Also included in NMLS round five was a site located at 15 Santana HL NW, however the applications received did not meet program requirements. The City will not proceed with the awarding of this site in this phase and it will be offered in a future NMLS round. "The need for affordable housing in our city is greater than ever,” says Mayor Jeromy Farkas. “Offering City-owned land to select providers at below market value helps to remove land cost, which is one of the largest barriers facing non-profit housing providers, and helps us to provide more homes for Calgarians.” Both housing providers must now carry out further due diligence to ensure the sites are viable for their projects, and must satisfy their pre-sale conditions, including land use amendments where applicable and development permit approvals. "We are honoured to have been selected through the City's Non-Market Land Sale to transform the Midfield Heights site at 155 Cirrus Close NE into high-quality, non-market housing.” says President of Liberty Housing Organization Oliver Trutina. “This opportunity marks an important step toward expanding affordable housing options and providing more Calgarians with safe, stable homes. We look forward to continuing our partnership with the City of Calgary to help close the housing affordability gap and build more inclusive communities." "The team at SORAH Project is thrilled to continue working with the City of Calgary to create sustainable, vibrant and culturally significant housing solutions for urban Indigenous peoples in the City,” says SORAH General Manager Max Lloyd. “The Dover project will see the construction of close to 100 townhomes, which is critical to helping address the need for affordable housing in Calgary.” Since 2019, NMLS has enabled nearly 1,000 perpetually affordable homes across 18 developments; 280 homes have opened their doors to date with more than 700 in active planning or construction. Learn more about the initiative and find housing resources at calgary.ca/affordablehousing .

title: Police investigate fatal pedestrian collision
summary: We continue to investigate a fatal pedestrian collision that occurred this morning in the community of Martindale. On Monday, Oct. 26, 2026, at approximately 5:40 a.m., a westbound driver attempted to turn into a parking lot at 135 Martindale Blvd. N.E. A pedestrian was laying on the sidewalk in front of the parking lot entrance and the driver passed over him. title: Western Inland Ports form alliance to strengthen Canada's trade corridors
summary: CentrePort Canada, Global Transportation Hub Authority, Leduc County, Edmonton Global and Edmonton Airports (Port Alberta), and The City of Calgary and Rocky View County (Prairie Economic Gateway) have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to create the Canadian Inland Ports Alliance (CIPA). The Alliance will align on major inland port initiatives, strengthening seaport-to-hinterland connectivity and supporting a more resilient, diversified, and competitive Canadian trade network. CIPA responds directly to growing pressures facing Canada's trade and transportation network, including congestion, shifting trade partners, supply chain disruptions, marine gateway constraints and the need for stronger inland capacity. The Alliance will help speed up coordinated action, increase interprovincial trade, expand access to global markets, and strengthen supply chain reliability. The MoU establishes a framework for formal collaboration on planning, advocacy, investment, and performance measurement. The agreement is intended to advance strategic planning focused on Canadian inland ports, aligning priorities, and advancing shared evidence to measure progress and outcomes. The parties will review progress annually and identify opportunities for further collaboration. Quotes “Inland ports play a vital role in strengthening Canada's trade and transportation networks. The Government of Canada is committed to expanding trade opportunities and building resilient supply chains. By investing in modern transportation infrastructure across the country, we are helping ensure the efficient movement of goods while supporting local jobs and economic growth.” - The Honourable Steven MacKinnon, Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons “Prairie Economic Gateway was created to help address Canada's trade challenges by increasing capacity in the trade network and creating new routes to more markets. This agreement shows how municipalities, inland ports and regions can work together to strengthen trade infrastructure, make supply chains more reliable and support a stronger Canadian economy.” - Mayor Jeromy Farkas, City of Calgary “Prairie Economic Gateway is a generational opportunity to strengthen our region's role in Canadian trade, attract investment and create long-term economic opportunity. By coordinating our efforts and planning across the trade corridor, we can help Western Canadian businesses move goods more efficiently and support a more resilient, diversified economy.” - Reeve Sunny Samra, Rocky View County “Canada's trade volumes are growing, and strong, integrated national trade corridors are integral to our sovereignty and connectivity. Inland ports build capacity and resiliency into our national transportation network. As Canada's largest and most established inland port, we have seen firsthand the value inland ports provide for Canadian businesses: More options to move their goods to market, room to invest and grow, and the ability to more easily build resilient and diversified supply chains.” - Carly Edmundson, President & CEO, CentrePort Canada Inc. “Port Alberta is a critical link in Canada's trade network, and the Canadian Inland Ports Alliance will unlock new value across it. By connecting Western Canada's inland ports more directly to global markets, we're opening new routes to market and real revenue opportunities for Canadian and international businesses ready to grow.” – Daryn Edgar, CEO Edmonton Global “As an airport CEO, I recognize that Canada's aviation network is part of a national, multimodal transport system. This MOU reflects our joint efforts to invest in data, deepen our understanding of trade flows, and modernize digital trade strategies—unlocking more efficient intermodal transport and delivering greater value for Canadians.” - Myron Keehn, President and CEO, Edmonton Airports “Trade has always been a cornerstone of Saskatchewan's economy. The Canadian Inland Ports Alliance unites key transportation and logistics partners to strengthen Canada's trade infrastructure, improve access to global markets and build a more connected and resilient supply chain network. Together, we are helping position Canada and Saskatchewan for long-term economic growth and competitiveness.” - Daniel Hersche, President and CEO, The Global Transportation Hub Authority “Leduc County proudly supports the Canadian Inland Ports Alliance, an initiative highlighting the importance of provincial and regional partnerships in driving economic growth across Alberta and Canada. Our County is uniquely positioned to help make this initiative a success by leveraging key assets. These include the Edmonton International Airport (YEG) with its 24/7 global cargo hub, the Nisku Business Park, home to more than 800 businesses and 15,000 employees, and our strategic access to major rail and road networks that move goods and services quickly and efficiently.” – Mayor Tanni Doblanko, Leduc County -30- About CentrePort Canada CentrePort Canada is a 20,000-acre inland port and Foreign Trade Zone. Located in the heart of North America, CentrePort connects to major national and international trade gateways and corridors, and is the only inland port in the country with direct access to tri-modal transportation – extensive truck, rail and air cargo operations. www.centreportcanada.ca About the Global Transportation Hub Authority The Global Transportation Hub Authority (GTH) is Saskatchewan's inland port and one of Canada's premier inland logistics hubs. Located in Regina, Saskatchewan, the GTH provides strategic access to rail, highway, and supply chain infrastructure that connects businesses to markets across North America and around the world. The GTH supports investment attraction, industrial development, and the efficient movement of goods, strengthening Saskatchewan's role in Canada's trade network. About Port Alberta Port Alberta helps businesses unlock new value from the Edmonton Metropolitan Region. In North America's northernmost major inland port. Here, air, rail, pipelines and highways converge, giving Canadian and international companies a direct path to new markets, new customers and new revenue. For businesses ready to grow, a world of opportunity starts here. About Prairie Economic Gateway Prairie Economic Gateway is a regionally approved, shovel-ready collaboration between The City of Calgary and Rocky View County to enable rail-served industrial development and economic diversification in the Calgary region. Gateway is envisioned as the centre of a future inland port supported by private sector investment. By extending trade infrastructure capacity beyond Canada's congested seaports and into the Prairies, the project is intended to strengthen national supply chains, open new opportunities for industrial development, and support long-term economic growth in Alberta and across Canada. title: Calgarians invited to help shape future of arts and culture
summary: As Calgary continues to grow and change, The City is inviting residents to help shape an updated cultural plan for Calgary through public engagement until Nov. 15. The cultural plan will help guide the future of arts, culture, music and Calgary's creative economy. More than a plan for funding, it will establish a long-term cultural vision to guide future investments, policy, partnerships and strategies as the city evolves. Input from Calgarians, partners, artists, organizations and communities will help inform the plan's direction. Arts and culture contribute to community wellbeing, vibrant neighbourhoods and communities, tourism, talent attraction and economic growth. An updated cultural plan will help ensure Calgary continues to benefit from those contributions while identifying opportunities to improve access to arts and culture across the city. "Arts and culture are part of how we experience Calgary every day," says Franca Gualtieri, manager of Arts & Culture at The City of Calgary. "Whether it's a festival, gathering place, cultural tradition or creative experience, these things help shape our city and connect us to one another. We're encouraging Calgarians to share what matters to them to help inform the updated cultural plan." The first Cultural Plan for Calgary was published in 2016 and helped provide a shared vision for arts and culture over the past decade. This project is an opportunity to build on that foundation and develop a cultural plan that supports Calgary for the next 30 years. Calgarians can participate by taking the online survey, joining an online information session or attending an open house. Details about all engagement opportunities are available at calgary.ca/culturalplan . Feedback gathered through this phase of engagement will be summarized in a What We Heard Report and used to help shape the next phase of public and sector engagement in spring 2027. The proposed cultural plan will be presented to Council in late 2027.

title: Man charged after breaching court-ordered release conditions in 48 hours
summary: We have charged a man with several offences after he is believed to have breached his court-ordered release conditions earlier this month. In August 2026, Sage Carson Elias Blaze YOUNGMAN, 20, of Calgary, was charged in relation to a robbery that occurred at a liquor store. At the time of the arrest, a loaded .22-caliber lever action rifle was seized from YOUNGMAN. On Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, YOUNGMAN was released with court-ordered conditions involving a 24-hour curfew and a weapons prohibition. At the time, the Calgary Police Service Offender Management Team began monitoring him. On Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026, members from our Offender Management Team observed YOUNGMAN downtown and confirmed he was in breach of his court-ordered release conditions. Officers from our Community Engagement Response Team (CERT) were nearby and successfully took YOUNGMAN into custody. At the time of his arrest, the following items were seized: A firearm Bear spray Approximately nine grams of methamphetamine Approximately eight grams of Fentanyl As a result, YOUNGMAN is charged with: Two counts of possession of a firearm contrary to a prohibition order Possession of a restricted firearm Possession of a firearm with a defaced serial number Unsafe storage of a firearm Possession for the purpose of trafficking Three counts of breach of a release order Two counts of breach of probation He will next appear in court on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. “We have found targeting repeat offenders is very efficient in promoting public safety, however it requires substantial resources and co-ordination not only from various areas within the Service, but with our external partners as well,” says Staff Sgt. Kerry Smith of the Calgary Police Service Offender Management Unit. “Our officers continue to dedicate a significant amount of time to monitoring high-risk individuals as we try and ensure they do not breach their conditions or reoffend, and that we intervene before they have the opportunity to victimize Calgarians.” Anyone with information about this incident is asked to contact police by calling 403-266-1234. title: Confined Space Rescue in the NW
summary: At approximately 8:40 a.m., Calgary Fire Department crews responded to a confined space rescue at a construction site in the 8000 block of 34 Avenue N.W. Upon arrival, firefighters located a construction worker who had fallen approximately 30 feet down a manhole at the site. Crews safely accessed the patient using air-monitoring equipment and initiated patient care, stabilizing the individual while preparing for removal. The Calgary Fire Department's Technical Rescue Team was dispatched and established a rope rescue system to safely extricate the worker from the confined space. Once stabilized and packaged for transport, the patient was successfully removed from the manhole using the rope rescue system. The patient's care was then transferred to Alberta Health Services, and the individual was transported to hospital in stable condition. Calgary Police Service also attended the scene to assist. As this incident involved a workplace injury, Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) was notified and was enroute to investigate. The Calgary Fire Department would like to recognize the coordinated efforts of all responding agencies whose collaboration contributed to the successful rescue. -30-

title: Joint operation results in 19 arrests and 87 warrants executed
summary: A joint warrant enforcement operation between the Calgary Police Service and Alberta Sheriffs has resulted in 19 arrests and the execution of 87 outstanding warrants. The recent two-day operation brought together members of our District 3 Community Engagement Response Team (CERT), Community Resource Officers (CRO), Patrol Officers and the Fugitive Apprehension Sheriff Support Team (FASST). The initiative focused on locating wanted fugitives, improving public safety and furthering investigations. The operation was planned over several weeks, with analytical resources preparing and reviewing approximately 130 information packages before officers were deployed. During the operation, members attended 62 residences throughout District 3. The operation resulted in: 19 individuals arrested. 87 warrants executed for charges including possession of dangerous weapons, drug trafficking, personation, possession of stolen property and possession of fake ID documents. “Our continuing partnership with the Alberta Sheriffs allows us to improve community safety, by coordinating resources to hold offenders accountable, while addressing ongoing concerns within the district,” says District 3 Insp. Travis Juska. “Strong collaboration between law enforcement agencies is essential to keeping Alberta communities safe. Operations like this demonstrate what we can accomplish when the Alberta Sheriffs and our policing partners work together, share resources and use our combined expertise to locate wanted fugitives and hold offenders accountable,” says Insp. Darren Thompson with the Alberta Sheriffs FASST. The Calgary Police Service extends its thanks to the Alberta Sheriffs for their continued collaboration and support.

title: Council appoints remaining members to Calgary's Water Utility Oversight Board
summary: Council's appointment of four members to Calgary's Water Utility Oversight Board (The Board) marks an important milestone in strengthening independent oversight of Calgary's water utility. Kate Chisholm, Corey Goulet, Edward McCauley and Kim Sturgess will join Stephen Stanley, who was named the inaugural Chair last month. These appointments complete the five-member board being established in response to recommendations from the Bearspaw South Feedermain Independent Review Panel. “We were looking for people who would bring different perspectives to the table, work effectively together and understand the important governance role of the WUOB,” said Steve Stanley, Board Chair. “Together, we have the breadth of experience needed to provide thoughtful, independent advice while keeping a clear focus on the long-term reliability and sustainability of Calgary's water utility.” The members were selected through a skills-based recruitment process supported by an external recruitment firm. It focused on finding individuals with experience in governance, regulatory environments, engineering, critical utility operations, finance, risk management, environmental science and executive utility leadership. “Independent oversight is an important part of a strong and accountable water utility,” said Michael Thompson, COO - Water Utility. “We welcome the perspective The Board will bring alongside Administration's operational knowledge and expertise. I look forward to working together to strengthen decision-making and support a water system Calgarians can rely on for generations to come.” The new members are: Kate Chisholm is an experienced corporate director with C-suite experience spanning legal and regulatory matters, risk management, environmental policy, sustainability and communications. A lawyer by training, she has held senior leadership roles with organizations including Capital Power Corporation, EPCOR Utilities and the Alberta Electric System Operator, and brings extensive board experience. Corey Goulet is a senior energy infrastructure executive with extensive experience in major capital projects, engineering and operations. A mechanical engineer by training, he has held senior leadership roles with Trans Mountain, TC Energy, Kiewit, Steelhead LNG and Tundra Energy Marketing, and brings significant experience working in regulated environments. Edward McCauley is an experienced leader and environmental scientist with extensive governance, research and organizational leadership experience. He has served as President and Vice-Chancellor of the University of Calgary since 2019 and has held leadership roles in water and environmental research, including with the Alberta Ingenuity Centre for Water Research and Alberta Water Research Institute. Kim Sturgess is an engineer and business leader with deep expertise in water management, governance and policy. She is the founder and former CEO of WaterSMART Solutions, where she spent more than two decades helping industrial, municipal and government clients improve the management of Alberta's water resources. She also brings extensive governance experience, including roles with the Alberta Water Council, Alberta Chamber of Resources board, Calgary Airport Authority and National Research Council of Canada. With the appointments now complete, board members will participate in onboarding and orientation before beginning their formal work. The first board meeting is planned for later this year.

title: Trust in The City reaches highest level since 2018 as resident confidence grows
summary: CALGARY – The City's 2026 Fall Research Results are now available to the public, prior to the presentation to City Council on October 27, 2026. The results suggest Calgarians are becoming more positive about life in Calgary and more confident in municipal government, while continuing to hold high expectations for infrastructure, safety and future growth. Quality of life, satisfaction with City services, trust in The City and perceptions of value for tax dollars all increased compared with fall 2025. “One of the clearest findings in this year's research is growing confidence in Calgary's future and in The City of Calgary as its municipal government,” says Chief Administrative Officer David Duckworth. “ That confidence is also reflected nationally, with Calgary outperforming comparable Canadian municipalities on key measures including quality of life, service satisfaction, trust and value for tax dollars. But greater confidence also comes with high expectations. Our responsibility is to turn that optimism into action and keep delivering for Calgarians as our city grows.” Confidence in Calgary is improving This year's research shows improvement across several key indicators that reflect how Calgarians feel about Calgary and municipal government. · 77 per cent rate their quality of life as good, up from 71 per cent last year. · 73 per cent are satisfied with City services, up from 67 per cent in fall 2025. · 49 per cent say they receive good value for their municipal tax dollars, up from 42 per cent in fall 2025. · 56 per cent trust The City, up from 47 per cent last year and the highest level recorded since 2018. Trust and service satisfaction continue to rise Trust and satisfaction showed some of the strongest gains in this year's research. Since last fall, trust in The City increased by nine per cent (47 per cent), while dissatisfaction declined from 24 per cent to 16 per cent. Service satisfaction also improved significantly, reaching its highest level since 2019. The findings suggest that trust grows when residents feel The City is running Calgary well, responding to community needs and working collaboratively. Perceptions of value for tax dollars are strongest when residents are satisfied with City services and believe public funds are being spent responsibly. Calgarians continue to prioritize transportation, infrastructure and safety While residents are expressing growing confidence in Calgary and municipal government, they continue to identify several issues they want The City to prioritize. · Traffic and roads remain the most frequently identified priority at 36 per cent. · Crime, safety and policing ranks second at 23 per cent. · Homelessness, poverty and affordable housing follows at 18 per cent. · Transit remains among the top priorities at 15 per cent. The research also found increased mentions of pedestrian safety, water infrastructure and aggressive driving compared with previous surveys. This year's findings suggest confidence is growing, while Calgarians remain focused on the issues that matter to them. The results suggest strong support for infrastructure investment, with 82 per cent of Calgarians agreeing now is a good time for The City to invest in new projects like roads, public transportation and local facilities. Residents recognize progress while continuing to expect visible improvements in the services and infrastructure that support Calgary's future. Calgary outperforms other major Canadian cities National Municipal Benchmarking results show Calgary scores above comparable municipalities on several key measures. Compared with national benchmarks, Calgary scores: · 8 per cent higher on quality of life · 7 per cent higher on service satisfaction · 12 per cent higher on trust · 6 per cent higher on value for tax dollars These results provide important context as many of the pressures affecting Calgarians, including affordability, growth and economic uncertainty, are also affecting municipalities across Canada. Research helps measure Calgarians' priorities and perceptions The results of this representative, third-party survey, together with additional research, provide City Council with insights into Calgarians' views on a range of issues, including quality of life, City services and Calgary's future. As one of the only cities in Canada to conduct biannual surveys on government performance and public sentiment, The City's public research results also help provide ongoing accountability and transparency to Calgarians, while identifying strengths and opportunities for improvement. The 2026 Fall Survey of Calgarians was conducted by Ipsos Public Affairs from August 4, 2026 to August 28, 2026 with 2,500 Calgarians, via telephone. The survey was conducted using numbers from both cell phones (70 per cent) and landlines (30 per cent) to obtain a random and statistically representative sample of Calgarians with a margin of error ± 2.0 percentage points, 19 times out of 20. The 2026 Fall Survey of Calgarians report as well as other research can be found at calgary.ca/insights . The fall survey presentation will be available on October 27. -30-

title: Safety in the classroom: Calgary Fire appeals to educators, parents and students for their continued partnership in annual School Fire Drill Program
summary: Calgary firefighters visit hundreds of schools across the city annually to perform school fire drills. All schools in Calgary must complete six fire drills per school year, and one of these drills should be attended by the Calgary Fire Department (CFD). Through this program, firefighters and school staff can practice and access their evacuation procedures, reinforce life safety messages with students and families and connect teachers with fire safety educational resources. The drills also reinforce the importance of planning and rehearsing an escape plan not only at school, but at the children's homes. CFD's appeal for fire safety awareness comes at a time where residential fires are on the rise. Although overall fire-related incidents were comparable to last year's levels, Calgary's single-family residential fires were up over 28% in September 2026 compared to 2025. On October 22, members of CFD, along with representatives from the Calgary Catholic School District, conducted a school fire drill at St. Elizabeth Seton School. Fire Chief Steve Dongworth, along with newly-appointed Junior Fire Chief Kean Hallisey, activated the fire alarm in the school, ensuring that it works, while evacuating children and staff safely. They also emphasized the importance of having a home escape plan in the event of an emergency. Greg Moore, Senior Officer, Occupational Health & Safety, Calgary Catholic School District said “by teaching our students about fire prevention and the importance of making safe choices, we're helping them build habits that can protect themselves, their families, their schools and their communities. We're grateful to the Calgary Fire Department for helping bring these lessons to life for our students”. “CFD is actively working with all the schools in Calgary to teach children about the importance of fire safety and practicing escape plans at home with their families” said Fire Chief Steve Dongworth. “We're helping students to build habits that protect themselves, their families and their schools.” To learn more about school fire drills, visit calgary.ca/schoolfiredrills -30-

title: Construction begins on Walden Fire Station and Library
summary: Residents in Calgary's growing southeast will gain a permanent fire station and a new public library in one shared community hub, with construction now underway on the Walden Fire Station and Library. With an estimated project cost of $34.2 million, the project will create Calgary's first integrated fire station and public library. The facility, located at 969 Walden Drive S.E., will include a permanent two-bay fire station and a new Calgary Public Library location serving residents of Walden, Legacy, Chaparral, Wolf Willow and surrounding communities. The facility is anticipated to open in 2028. “This project reflects the kind of thoughtful infrastructure investment that helps build a more connected, resilient and livable Calgary,” says Mayor Jeromy Farkas. “By bringing essential services together in one location and making efficient use of public resources, we're creating lasting value for residents and helping build thriving communities.” The Government of Alberta contributed $4.1 million toward the project through the Local Government Fiscal Framework and the former Municipal Sustainability Initiative, supporting the delivery of this investment in Calgary's southeast. "The Walden Fire Station and Library is a prime example of creative thinking about municipal infrastructure,” says Dan Williams, Alberta Minister of Municipal Affairs. “ Through Municipal Affairs ' more than $4 million investment, our government is proud to help create family-focused spaces that will improve livability and inspire Calgary citizens long into the future." "This project represents the first public civic infrastructure built in Ward 14 since 1976,” says Landon Johnston, Councillor for Ward 14. "It represents the start of what we hope to be many, many more examples of reinvestment of property tax dollars into Ward 14 in the years to come. I will work to ensure future projects are delivered more efficiently." The facility is being built on the site of the existing Walden Temporary Fire Station and will help meet the long-term service needs of southeast Calgary. The temporary fire station has served the area since 2020 and will remain fully operational during construction, ensuring uninterrupted emergency response while the new permanent station is built. Once the permanent facility becomes operational, the temporary station will be removed. "This new station will strengthen our ability to provide timely emergency response in Calgary's south and ensure firefighters have the facilities, equipment and resources they need to serve the community effectively," says Steve Dongworth, Fire Chief, Calgary Fire Department. "As these communities continue to grow, investments in emergency services help us maintain the high standard of service Calgarians expect." The new full-service Library will include collections, children's spaces, technology, meeting rooms and programming space in Calgary's growing southeast, where demand for Library service continues to increase. “Walden Fire Station and Library brings long-needed, important civic infrastructure to a community who will now have a place to gather and connect together,” says Sarah Meilleur, CEO, Calgary Public Library. “Calgary Public Library and Calgary Fire have worked together for many years to support communities through programming, learning opportunities and public safety education. Walden is the first location where that partnership will be reflected in the building itself, bringing emergency services and lifelong learning together in one community hub.” About the Walden Fire Station and Library The Walden Fire Station and Library will be Calgary's first combined fire station and public library, bringing together two important community services in one location. Building on a long-standing partnership between Calgary Fire and Calgary Public Library, the facility will support fast and reliable emergency services while providing a welcoming place to read, learn and gather for residents of Walden, Legacy, Chaparral, Wolf Willow and surrounding communities. It will include: · A 15,000-square-foot, two-bay permanent fire station. · A 11,000-square-foot Calgary Public Library location. · Parking for staff and the public. For project updates and more information, visit the Walden Fire Station and Library project webpage or contact the project team at Walden@calgary.ca.

title: Calgary Community Associations mark milestones and create new ways to connect
summary: Across Calgary, The City's community partners including more than 160 community associations, are celebrating milestone anniversaries while volunteers turn local ideas into welcoming events, useful amenities and new ways for neighbours to connect. So far this year, some notable anniversaries include the Sandstone MacEwan Community Association marking 40 years, the Brentwood Community Association celebrating 50 years, the North Haven Community Association celebrating 60, the Triwood Community Association marking 65 years and the Rosedale Community Association reaching their 75 th anniversary. These community association milestones, which are only a few, reflect decades of community residents giving their time, ideas and care to strengthen Calgary's communities. This year's celebrations are part of the larger story of partnership with Calgary's community associations, including the Kincora Community Association's work on a new playground to create another space for families to gather. The Symons Valley Leisure and Amenities Society submitted a development permit for the first stage of a community sport and recreation hub, the Coach Hill Patterson Heights Community Association broke ground on a community space, while the Hidden Valley Community Association's member discount program is building connections between residents and local businesses. “We partner with Calgary community associations to make life better for all Calgarians. This close partnership allows us to work together to create and sustain vibrant and healthy communities across the city,” said Tim Mowrey, Manager, Community Partners for The City. “We encourage all Calgarians to attend events, become members of their community association, volunteer or serve on your community association Board.” Community association events are also bringing neighbourhoods together in creative ways, including the West Springs and Capitol Hill Community Association's hosting successful Neighbour Day activities in June, the Mahogany Community Association hosting a community screening event for the new Toy Story movie in July and the Rutland Park Community Association receiving the Inspiring Neighbourhood Grant funding for two sea can storage containers to be painted with beautiful murals. In the community of Redstone, the community association 's third annual Stampede Breakfast drew an amazing crowd of 7,000 people, with Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith both attending. The Elbow Park Community Association replaced a vandalized and broken sundial in the Gerry Shaw Garden, the Montgomery Community Association welcomed families to its Great Big Family Picnic in August, while the Sage Hill Community Association invited residents to their community duck hunt in April and the Ranchlands Community Association held a 'Dog Mayor' contest with Shiba Inu Kero announced as the winner last month. Calgary's community associations represent more than 250 communities. The Federation of Calgary Communities is also a partner of The City in supporting community associations as they work to offer social, recreational, and educational opportunities close to home, take care of gathering spaces and buildings, and help Calgarians have a voice in community life. More than 16,000 volunteers support Calgary's community associations with thousands of hours each year. Learn more about Calgary's community associations . -30-

title: Largest missing-person response in CPS history leads to recommendations for future critical incidents
summary: Today, we are publicly releasing the key themes from our operational and investigative review of the search for 11-year-old Parker. The review was undertaken internally to identify lessons learned, recognize what worked well and recommend practical improvements for future missing-person investigations, major searches and other prolonged critical incidents. It does not assess the performance of individual employees or partners, nor does it reinvestigate the circumstances of Parker's disappearance. The search for Parker became the largest missing-person response in CPS history, involving a sustained, multi-agency operation, extensive community participation and significant investigative, search, technological and communications resources. The review found that members, partner agencies, volunteers and community members demonstrated extraordinary commitment throughout the response while also identifying opportunities to strengthen organizational systems and processes for future incidents. The review found a number of significant strengths across the response, including: Investigation-led search management Public awareness and community engagement Technology and digital evidence capabilities Strong partnerships and interagency collaboration The professionalism, compassion and adaptability demonstrated by members and partners throughout the response The review also identified opportunities to strengthen organizational systems related to: Scalable resourcing and operational sustainability Command integration and incident management Tip, task and canvass management Public alerting and partnership frameworks Technology readiness and scalability Member wellness and operational resilience One of the key findings involved the unprecedented volume of information received during the investigation. The response generated approximately 1,000 formal investigative tips, more than 90,000 direct social media messages, thousands of emails and approximately 10 terabytes of CCTV footage. The review found that while this information provided significant investigative value, existing systems were not designed to easily manage information at that scale during a prolonged critical incident. The review found that additional capacity and stronger organizational systems would have helped the CPS receive, assess, assign and track the extraordinary volume of information more efficiently. It does not conclude that different resources, systems or processes would have changed the outcome. Rather, it identifies opportunities to improve future responses through better coordination, continuity, information management and operational planning. The review also acknowledges the provincial review on alerting is underway and the recent findings released by The City related to the initial 9-1-1 response. The CPS recognizes and respects The City's review process and responsibilities. The CPS review examined the police response, including investigations, search operations, public engagement, communications, technology and partnerships. It identifies Calgary 9-1-1 as an essential partner in future policy development, training, information sharing, tip management and major incident planning. Formal recommendations were identified across investigations, search management, incident command, strategic communications, partnerships and public alerting, tip management, technology and member wellness. These recommendations will inform future policy development, training, exercises, technology investments and operational planning. We recognize that renewed discussion of this case may be difficult for Parker's family, members involved in the response and many others in our community. The release of these key themes is intended to support transparency, accountability and continuous improvement while honouring the collective effort invested in the search for Parker. The Calgary Police Service Victim Assistance Support Team (VAST) is a free service that provides support, resources and information to victims of crime and tragedy. For anyone who needs support, VAST can be reached at 403-428-8398 or toll-free at 1-888-327-7828. More information is available at https://www.calgary.ca/cps/community-programs-and-resources/victims-of-crime/victim-assistance-support-team.html Key themes from the review: Extraordinary commitment from members and partners Members worked prolonged hours, volunteered outside their regular duties and remained focused on locating Parker and supporting his family. The review found that investigators, search managers, operational commanders, support staff and partners demonstrated extraordinary professionalism and determination. More than 800 searcher deployments were contributed during the response, with personnel from across the CPS and numerous partner agencies stepping in to support investigative, search, operational and community engagement efforts. The review repeatedly notes that many successes were achieved because of the commitment and adaptability of people across the organization. Scalable resourcing and operational sustainability The response tested the CPS' ability to sustain staffing, preserve knowledge, relieve personnel and coordinate resources over an extended period. As the investigation grew more complex, maintaining continuity became increasingly important. The review found that key personnel developed extensive knowledge that was difficult to transfer between shifts or personnel rotations and that many support functions were scaled up through individual initiative rather than formal surge plans. The review recommends a more formal and scalable approach to investigative staffing, relief planning, knowledge transfer, resource generation and operational continuity during prolonged critical incidents. Investigation-led search management The review found that search operations were most effective when guided by current investigative information and when search findings were continuously fed back into the investigation. Search managers, investigators, geomatics specialists and partner agencies worked together to adjust priorities as new information emerged, rather than relying solely on traditional search practices. The review reinforces the importance of maintaining a close connection between investigative and search functions and recommends updates to policy, training, documentation and governance to align with current standards and emerging best practices. Clearer command integration As the response evolved, additional planning, logistics and resource coordination functions were introduced to support the investigation and search effort. The review found that these functions provided significant value, but that roles, responsibilities and activation thresholds were not always clearly understood across all groups involved in the response. It recommends greater clarity around how investigators, search management, the Real Time Operations Centre, Major Events and Emergency Management and incident-management functions work together during prolonged critical incidents, supported by policy updates, training and exercises. Communications as an operational function The review found that communications became much more than a public information function. Media engagement, public appeals, social media content, community outreach and family communications directly influenced investigative outcomes by generating leads, encouraging evidence submissions, directing public action and countering misinformation. Communications professionals also managed significant volumes of public engagement throughout the response. As a result, the review recommends embedding Strategic Communications further within major-incident command structures and ensuring communications capacity is considered when planning for large-scale public engagement campaigns. Partnerships and public alerting The response relied heavily on partnerships with government agencies, search-and-rescue organizations, community partners, the Missing Children Society of Canada and members of the public. Public awareness efforts, including the Alberta Emergency Alert, MCSC Rescu platform, extensive media coverage and social media outreach, helped expand awareness of Parker's disappearance far beyond Calgary. The review found these partnerships and alerting tools generated significant public participation and investigative information, while also creating substantial operational demands. It recommends clearer alerting frameworks, a more formalized relationship with MCSC and continued CPS involvement in discussions around future alerting tools for vulnerable missing persons. Centralized tip, task and canvass management The review found that one of the greatest challenges was not generating information, but managing the unprecedented volume of information received. Approximately 1,000 formal investigative tips, more than 90,000 direct social media messages, thousands of emails and significant volumes of digital evidence were received through multiple intake channels. Investigators often had to reconcile duplicate information, determine ownership and verify follow-up across separate systems. The review recommends a centralized tip-management system, consolidated canvass tracking, clear ownership and stronger information-sharing standards to improve coordination and reduce duplication during future major incidents. Technology as a core operational capability Technology played a critical role throughout the response and significantly expanded what was operationally possible. Mapping tools, video analytics software, drones, digital evidence platforms and public evidence-submission tools supported evidence collection, information sharing, search coordination and investigative decision-making. However, the review found that supporting infrastructure, server capacity, licensing models, technical support and trained-user availability were strained by the scale of demand. It recommends additional investment in technology readiness, training and scalability to support future major incidents. Member wellness The review recognizes member wellness as an operational-readiness issue rather than solely an individual responsibility. The sustained nature of the response exposed members to long hours, high workloads, emotionally difficult circumstances and intense public scrutiny. While wellness supports were made available, the review found that future major incidents would benefit from wellness being formally integrated into planning, operations and demobilization processes from the outset. Recommendations include proactive outreach, clear wellness activation processes and stronger coordination between operational and wellness teams during prolonged critical incidents. Statement from Parker's Family

title: Police seeking bus passengers after fatal collision

title: Water main repairs impacting traffic on 14th Street S.W. - Boil Water Advisory still in effect.
summary: On Friday, October 16, City crews began repairs on a water main that supports the community of Eagle Ridge and Heritage Park. During the repairs, they experienced an unanticipated depressurization of the pipe and could not guarantee the water quality. As a precaution, Alberta Health Services ordered a Boil Water Advisory. This issue is not related to the Bearspaw South Feeder Main, nor is it impacting Rockyview General Hospital. To complete repairs, two northbound and two southbound lanes on 14th Street S.W. between 75 Avenue S.W. and Heritage Drive. S.W. will be closed until further notice, leaving one lane open in each direction. Depending on the condition of the pipe we may need to adjust the lane closures to complete the repair. This is a challenging repair and will take some time to complete. Significant traffic delays are likely. Please use alternative routes if possible and follow all signage and detours. All residents within the affected area are advised to bring all tap water to a rolling boil for one full minute prior to any consumption, including: Drinking, including coffee and tea Cooking Brushing teeth Cleaning raw foods Preparing infant formula or juices Making ice, etc. In-home water filters are not sufficient and water in them must still be boiled before use. You may instead choose to purchase bottled water for consumption for the duration of this advisory. Water wagons are being provided, and their location will be available on calgary.ca/boilwater . When cleaning: If you are not using a dishwasher, water used for cleaning surfaces or dishes should be boiled. Water used for bathing and laundry does not require boiling. For businesses: Food Service Establishments, Care Providers and Personal Service facilities should contact Environmental Public Health at 1-833-476-4743 for direction. This advisory will remain in effect until further notice. Affected residents will be contacted directly when the advisory is lifted and updates will be available on calgary.ca/boilwater . The City of Calgary is working closely with Alberta Environment and Protected Areas and Alberta Health Services to resolve the water quality concerns. For health-related questions and further information about boil water procedures, please contact Health Link at 811 or visit myhealth.alberta.ca/Alberta/Pages/Boil-water-advisory-how-to-use-water-safely.aspx

title: Youth charged, two additional suspects sought in armed robberies
summary: We have charged one teen in relation to two armed robberies that occurred in June 2026, and are looking for the public's help to identify two additional suspects. On Tuesday, June 16, 2026, at approximately 9 p.m., it is believed three suspects entered Carrie's VIP Body Care, located at #7A, 2016 25 Ave. N.E., one of which was armed with a firearm. At the time, those inside the business hid in a back room, called police, and did not interact with the suspects. The suspects fled in a black Jeep Grand Cherokee believed to be stolen. Later that evening, at approximately 10:20 p.m., it is believed the same three suspects entered Bud Mart, located at 20 Copperpond Passage S.E., once again armed with a firearm. The suspects threatened and assaulted an employee and a customer before fleeing the business with cannabis products and cash. Police were contacted and launched an investigation. On Tuesday, June 23, 2026, police located the Jeep Grand Cherokee believed to be involved in the robberies in the southwest community of Woodbine. Investigators located evidence inside the vehicle and were able to identify a suspect. On Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026, police located and arrested the suspect at a residence located in Saddle Ridge. On Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026, a search warrant was executed at the suspect's residence and officers seized: · A cellphone · A loaded handgun · Ammunition As a result, a 17-year-old male is charged with: · Three counts of failure to comply · One count of possession of stolen property over $5,000 · One count of pointing a firearm · Two counts of possession of a weapon for a dangerous purpose · Two counts of disguise with intent · Two counts of robbery with a restricted or prohibited firearm · Further charges are pending He will next appear in court on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. The youth cannot be named under the provisions of the Youth Criminal Justice Act. Police are also looking for the public's help to identify the remaining two suspects who are believed to be involved in the robberies. The first suspect is described as man, approximately 18 to 20 years old. He was last seen wearing a face mask, a black sweatsuit, black gloves with a white pattern and black running shoes. The second suspect is described as male, approximately 16 to 18 years old. He was last seen wearing a face mask, a black sweatsuit and black running shoes. Due to provisions under the Youth Criminal Justice Act, images showing a youth's face cannot be released. However, an image showing the youth from the side, including the clothing he was wearing at the time of the incident, is available. The investigation remains ongoing. Anyone with information about this incident, or the identity of the suspects, is asked to contact police by calling 403-266-1234. Tips can also be submitted anonymously to Crime Stoppers through any of the following methods: TALK: 1-800-222-8477 TYPE: www.calgarycrimestoppers.org APP: P3 Tips Case #: CA26265380/5624

title: Update #2: Suspect identified and charges laid in random sexual assault
summary: In August 2026, we sought the public's assistance in identifying a vehicle believed to be involved in a random sexual assault at the Southland CTrain Station. title: Calgary Fire Department highlights multi-agency response to fatal transit bus collision and fire
summary: At approximately 1:10 p.m. on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026, Calgary Fire Department (CFD) crews were dispatched to the 800 block of Saddletowne Circle N.E., near the intersection of 80 Avenue N.E., for a multi-vehicle collision involving two Calgary Transit buses. Upon arrival, firefighters encountered several severely damaged vehicles, multiple patients with varying degrees of injury, and one transit bus driver trapped inside their vehicle. A second transit bus was involved in a significant fire, with flames and heavy smoke visible from the vehicle. Recognizing the complexity and severity of the incident, firefighters immediately stretched hose lines and began knocking down the fire while requesting additional resources. A mass casualty incident was subsequently declared. As Calgary Police Service (CPS) officers and Emergency Health Services (EHS) personnel arrived on scene, firefighters worked simultaneously to extinguish the bus fire, stabilize the trapped driver and support patient care operations. Calgary Fire Department established the Unified Command Post, providing a central location for incident command and coordination between CFD, CPS, EHS, Calgary Transit and other supporting agencies throughout the response. The CFD Technical Rescue Team was deployed to support the advanced extrication of the trapped bus driver. Working in close coordination with EHS personnel, technical rescue firefighters safely and efficiently removed the driver from the vehicle and transferred them to awaiting medical care. Following extinguishment of the fire, CFD Hazardous Materials specialists worked alongside Calgary Transit personnel to assess the compressed natural gas (CNG) system and confirm it had been safely vented, eliminating any ongoing risk to responders or the public. During suppression and search operations related to the bus fire, firefighters located three deceased persons. Calgary Police Service subsequently confirmed the three individuals were passengers aboard the second transit bus who died following the collision and subsequent fire. This was an exceptionally challenging incident for all responding personnel. Firefighters arrived to find multiple injured patients, a trapped bus driver and a transit bus on fire, requiring simultaneous rescue, firefighting and patient care operations. Throughout the incident, responders from CFD, Calgary Police Service, Emergency Health Services, Calgary Transit and 9-1-1 communications worked together under difficult circumstances to provide the highest level of service possible. CFD acknowledges the professionalism, teamwork and dedication demonstrated by all personnel involved in this tragic event. CFD Fire Investigators attended the scene and have begun investigating the origin and cause of the bus fire. Their investigation is proceeding concurrently with the collision investigation being conducted by Calgary Police Service and the death investigation being conducted by the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner. -30-

title: Three deceased following multi-vehicle collision
summary: Update: The third deceased passenger has since been identified, and their next of kin have been notified. Our Traffic Section continues to investigate a multi-vehicle collision in northeast Calgary that resulted in three fatalities and left one person with life-altering injuries. At approximately 1:10 p.m., on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026, a City of Calgary transit bus was travelling northbound in the 800 block of Saddletowne Circle N.E., approaching the intersection of 80 Avenue N.E. It is believed the bus struck a truck travelling in the same direction. The truck entered an adjacent lane, where it sideswiped a SUV before continuing forward and striking the rear of a box truck. The bus continued northbound and struck the rear of a sedan, pushing the vehicle through the intersection. The sedan then travelled toward Saddletowne Circle N.E., where it struck a truck. Both vehicles eventually came to rest. The bus continued northbound and struck the rear of a second City of Calgary transit bus. Both buses travelled a short distance following the collision before coming to a stop. During the collision, the natural-gas tanks on the second bus ignited. The second bus continued forward before striking a sedan. Within seconds, the fire intensified resulting in an explosion and significant fire inside the bus. Three passengers on the second bus were found deceased. Two have since been identified and their next of kin have been notified. Efforts to identify the third individual remain ongoing. The driver of the second bus was able to exit the vehicle. The driver of the first bus was transported to hospital with life-altering injuries. The remaining drivers involved in the collision were either uninjured or sustained minor injuries. As a result of the multi-vehicle collision, 16 people sustained minor injuries, including an officer who is now recovering at home. At this time, it is too early to determine whether impairment, speed or distraction contributed to the collision. All possible factors remain under investigation. Anyone who was affected by witnessing this incident is encouraged to connect with our Victim Assistance Support Team (VAST) by calling 403-428-8398 or toll-free at 1-888-327-7828. VAST is a free service provided to victims of crime and tragedy. More information is available at: https://www.calgary.ca/cps/community-programs-and-resources/victims-of-crime/victim-assistance-support-team.html Anyone with information about this incident is asked to contact police by calling 403-266-1234. title: Water restrictions take effect Nov. 4 as Bearspaw South Feeder Main enters final steps of construction
summary: Calgary is one step closer to a stronger and more reliable water system as crews prepare to connect the new Bearspaw South Feeder Main into the existing water system, beginning November 4. While this work is underway, city-wide Stage 4 outdoor water restrictions and indoor water conservation will be needed for approximately four weeks to reduce demand while the water supply is limited. This connection marks one of the final steps of installation for the new feeder main. Once connected, crews will begin the final commissioning work required to bring the new pipe into service by the end of this year. "The November connection is a significant phase of the project because it is when the new feeder main will be integrated into Calgary's existing water system," said Michael Thompson, Chief Operating Officer - Water. "Over the past several months, our focus has been on advancing construction while securing the specialized materials needed to complete this work. With the majority of those materials now on-site in Calgary and the rest of the materials scheduled to arrive on time, we're positioned to move into this final phase and deliver on a key investment in Calgary's water infrastructure that will help reduce the risk of future major disruptions." Water restrictions required during connection work To safely complete the connection of the new pipe, the existing Bearspaw South Feeder Main must be temporarily shut down. During this period, the amount of water that can be distributed across the city will be significantly reduced to 500 million litres a day. We need to stay below this number and ensure we have sufficient water for everyone, including firefighting, if needed. As a result, city-wide Stage 4 outdoor water restrictions and indoor water conservation measures will be required beginning Nov. 4 for approximately four weeks. No outdoor water use will be permitted during this time and we're asking all Calgarians and our neighbours in Airdrie, Chestermere, Strathmore and Tsuut'ina Nation to save water indoors by taking the following actions: Run dishwashers and laundry only when full. Flush toilets only when needed. Take shorter showers. Aim for three minutes. "We know Calgarians have already done a tremendous job reducing water use when needed," said Thompson. "The actions people take during this period will help us complete this work safely and successfully while protecting water services across the city.” Once the new feeder main has been connected, crews will focus on preparing the new line for service. This includes disinfecting the pipe, filling it with water and completing the water quality testing required before the new feeder main can be brought into operation. This process will take approximately two to three weeks. The project remains on track for the new feeder main to be fully operational by the end of the year.
