title: Operation Silent Night helps lower vehicle noise levels on 17 Avenue S.W.
summary: Noise monitoring data shows measurable reduction in loud vehicle activity during targeted enforcement initiative A data-driven approach to reducing excessive vehicle noise is delivering results on one of Calgary's busiest corridors. Noise monitoring data collected during Operation Silent Night shows measurable improvements in sound levels and a reduction in loud vehicle activity along 17 Avenue S.W., an area identified as Calgary's highest-priority vehicle noise hot spot. To evaluate the impact of the initiative, The City analyzed data from a noise monitor near Tomkins Park and compared results from the August 2026 enforcement period with the same period in 2025. The findings show a significant reduction in loud vehicle events and overall noise levels. During enforcement hours, loud vehicle events decreased from 357 events in 2025 to 267 events in 2026, a reduction of 25.2 per cent. Across the full analysis period, loud vehicle events decreased from 801 to 715, a reduction of 10.7 per cent. Average sound levels during enforcement hours also fell from 71.18 dBA to 68.80 dBA, a decrease of 2.38 decibels. “The results show that when drivers understand the rules and see a visible enforcement presence, we can make a meaningful difference in reducing excessive vehicle noise and improving the quality of life for residents and businesses,” said Brad Johnson, Inspector and head of the Traffic Safety Team. The strongest reductions were observed during active enforcement periods, suggesting a positive impact from increased awareness and officer presence. While factors such as weather, traffic volumes and special events can influence sound levels, the monitoring data indicates a clear improvement during the operation period. The results also highlight the value of Calgary's citywide noise-monitoring network. The monitors provide objective information about loud vehicle activity, helping The City identify noise hot spots, understand trends and evaluate the effectiveness of initiatives aimed at improving community livability. Operation Silent Night demonstrates how data, technology and targeted enforcement can work together to reduce excessive vehicle noise and support quieter, more enjoyable public spaces for residents, businesses and visitors. -30-

title: Downtown Safety Project Receives Provincial Planning Award
summary: A Calgary initiative focused on creating safer and more welcoming public spaces has received province-wide recognition from the Alberta Professional Planners Institute (APPI). The award recognizes a Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design (CPTED) project led by The City of Calgary in partnership with DIALOG. The project examined 10 locations across downtown Calgary, exploring how design, community input and collaboration can help improve safety and the experience of people using public spaces. What set the project apart was its focus on implementation. Rather than producing recommendations alone, the team worked closely with businesses, community organizations, operational teams and subject matter experts to identify practical solutions that could be put into action. Several improvements are already underway or complete, including lighting enhancements, safety infrastructure and other measures designed to improve public spaces for residents, visitors and businesses. "This recognition reflects the incredible collaboration behind the project," said Darshan Tailor, Business Strategist with The City of Calgary. "Businesses, community organizations, City teams and technical experts all contributed their knowledge and experience. Together, we developed practical solutions that are helping create safer public spaces." Collaboration was central to the project's success. Interested parties from across sectors helped identify challenges, share local insights and shape recommendations that were both meaningful and achievable. This partnership-based approach ensured the project delivered practical outcomes rather than a stand-alone study. The recognition highlights the importance of investing in public spaces that support a vibrant downtown. Safer, more welcoming environments help encourage people to live, work, visit and spend time in the core, benefiting residents, businesses and the broader community. The project assessed 10 downtown locations and produced implementation-focused action plans designed to translate safety recommendations into tangible improvements on the ground. The APPI award recognizes planning excellence and innovation, celebrating projects that create positive impacts for communities across Canada.

title: Calgary Fire Responds to Early Morning Carbon Monoxide Incident
summary: At around 5:00am, fire crews were dispatched to the 2700 block of 12 Avenue SE to investigate a carbon monoxide (CO) incident. Crews arrived at a three-story multi-unit residential complex and reported a strong exhaust odor on entry to the building. A resident had called 9-1-1 as their unit CO alarm was active. Firefighters detected levels peak levels of over 150 ppm in the complex and activated the building fire alarm to evacuate all the occupants as any levels above 50 ppm are considered dangerous. Calgary Transit was contacted and two buses attended the scene to provide for warm shelter for occupants. 62 people were evacuated onto the buses, while other occupants self-evacuated to other areas on their own. No injuries were reported. Firefighters were able to locate the source of the CO as a roof top ventilation unit and gas was shut off to the unit. ATCO gas attended and confirmed the source, and fire crews ventilated the building until there was no CO levels detected. It was determined to be safe to allow everyone to re-occupy the building and responsibility turned back over to the property manager. As part of Fire Prevention Week, this year, on October 8, the Calgary Fire Department and ATCO will be visiting homes in the Temple community, offering to install, test and replace smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, as well as remind residents about the importance of knowing how to use lithium-ion batteries safely. The Calgary Fire Department reminds all residents that working carbon monoxide alarms save lives, as was the case in this morning's incident. Most commonly, the main source of CO gas in your home is your furnace, but any household appliances which run on fuels, like natural gas and propane and even fireplaces can be a source. Schedule routine maintenance and inspections performed by qualified personnel to ensure these appliances are working properly. As weather conditions continue to cool down, another common source of CO is from vehicles. Never idle vehicles inside enclosed spaces, such as garages or near air inlets to buildings. A CO alarm that is continuously repeating a 4-beeping pattern means it detects CO and everyone should get out and call 9-1-1. Let the Emergency Communications Officer know if anyone is experiencing the symptoms of CO exposure. CO alarms should be installed on every level of the home including the basement and most importantly be placed near bedrooms so people can hear them where they sleep. CO alarms can be purchased at any hardware stores. Caution should be taken when ordering any CO alarms online and ensure that alarms meet Canadian safety standards. For more information on carbon monoxide safety, visit calgary.ca/fire and ATCO Gas -30-

title: Attendants keep park washrooms open and clean for everyone
summary: A tourist trying to navigate the city, a family visiting a festival downtown or an individual who doesn't have regular access to a private bathroom. What do they all have in common? At some point, they are going to need to find a washroom, and they all hope to find one that is safe and clean. Keeping public washrooms open, accessible and tidy requires consistent monitoring. This is where the Parks & Open Spaces Washroom Attendant Program comes in. Washroom attendants fulfill a variety of tasks during their shifts including checking and cleaning washrooms between visitors, monitoring the space so that everyone has access to the washrooms (wellness checks after someone has been in the washroom for more than 15 minutes), de-escalating situations where necessary and calling for help if someone is in medical distress. At the Devonian Gardens washrooms, attendants often see tourists who still have their suitcases with them. "We might be their first impression of Calgary," said Washroom Attendant Paul. " Tourists often think they need to pay to use our washrooms and we say, 'It's free,' they tell us that in Europe you have to pay for the toilet paper. They are often shocked that it's free AND clean." Parents with children are very appreciative that they can access a family washroom that is monitored. “They want to take their child to someplace clean," said Paul. Paul is one of the many attendants that monitor and cares for the public washrooms in select downtown parks as an employee of Hiregood . “Hiregood is a social enterprise that creates meaningful, long-term employment for people who are too often overlooked in the traditional workforce,” said Jodi Phelan, Chief Executive Officer for Hiregood. “We provide real services for our customers while creating real jobs in the community. This program is a perfect example of what that can look like. Our attendants aren't just keeping the washrooms clean. They are creating safer, more welcoming spaces for everyone who uses them.” Taren Yellowbird said that working as an attendant can be humbling, has challenged her in ways she needed to be challenged and is also more of a personal vocation than just a job. After university and working for outreach organizations, she was looking for meaningful work and then found this position, calling it "the best decision ever" to move to Calgary and become a washroom attendant. "My sister died on the streets from a heart attack and my niece died two weeks ago from an overdose so this is very personal, doing this work helps me grieve,” said Taren. “My sister and my niece — no one found them in time; no one was there." Attendants say a variety of individuals use the washrooms including the elderly, families, people who work downtown, those attending an event or have an appointment and plenty of tourists. Part of the success of the program comes from creating a community of support within these parks that includes the Parks maintenance staff, security and the attendants. When they are all working together, it improves the park experience for everyone said Washroom Attendant Samuel Kairu. "People come by and say good things about having us here," said Samuel. "They remember a time when people didn't have access to a washroom here, when it was shut down. Now it is good, many people feel at peace here. We often have 70 people per shift, sometimes 100 people. During an event we had 450 during one shift!" The attendants also build a rapport with people who frequent the park, providing information about helpful resources and acting as another set of eyes and ears to ensure the space is welcoming for everyone using it. Washroom Attendant Channsey Sung was unhoused when she was younger and said she has a lot of empathy for the people who are in a similar situation now. " I worked hard to get out of that situation," said Channsey. "If you don't have a home, it's hard to get work. If people ask us, we will tell them about programs that can help them get off the street." Attendants see folks using the washrooms before they take the CTrain home, while they are shopping and others are park regulars. "There are many people who come here on a regular basis to get ready for work or to get cleaned up before going to dinner; it's part of their routine," said Gilbert McComb, Washroom Attendant. "I believe we are showing that we care and that there is compassion for everyone. People need to take care of the necessities of life to be able to make changes and be a more productive part of society." One washroom attendant, who asked to remain anonymous, said that the attendants create a community of people who care for each other in these parks. She shared one story about a young woman who visited the park often, who had two dogs and was living on the street. "She would come by and we would check in on her and the dogs, we got to know her and she got to know us. We would talk about where she wanted to go and what she wanted to do. She ended up calling her grandfather, cleaned herself up and now she is back working again. We help a lot of people who want to take the help, that's very satisfying!" Visitor surveys provide feedback that guides the Washroom Attendant Program and helps measure its success. Survey feedback collected in 2025 and 2026 shows that 97% of visitors are likely to return due to positive experiences. Before the program was launched in 2023, public concerns about safety and cleanliness were common, and many facilities were often closed for extensive vandalism repairs. Thanks to this program, repairs have been reduced and washrooms at program locations are open every day. In previous years, some public washrooms were closed for 10 out of 12 months due to vandalism. “Over 80 per cent of people who filled out our customer satisfaction survey for the program in 2025 said that the presence of an attendant made these washrooms feel safe and welcoming,” said Joy Norstrom, Parks Issues Strategist, adding that they collected 880 surveys during the first three quarters of 2025. “Parks are important public spaces, and we want them to be accessible, safe and peaceful places where everyone is welcome. The Washroom Attendant Program helps us achieve this in these downtown parks.” Jodi said she is immensely proud of the Hiregood attendants who help create safer public spaces. “Public washrooms are something most of us don't think about until we need one,” said Jodi. “Having access to a clean, safe washroom is a basic need, whether you're a tourist, a family with children, someone working downtown or someone experiencing homelessness. Everyone deserves to be treated with dignity."

title: Rocky Ridge Athletic Park opens new opportunities for sport in northwest Calgary
summary: Calgarians have more room to practice, play, train and compete with the opening of Rocky Ridge Athletic Park, a major new addition to Calgary's public recreation system. The $26-million athletic park features two multi-use, artificial turf fields, along with washrooms, parking, spectator seating and field lighting that extends playable hours and supports increased use throughout the season. Located next to Shane Homes YMCA at Rocky Ridge, the new City-operated park expands access to high-quality outdoor sport space for northwest Calgary and the wider community. “Recreation spaces help build healthy communities and create opportunities for Calgarians to connect through sport,” said Mayor Jeromy Farkas. “Rocky Ridge Athletic Park is an investment in Calgary's growing northwest and in the public recreation system our city needs for the future. These new fields will give more kids, families and sport organizations access to quality spaces where they can play, compete and build lasting connections.” The two new fields bring Calgary's athletic park network to 15 athletic parks with 31 soccer fields across the city, adding much-needed capacity and helping respond to growing demand for bookable field space. The additional capacity also gives The City greater flexibility to manage field use, support the recovery of natural grass fields and provide more playing opportunities. “Quality fields are essential to giving youth the opportunity to develop their skills, build confidence and experience the benefits of team sport,” said Bernie Morton, president of Calgary Minor Soccer Association. “These new fields will provide more opportunities for kids to practice and compete while helping meet the strong and growing demand for soccer space in Calgary. We appreciate The City's investment and its continued work with sport organizations to strengthen recreation opportunities for Calgarians.” The opening of Rocky Ridge Athletic Park demonstrates how investment in public recreation can add capacity and improve access as Calgary grows. The park forms part of The City's broader work to renew aging recreation infrastructure, respond to increasing demand and provide recreation spaces that support health, quality of life and community connection. Through GamePLAN, The City's 25-year vision and strategic framework for public recreation, Calgary is taking a long-term, system-wide approach to renewing existing facilities, adding capacity and improving how Calgarians access recreation spaces and services. Council adopted GamePLAN and established Making Waves as the service level for public recreation facilities and amenities in 2025, which has a long-term goal of increasing bookable hours at fieldhouses and athletic parks by 2.5 times. Rocky Ridge Athletic Park is part of the larger Rocky Ridge Athletic Complex . Design work for a future fieldhouse is underway, with construction dependent on future funding approval. As a Wave 1 GamePLAN priority, funding for fieldhouse construction will be considered through the 2027-30 Service Plans and Budgets process. The fields can accommodate soccer and other field sports and are available to user groups through The City's booking and process. For booking information, visit the Rocky Ridge Athletic Park webpage . Quick facts Council approved Rocky Ridge Athletic Park in 2021 as part of the Capital Investment Strategy. Construction began in September 2024 and was completed in 2026. The $26-million park includes two artificial turf, multi-use fields, along with washrooms, parking, spectator seating and field lighting that extends playable hours and supports increased use throughout the season. The new fields bring Calgary's City-operated athletic park network to 15, with 31 soccer fields across the city. The park is located at 9700 Country Hills Blvd. N.W., adjacent to Shane Homes YMCA at Rocky Ridge. User groups can book the fields through The City's booking and allocation process. -30-

title: Safe Charging is a Superpower - Fire Prevention Week, October 4-10, 2026
summary: Kean Hallissey, age 12, was named Junior Fire Chief in a ceremony today at the Alberta Children's Hospital. Fire Chief Steve Dongworth made the announcement and presented Kean with a fire helmet and special certificate honouring his appointment. Each year during Fire Prevention Week, the Calgary Fire Department (CFD) appoints a Junior Fire Chief to act as Calgary's fire safety ambassador. This program has been running since 2016 in partnership with the Alberta Children's Hospital. Kean's duties will include promoting this year's Fire Prevention Week theme, “Charge into Fire Safety - Safe Charging is a Superpower.” As part of Kean's first day, he went for a ride in a fire engine and had lunch with firefighters and his family at the Alberta Children's Hospital. “Our Junior Fire Chief plays an important role in helping to raise fire safety awareness for everyone, especially young people,” said Chief Dongworth. “Just like our Community Safety Team and the 1800 other firefighters in our service, the Junior Fire Chief helps to us communicate important fire safety messages with our family, friends and community.” “We're honoured to continue this meaningful partnership with the Calgary Fire Department, recognizing a remarkable child whose courage and character embody the spirit of the Junior Fire Chief program.” said Stacy Kelly, Special Events Coordinator at the Alberta Children's Hospital. “The program helps to promote important initiatives and our shared values around safety, teamwork and leadership.” Kean joins the Calgary Fire Department at a time when Calgary is seeing increasing fire risks from consumer and household devices due to lithium-ion battery fires. “With more lithium-ion battery fires, residential fires, overdoses and other medical calls, Calgary Fire is expected to see its greatest-ever number of incidents in 2026,” said Chief Dongworth with a minimum projection of 94,000 incidents by end of year. We're also seeing growth in emerging risks such as urban wildfire and fireworks usage.” Lithium-ion fires can be hard to extinguish and difficult to control. Batteries contain high amounts of stored energy which, once ignited, cause thermal runaway, leading to rapid overheating, explosions and toxic gases. Damaged batteries, overcharging, and improper use of batteries and chargers are common causes of fires. Use of off-brand or discounted high-capacity batteries is also highly associated with greater fire risk, as is modifying electronics in any way. Know how to charge & recycle safely Calgarians are encouraged to: Buy and use safely : Purchase products from reputable vendors and look for a “UL” or “CSA” stamp on the product to ensure it meets safety standards. Don't damage or modify your devices and their batteries. Charge safely : Do not overcharge devices; unplug them or remove the battery once fully charged. Do not charge under pillows, on beds or on couches where batteries can overheat. Recycle responsibly : Recycle your batteries at designated collection sites across Calgary. Find out more at calgary.ca/chargesafe . By responsibly recycling batteries, hazardous materials are kept out of the garbage and landfills. Recycling also allows for the recovery and reuse of valuable resources, which can be used in the manufacturing of new products, like stainless steel products or even new batteries. Find out more about how to safety manage and dispose of batteries, including free drop off locations across Calgary: calgary.ca/chargesafe . For more information about Fire Prevention Week, visit calgary.ca/firepreventionweek . -30- Fire Prevention Week – Fast Facts 2026 is currently on track to see the most ever lithium-ion battery fires on record in Calgary, mostly caused by e-scooters, e-bikes and battery packs. While lithium-ion battery fires are not as frequent as structure fires, they doubled in Calgary between 2024 to 2025, from 10 to 21 incidents. With more lithium-ion battery fires, residential fires, overdoses and other medical calls, Calgary Fire is expected to see its greatest-ever number of incidents in 2026 with a minimum projection of 94,000 incidents by end of year. Previously, 92,923 incidents in 2023 represented the most calls for help in a single year for Calgary's 141-year-old fire service. Incident volumes have increased with Calgary's continued population and geographic growth, from 61,064 incidents in 2020 to 92,248 in 2025 – a 51% increase. CFD is also seeing growth in emerging risks such as urban wildfire and fireworks usage.

title: Community previews 2026 Grey Cup Legacy Project at Fonda Park
summary: Community members, young athletes and Calgary Stampeders players got an early look at Fonda Park's new flag football fields at a community preview event on Saturday, Oct. 3. The City of Calgary is delivering three new flag football fields at Fonda Park (1017 Fonda Ct. S.E.) in partnership with the Stampeders Foundation's 2026 Grey Cup Legacy Project. The fields respond to the rapid growth of flag and touch football in Calgary, a sport gaining popularity with youth and adults alike, while bringing more opportunities to participate closer to families in the surrounding communities. "Fonda Park was selected because it already has the infrastructure, the transit access and parking needed to support increased recreational use," said Deputy Mayor Dan McLean. McLean noted that the project repurposes underused playfields, including an underused baseball diamond, while keeping valued community amenities like the skate slab and playground. Two of three fields are complete and will be open for booking starting April 2027, while the third field will begin construction next spring. The event focused on what the fields are for: getting kids to play. Stampeders Jaylon Hutchings and Folarin Orimolade joined young athletes on the field for a try-it session open to all ages. A permanent home for flag football The fields bring organized flag football to an area of the city that hasn't had local access before. "Most kids don't stop playing sports because they lose interest. They stop, or never start, because it's too expensive, too far away, or too hard to fit into family life”, said Logan Ruzycki, a coach with the YYC Flag Football League. "If you were a kid in this part of the city and wanted to play flag football, it usually meant a long drive." Ruzycki noted that flag football needs little equipment, is low-contact, and lets boys and girls of all sizes and skill levels play together from day one. "But sport is only as accessible as the place you play it." Better use of park space, more access to sport The Fonda Park Playfield Enhancements project supports two of The City's long-term strategies for parks and recreation: GamePLAN and Connect: Calgary's Parks Plan . Together, they guide how The City can make better use of existing public spaces, respond to changing recreation needs and bring more opportunities closer to where Calgarians live. Connect calls for multifunctional parks that can serve a range of community needs. At Fonda Park, that means adding dedicated sport fields without taking away what neighbours already use and value. Fonda Park remains a community park first: when the fields aren't booked for organized sport, they're open and free for public use. The project also reflects GamePLAN's Level the Playing Field and Change the Game principles. It increases access to recreation in a traditionally underserved area, removes barriers like travel distance, and repurposes underused space to meet changing sport and recreation needs. A Grey Cup legacy The Stampeders Foundation's 2026 Grey Cup Legacy Project is contributing $500,000 toward the project, alongside City funding through Recreation & Social Programs and the Parks & Playground Amenities (PAPA) program. The fields are a lasting, community-level legacy of the 2026 Grey Cup Festival. "You don't have to play professional football to learn hard work, teamwork and resilience. You just need an opportunity to play the game," said Calgary Stampeders president Jay McNeil.

title: ECCO Fire Remains Under Control as Monitoring Continues
summary: Calgary Fire Department and partner agencies continue suppression, containment and monitoring efforts at the ECCO fire site in southeast Calgary. The incident remains under control and stable. Crews continue to use specialized landfill-fire suppression techniques, including soil capping and management of localized venting areas, as part of ongoing containment efforts. Specialized landfill-fire experts have been engaged to assess the incident and provide recommendations. Current tactics are based on those recommendations. The incident remains classified as under control and stable. Air-quality monitoring conducted by provincial partners has not identified any new exceedances of Alberta Ambient Air Quality Objectives or Guidelines during the Sept. 28 to Oct. 5 reporting period. Air Quality Health Index (AQHI) readings remained primarily in the low-risk category, while monitoring stations around the site continued to report low concentrations of fine particulate matter (PM2.5). Alberta Environment continues to support ongoing air-quality monitoring and has reported no significant changes in regional air-quality conditions related to the incident. Calgary Fire Department is aware that some residents have reported stronger odours in nearby communities in recent days. Residents may continue to notice periodic odours, smoke or occasional visible flames during suppression activities. The City has previously advised that these conditions can occur as crews access and extinguish buried burning material within the landfill. The Calgary Fire Department will continue to provide updates as operations progress. -30-

title: Charge into Fire Safety - Safe Charging is a Superpower!
summary: Fire Prevention Week runs from October 4-10, and this year the Calgary Fire Department (CFD) is urging all Calgarians to learn how to use and dispose of lithium-ion batteries safely. Firefighters are seeing an increase in battery fires in homes, garages and businesses across the city. Lithium-ion batteries power many everyday electronics, including phones, laptops, power tools and e-bikes. If not handled correctly, damaged, or overcharged, they can overheat and cause fires or explosions. “Fires caused by lithium-ion batteries are especially dangerous, to Calgarians and firefighters,” said Jeff Budai, Community Safety Coordinator with CFD. “They can burn with extreme heat and speed, making them difficult to extinguish. We urge everyone to take precautions when using these types of batteries and to learn what to do if the battery is smoking, releasing a chemical smell or producing flames. It might help to save your life.” Since 2015, Calgary has experienced over $46 million in property losses due to lithium-ion battery fires, with $38 million in losses in 2025 alone. While lithium-ion battery fires are not as frequent as structure fires, they doubled in Calgary between 2024 to 2025, from 10 to 21 incidents. 2026 is currently on track to see the most ever lithium-ion battery fires on record, with 20 fires, mostly caused by e-scooters, e-bikes and battery packs. With the growing local and international trend in battery fires, the Calgary Fire Department has published a new “ What to do with your lithium-ion battery ” guide to calgary.ca/chargesafe , which helps residents to identify when to call 9-1-1 and where to dispose damaged batteries. Quick tips to avoid battery fires Buy safely: Purchase products with lithium-ion batteries only from reputable vendors. Look for a “UL” or “CSA” stamp on the product to ensure it meets safety standards. Charge safely: Use only the cables that come with the device and charge devices on a hard, flat surface. Do not overcharge devices; unplug them or remove the battery once fully charged. Do not charge under pillows, on beds, or on couches where batteries can overheat. Recycle responsibly: Properly recycle lithium-ion batteries at designated collection sites to prevent fire hazards. For more information about lithium-ion batteries, please visit calgary.ca/chargesafe Family-friendly events During Fire Prevention Week, we are hosting several events to help Calgarians learn about the importance of charging and recycling lithium-ion batteries safely. Calgarians of all ages are invited to drop by to talk to the firefighters, tour the fire trucks and enter to win some great prizes. October 4 Fire Station Open House Location: Fire Station 30, 6 McKenzie Towne Gate SE Time: 1 - 4 p.m. October 7 Meet Calgary firefighters to learn about fire prevention and enjoy a free VR experience Location: CF Chinook Centre Time: 3 - 7 p.m. October 10 Meet Calgary firefighters to learn about fire prevention and enjoy a free VR experience! Location: Sunridge Mall Time: 10 a.m. - 4 p.m. Did you know? Battery fires at City landfills and recycling facilities are increasing due to improper disposal, with over 50 fire incidents reported at City landfills and recycling facilities in 2025. Since 2015, Calgary has experienced over $46 million in property loss due to lithium-ion battery fires, with $38 million in losses in 2025 alone. While lithium-ion battery fires are not as frequent as structure fires, they doubled in Calgary between 2024 to 2025, from 10 to 21 incidents. 2026 is currently on track to see the most ever lithium-ion battery fires on record, with 20 fires, mostly caused by e-scooters, e-bikes and battery packs. About Fire Prevention Week Fire Prevention Week is held annually by fire departments across North America. Fire Prevention Day was proclaimed in Canada in 1919 to commemorate the Great Chicago Fire of 1871, as well as a major fire that destroyed the Centre Block of the Parliament buildings in Ottawa on February 3, 1916. In 1922, Fire Prevention Day expanded to Fire Prevention Week. For more information about Fire Prevention Week, please visit calgary.ca/firepreventionweek -30-

title: Calgarians can recycle more starting October 1
summary: New recyclable packaging materials accepted in blue carts under Alberta's Extended Producer Responsibility framework. Starting October 1, Calgarians will be able to recycle more packaging materials through their blue carts and community recycling depots as Alberta expands residential recycling programs under its Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) regulations. The expanded program gives residents more opportunities to recycle common household packaging that previously belonged in the garbage. Newly accepted materials include: Foam packaging such as foam blocks, takeout containers and egg cartons. Food and body aerosols such as cooking spray, sunscreen and hairspray. Flexible plastic bags and wrappers such as chip bags and granola bar wrappers. Tubes such as toothpaste and deodorant containers. “For Calgarians, recycling is part of everyday life, and this change means more of the packaging residents use can now be recycled through the city's residential recycling system,” said Sharon Howland, Leader, Program Management, Waste & Recycling Services. “It's a practical improvement that makes recycling easier and more convenient for households across the city while supporting a more consistent recycling system across Alberta.” To ensure materials can be successfully sorted and recycled, all recyclables should be empty, clean and loose before being placed in blue carts. Empty containers of liquids and food residue. Clean containers by rinsing or wiping them out. Place recyclables loose in the cart, not in bags. The City of Calgary will continue collecting blue carts on the current collection schedule, with no changes to pickup service. Residents will not see any changes to their ENMAX bills when the new recycling changes take effect on October 1. Through Alberta's EPR framework, producers are taking on most of the costs of residential recycling. As a result, The City's Blue Cart fee for single-family households was reduced on April 1, 2025, saving households $7.17 annually. The expanded program applies to both single-family households and multi-family properties. Multi-family property managers and condo boards can register with Circular Materials to access free recycling collection services and the expanded list of accepted materials. Residents can learn more about the new recycling program and view the complete list of accepted materials at calgary.ca/recyclemore or contact 311 for assistance. NOTE to media: City-provided b-roll will be posted on the Newsroom later today and can be accessed here , when available. -30- About Alberta's Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) framework: The expanded list of accepted materials is part of Alberta's Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) framework, which creates a more consistent residential recycling system across the province. Residents across Alberta will be able to recycle the same accepted packaging materials, regardless of where they live. Under EPR, producers such as manufacturers and brands are responsible for managing the packaging and paper products they supply once those materials become waste. The first phase of Alberta's EPR regulations came into effect on April 1, 2025. The second phase expands the range of materials accepted in residential recycling programs.

title: The City and partners confirm future Indigenous Gathering Place will be located at The Confluence
summary: In support of the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, The City, the Indigenous Gathering Place Society (IGPS) and The Confluence Historic Site & Parkland have confirmed that the future Indigenous Gathering Place will have a permanent home at Moh'kinsstis, where the Bow and Elbow rivers meet. The decision marks a significant milestone following years of Indigenous community leadership, Elder guidance, advocacy, engagement and partnership. A portion of the City-owned lands currently leased to The Confluence will be reallocated to IGPS for the future Indigenous Gathering Place. The exact location and size of the parcel will be determined through the next phase of work between IGPS, The City and The Confluence. “This is a significant milestone in a journey that has been guided by Elders and Indigenous community for many years,” says Buddie Dixon, co-chair, Indigenous Gathering Place Society. “Moh'kinsstis has been a place of gathering since time immemorial. Knowing the Indigenous Gathering Place will have a visible and permanent home here brings us one step closer to creating a place where Indigenous Peoples can gather, practice culture, share knowledge and strengthen community for generations to come.” Moh'kinsstis has been a place of gathering and significance for Indigenous Peoples since time immemorial. Its history extends far beyond the establishment of Fort Calgary in 1875. The future Indigenous Gathering Place will be rooted in this much longer relationship between Indigenous Peoples and the lands and waters where the Bow and Elbow rivers meet. The Confluence Historic Site & Parkland Society (formerly the Fort Calgary Preservation Society) acquired operations of the 42-acre site in 1985. In recent years, the civic partner has evolved to centre the land's Indigenous significance through programming, exhibits and committed land stewardship. “For close to four years, The Confluence has focused on building relationships with Indigenous community members and developing offerings like the Confluence Reciprocity Program and the Holy Gathering Place, which actively welcome and support Indigenous-led initiatives to the site,” said Jennifer Thompson, president of The Confluence. “We believe that a neighbouring Indigenous Gathering Place will be complementary to that work.” The City, the Indigenous Gathering Place Society, and The Confluence will now work together to identify the specific parcel for the future Indigenous Gathering Place and determine the changes required to the existing land lease. “Confirming a future home for the Indigenous Gathering Place at Moh'kinsstis is an important step in The City's commitment to reconciliation,” says Mayor Jeromy Farkas. “This is a vision that Elders and Indigenous community have carried forward for many years. We are committed to working with the Indigenous Gathering Place and The Confluence to establish a home where their vision can take root for generations to come.” Mayor Farkas, Jennifer Thompson and Buddie Dixon were at an event for the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation commemoration at The Confluence, to share the news. -30-

title: Prolific offender facing 32 charges
summary: We have arrested a repeat offender who was wanted on 10 outstanding warrants. In the evening hours of Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026, the offender was seen entering a new-home construction site located in the 4800 block of Voyageur Drive N.W., and operating a motor vehicle contrary to a release order. He was arrested without incident, and officers seized a sawed-off shotgun with a defaced serial number along with ammunition. As a result, Logan Donald SMITH, 29, is charged with: Two counts of possession of a controlled substance Two counts of driving while prohibited One count of break and enter to commit One count of possession of break and enter tools Two counts of theft of a motor vehicle One count of mischief over $5,000 One count of possession of stolen property One count of unsafe storage of a firearm Two counts of carrying a concealed weapon One count of unauthorized possession of a prohibited weapon One count of possession of a firearm without holding a license One count of possessing a prohibited firearm with accessible ammunition One count of possessing a defaced firearm Two counts of breaching a prohibited firearms order 13 counts of breaching a release order SMITH remains in custody and is scheduled to next appear in court on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026. title: Joint operation results in 15 arrests and 51 warrants executed
summary: A joint warrant enforcement operation between the Calgary Police Service and Alberta Sheriffs has resulted in 15 arrests and the execution of 51 outstanding warrants. The recent two-day operation brought together members of our District 2 Patrol and Patrol Support Teams and the Fugitive Apprehension Sheriff Support Team, FASST. The initiative focused on locating wanted individuals, improving public safety and furthering investigations. The operation was planned over several weeks, with analytical resources preparing and reviewing approximately 120 information packages before officers were deployed. During the operation, members attended 66 residences throughout Calgary. The operation resulted in: 15 individuals arrested 51 warrants executed, including one Canada-wide warrant Five criminal charges laid 34 investigations In addition to arrests, investigators gathered information about the possible whereabouts of wanted individuals, verified addresses, developed new investigative leads and updated records to support future enforcement efforts.

title: From rendering to reality: Sunnyside Flood Barrier complete, strengthening Calgary's flood resilience
summary: With the completion of the Sunnyside Flood Barrier, Calgary has achieved a significant milestone in building a more flood-resilient city. Now operational, the barrier provides critical protection for the communities of Sunnyside and Hillhurst, reducing flood risk to homes, businesses, and essential infrastructure. As a key component of Calgary's Flood Resilience Plan, the project reflects years of planning, collaboration and investment to strengthen resilience, connectivity and public spaces in Sunnyside and Hillhurst. "The completion of the Sunnyside Flood Barrier is a major achievement for Calgary and a significant step forward in our efforts to build a more flood-resilient city,” said Mayor Jeromy Farkas. "This project strengthens our ability to withstand future flood events while creating lasting community spaces that Sunnyside residents and visitors can enjoy for generations to come." The flood barrier provides the communities of Sunnyside and Hillhurst with protection from a one-in-100-year flood event, meaning a flood with a one per cent chance of occurring in any given year. The project represents a total investment of $73 million over a decade, from initial planning through to completion, delivering a significant step forward in reducing flood risk and strengthening Calgary's long-term resilience. Spanning 2.4 kilometres, the barrier combines permanent flood walls, sheet pile walls, demountable flood walls and deployable flood protection systems to reduce flood risk while maintaining community access, strengthening connections to the Bow River and preserving the character of the surrounding area. Michael Thompson, Chief Operating Officer – Water Utility notes the importance of investing in Calgary's flood resilience. “Building a flood barrier Calgarians can rely on means preparing in advance for extreme events and reducing their impacts when they occur. The Sunnyside Flood Barrier is an important example of how long-term planning and investment help protect people, homes and businesses from river flooding." Community input played a significant role in shaping the project and the public spaces surrounding the barrier. Through planning and design, Sunnyside and Hillhurst residents and The City of Calgary Council emphasized the importance of preserving connections to the Bow River, enhancing public spaces and honouring the community's history. As a result, the project includes nine new seating areas, two food truck pads, improved pathways and public spaces along the river for people walking, wheeling and cycling, along with approximately 200 new trees, including 68 Memorial poplar clone trees, and additional landscaping enhancements. Four key public spaces were also enhanced throughout the project, which include the Calgary Soldiers' Memorial, Peace Bridge North Shore, 7 Street N.W. lookout and Prince's Island Pedestrian Bridge & Bow River access. “What began as a vision on paper has now become a lasting investment in Calgary's future,” said Martin Pritchard, Manager of Linear Infrastructure Delivery. “Guided by community input and brought to life through the collective expertise of multiple project teams, the Sunnyside Flood Barrier delivers critical flood protection while enhancing public spaces and celebrating the unique history and character of the community.” Since the 2013 flood, over $1.3 billion has been invested in flood mitigation and resilience projects throughout Calgary. Mitigation work that is already complete or is underway has reduced Calgary's flood risk by approximately 70 per cent and our flood damages by $118 million every year. Through a coordinated approach that combines upstream, community-level and property-level flood protection measures, The City continues to strengthen resilience across Calgary's river valleys. Investments in Calgary's flood protection directly support the future of Calgary's communities, businesses, and infrastructure. The Sunnyside Flood Barrier is now operational and protecting the community, while final landscaping and public realm enhancements continue. Landscaping and pathway work are expected to be completed by the end of October 2026. For the latest information, visit www.calgary.ca/sunnysidebarrier . -30-

title: ECCO Landfill Fire Update- Sept 24
summary: The Calgary Fire Department (CFD) continues suppression efforts at the ECCO Recycling facility landfill fire in southeast Calgary. The fire remains contained to the landfill site as crews continue working toward full extinguishment. Today, crews continued capping operations by removing debris, flattening affected areas and spreading additional dirt and clay across the site. These efforts help isolate remaining heat sources and support extinguishment efforts. As capping operations continue, crews are observing reduced visible smoke from portions of the site. New drone footage captured over the site today provided an updated aerial view of conditions, helping inform planning and ongoing capping operations. An engineering consultant also attended the site to assess conditions and provide technical expertise in support of ongoing incident management and recovery planning. As the incident enters a longer-term phase, incident management is transitioning to a remote command model. CFD will continue to monitor site conditions, coordinate suppression activities and support ongoing work at the site. Information provided to CFD by Alberta Health Services indicates that recent air quality monitoring has not identified any new exceedances at monitoring locations supporting the incident response. Alberta Health Services notes that air quality can vary significantly over short distances due to wind patterns, terrain and local conditions, with the greatest potential for impacts occurring in areas directly downwind of the fire. Residents may continue to notice occasional smoke, odours or isolated flare-ups from the site. These flare-ups can occur as crews expose and extinguish buried burning material and do not necessarily indicate the fire is expanding beyond the landfill area. Capping operations, monitoring and site rehabilitation activities will continue until the fire risk has been fully mitigated. As operations continue to stabilize, CFD will transition from daily public updates to a weekly update schedule. Additional updates will be issued as required should significant developments occur at the site. For the latest information on the landfill fire, visit Calgary.ca/landfillfire -30-

title: Calgary police release results of commercial vehicle inspection
summary: The Calgary Police Service recently completed its three-day fall commercial vehicle inspection in high-volume traffic areas around Calgary. The checks were conducted from Tuesday, Sept. 15, through Thursday, Sept. 17, 2026, in partnership with Sheriff Highway Patrol (SHP), Alberta Transportation Vehicle Safety and Economic Corridors, Airdrie Bylaw, and The City of Calgary. In that time, a total of 197 vehicles were inspected, with the following results: · 100 vehicles were found to have critical defects that placed them out of service. (51 per cent) · 36 vehicles were found to have major defects that required attention. (18 per cent) · 61 vehicles passed with no critical defects. (31 per cent) A total of 98 violation tickets were issued. Additionally, one driver was charged for operating a commercial vehicle without a valid license. Among the most common defects to be found were worn tires, poorly secured cargo, and inadequate brakes. Additionally, defective headlights, faulty steering systems, and leaking fuel tanks were also found. “Commercial vehicle drivers perform a critical service for Calgarians, transporting important goods we all rely on,” said Insp. Robert Patterson, with the Calgary Police Traffic Unit. “However, it's critical that those vehicles meet all legal standards to ensure the safety of everyone on the road.” The percentage of vehicles placed out of service during this inspection (51 per cent) was slightly higher than during the inspection event that took place in the spring (48 per cent). Photos of some of the vehicle violations detected during the most recent inspection are available on The City Of Calgary Newsroom. The North American Standard Out-of-Service Criteria is the pass-fail criteria for inspections and identifies critical violations that can prohibit a motor carrier or driver from operating a commercial motor vehicle for a specified period of time, or until the condition is corrected. A list of the requirements and resources are available on the CVSA website, including a North American Standard Roadside Inspection Vehicle Cheat Sheet at www.cvsa.org/inspections/resources .

title: Bearspaw South Feeder Main Construction Progress Continues with 80% of Replacement Steel Pipe Installed
summary: The Bearspaw South Feeder Main Replacement Project continues to advance on schedule, with approximately 80 per cent of the new feeder main pipe now installed in the ground across Stages A and B. “We are pleased to have more than 90 per cent of the project materials required to complete the project on-site in Calgary, including 93% for the steel pipe,” said Darren Finney, Manager, Major Projects. “Crews continue to make strong progress across both stages, and we remain on track for the new feeder main to be in service by the end of the year.” Stage A construction update Stage A construction began in January and used microtunnelling to complete approximately 3.7 kilometres of tunneling beneath existing infrastructure. Installation of both the concrete carrier pipe and the new steel feeder main between the Shaganappi Pump Station and 73 Street N.W. is now complete. Stage A construction remains underway in the area, with crews continuing valve chamber installation, pipe welding and work on supporting infrastructure. Stage B construction update Stage B open-cut construction along 34 Avenue N.W. in Bowness began in June and remains on schedule. More than 1.6 km of steel feeder main pipe has been installed, representing approximately 61 per cent of the Stage B alignment. Pipe installation is complete on seven of the 13 blocks with another three currently underway. Stage B construction continues in sections, with four crews working simultaneously. Roadways, sidewalks and property access are being restored as construction advances. Landscaping restoration will continue into Spring 2027. Looking ahead The Bearspaw South Feeder Main will need to be shut down to connect the new feeder main to the existing water system. Pipe tie-in connections at various locations along the new feeder main pipe will include open-cut construction similar to ongoing Stage B construction. Stage 4 outdoor water restrictions and indoor water conservation will be required during this time. Feeder main commissioning is estimated to begin in December. Once the pipe is connected, the water restrictions will be lifted, but we still need to fill, disinfect and complete water quality testing before the new feeder main is in service. These estimated date ranges are subject to change based on construction timelines and project logistics. Parkdale Boulevard Repairs Additional repairs will be completed this fall on the feeder main between the Shaganappi Pump Station and the Memorial Pump Station along Parkdale Boulevard and Memorial Drive N.W. Recent condition assessments identified locations on the 1500 mm section of the Bearspaw South Feeder main along Parkdale Boulevard that require proactive repairs. While the 1500 mm and the 1950 mm pipe, which is the pipe currently being replaced, are both part of the same feeder main, they are separate sections with different condition profiles. Assessments of the 1500 mm between the Shaganappi Pump Station and the Memorial Pump Station, show it remains in good overall condition and does not require replacement. Instead, targeted repairs at specific locations will help maintain the pipe's long-term reliability. The repairs will involve 24/7 construction, excavating locations, removing sections of pipe and replacing them with new steel segments. Community support We continue to work directly with residents, businesses and property owners affected by construction. Anyone with questions or concerns can contact the project team. Community members are encouraged to attend upcoming information sessions and can register online at calgary.ca/bearspawfeedermain . They can also visit the project's Community Resource Centre at the Bowness Community Association. Office hours are Monday and Wednesday: 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., Tuesday and Thursday: 10 a.m. to 7 p.m. The Bearspaw South Feeder Main Construction Liaisons are available at the Community Resource Centre on Wednesdays from 10 a.m. to 12 p.m. For project information and construction updates, visit calgary.ca/bearspawfeedermain

title: ECCO Landfill Fire Update- Sept 23
summary: Suppression efforts at the ECCO landfill fire in southeast Calgary continue to make steady progress as crews focus on reducing remaining hot spots and expanding the use of compacted soil and clay across affected areas of the site. Clean fill is being delivered to the site as crews continue placing and compacting material over areas affected by the fire. Additionally, fire breaks are being made by removing debris, flattening and compacting the area followed by spreading clean fill in unaffected areas to prevent fires from spreading. An excavator equipped with a tamping attachment is being used to increase compaction on portions of the pile, helping reduce pathways that allow heat, smoke and air to move through the material. Specialized contractors remained on site today monitoring conditions and addressing isolated hot spots. While overall fire activity has decreased in recent days, crews continue to closely monitor areas where residual heat remains and respond to changing conditions as required. Alberta Environment and Protected Areas continue environmental and air quality monitoring related to the incident. Recent monitoring has generally identified low-risk air quality conditions in surrounding communities, and monitoring resources remain available should conditions change. Residents can continue to monitor current air quality conditions through Alberta's Air Quality Health Index and provincial incident monitoring updates. The latest information, frequently asked questions and previous updates are available at calgary.ca/landfillfire -30-

title: Three men facing 20 charges in weapons seizure
summary: Earlier this month, members of our Gun Violence Enforcement Team arrested and charged three men who were found to be in possession of prohibited firearms and in violation of release orders, with one man wanted on outstanding warrants. On Thursday, Sept. 10, 2026, police executed a search warrant in the 100 block of Covington Rise N.E., resulting in the seizure of the following: A Glock 17 handgun An H&R Arms Company .22 calibre revolver A 3D printed Glock 18 handgun A 3D printer A 3D printed Glock magazine A 3D printed silencer A replica BB gun As a result of the investigation, Robert CVITANOVIC, 55, is charged with: Two counts of failing to comply with a release order One count each of unsafe storage of a firearm, possession of an unauthorized firearm and possession of a prohibited or restricted firearm with ammunition Three counts of breaching a firearms prohibition order CVITANOVIC is schedule to next appear in court on Friday, Sept. 25, 2026. John Wayne KIRBY, 44, is charged with: Two counts of failing to comply with a release order One count each of unsafe storage of a firearm, possession of an unauthorized firearm, possession of a prohibited or restricted firearm with ammunition and breach of a firearms prohibition order KIRBY is scheduled to next appear in court on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026. Travis Ricky Cameron ROBILLARD-BALL, 35, is charged with: Two counts of failing to comply with a release order One count of possession of a prohibited device knowing its possession is unauthorized Three counts of breaching of a firearms prohibition order ROBILLARD-BALL is scheduled to next appear in court on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. “Every crime gun we seize is one less weapon that can be used to harm someone in our community,” says Staff Sergeant Matt Gow of the Calgary Police Service Organized Crime Enforcement Unit. “Removing these firearms from the hands of offenders is one of the most important ways we can prevent violence and keep Calgarians safe.” Addressing gun violence continues to be a priority for our Service. Through investigation, prevention, and enforcement activities we have coordinated our resources to reduce victimization and enhance community safety. Our efforts to address gun violence rely on strong community support. If you have information that could help an investigation, such as witnessing suspicious behaviour or vehicles, please contact police. Even something small can have a great impact on an investigation. Anyone with information about this incident is asked to contact police by calling 403-266-1234. Tips can also be submitted anonymously to Crime Stoppers through any of the following methods: TALK: 1-800-222-8477 TYPE: www.calgarycrimestoppers.org APP: P3 Tips CA26412627/5053

title: Charges laid after hate-motivated assault
summary: Two men have been charged after a hate-motivated assault in July. On Thursday, July 2, 2026, police were called for reports of a woman in medical distress outside of a restaurant in the 9600 block of Macleod Trail S.W. Witnesses reported that the woman had been using a portable washroom when two men walked up to the washroom and tipped it over with the door toward the pavement, leaving the woman trapped inside. The men then fled. The witnesses assisted the woman out of the washroom, called police and rendered first aid on the scene. The victim was transported to hospital for exposure to waste matter and toxic chemicals. She has since recovered. Following an investigation by our Hate Crime Prevention Team, which included reviewing CCTV and speaking with witnesses and the victim, it is believed the men made comments targeting the victim based on gender and ethnicity, and hate-motivation has been deemed a factor in the assault. As a result, two men were arrested in connection with the incident. Tyson David CANN, 24, of Calgary, was charged with one count of assault causing bodily harm and will next appear in court on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. Fynn Storm FERRIER, 24, of Kimberley B.C., was charged with one count of assault causing bodily harm and will next appear in court on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. “This was a degrading and harmful assault that left the victim trapped, injured and in need of medical care,” says Sergeant Chelsea Francois of the Calgary Police Service's Hate Crime Prevention Team. “Hate-motivated crimes have a deep impact, not only on the person targeted but on the broader community. There is no place for hate in our city. If you see hate, report it.” Any evidence of hate motivation is considered by the courts after a person is found guilty of the connected crime. If the judge decides during sentencing that hate was a motivation for the offence, it is an aggravating factor that can add to the convicted person's sentence. Hate-motivated crimes are recognizable crimes, like assault, theft, vandalism or any other crime, where the offender was motivated by bias, prejudice or hate that is based on one of nine personal characteristics of the victim. Visit www.reporthate.ca for more information on how and why to report. Anyone with information about this incident is asked to contact the Calgary Police Service non-emergency number at 403-266-1234. Tips can also be submitted anonymously to Crime Stoppers through either of the following methods: TALK: 1-800-222-8477 TYPE: www.calgarycrimestoppers.org APP: P3 Tips CA26292939/5299

title: Wood From City Tree Removals Benefits Animals at The Wilder Institute's Calgary Zoo
summary: Wood from trees removed and pruned as part of City of Calgary urban forest maintenance is getting a second life thanks to a partnership with The Wilder Institute's Calgary Zoo. The removals were completed to proactively manage safety risks for dead and dying trees. Rather than going directly to compost, suitable branches, logs and other woody material from the removals have been provided to the zoo, where they are being put to use to support the animals in their care. The material is being used for habitat enrichment and browse (food) for a variety of animals including moose, giraffes, camels, gorillas, monkeys and hippos, providing new opportunities for the animals to snack, explore, forage, climb and play. “The urban forest plays an important role in Calgary's quality of life. This partnership shows how we can continue generating value even after a tree's lifecycle has ended,” said Wayne Driscoll, Urban Forestry Superintendent, Calgary Parks and Open Spaces. “By connecting City operations with community partners like The Wilder Institute's Calgary Zoo, we are advancing sustainability, reducing waste, and creating meaningful benefits for both people and animals.” Hundreds of members from the zoo's community of volunteers played an integral role in the removals by helping strip branches of leaves, bag woody material, leaves and seeds, cut and sort smaller branch materials into containers for transport and move bagged materials to trucks for transport. There was a lot of work to be done, and the volunteers were there with enthusiasm and big smiles. The City and zoo extend their thanks to everyone who helped make the effort a success. The removals translated into: 304, 6–7-kilogram bags of browse 10, 16–22-kilogram silage barrels of woody material 1.5 truckloads of bagged branches Numerous large logs to be used as “furniture” in animal habitats “We're always excited to receive wood like this because it gives us new opportunities to enrich the lives of the animals in our care,” said Katharine Varzé, Horticulture Manager with the Wilder Institute's Calgary Zoo. “Whether it's fresh browse for animals to eat or larger logs that become part of their habitats, there are lots of ways we can put this material to use. It's pretty special to see trees from Calgary's urban forest find a second life here at the zoo." The City regularly completes tree risk assessments, pruning and removals of trees that are dead, declining or pose a public safety risk as part of its ongoing care to support the long-term health of Calgary's urban forest. As part of this work, Urban Forestry is looking for new ways to make good use of the removed wood material where possible. The collaboration with The Wilder Institute's Calgary Zoo is just one example of how partnerships can help put removed material to good use while supporting animal care and wellbeing. Calgary Parks is also currently working with the zoo to provide removed invasive caragana plants as a snack for the resident giraffes. The Wilder Institute's Calgary Zoo and Calgary Parks social media channels will feature more photos and stories of the animals benefiting from the wood provided in the coming weeks. We invite Calgarians to follow along to see how the trees continue to make a positive impact: Facebook: facebook.com/thecalgaryzoo , facebook.com/cityofcalgaryparks Instagram: instagram.com/thecalgaryzoo , instagram.com/calgaryparks * Photos courtesy of The Wilder Institute's Calgary Zoo

title: City implements stronger fireworks enforcement to improve public safety
summary: The City of Calgary is taking action to improve public safety by strengthening fireworks enforcement and introducing a new offence to deter unauthorized fireworks use. Council approved amendments to the Fire Operations and Fees Bylaw that will come into effect on September 22, 2026. The bylaw changes will increase fines for selling fireworks from $750 to $3,000 and increase fines for discharging fireworks without a permit from $500 to $1,000. The City of Calgary's review found that Calgary's current penalties are lower than those in comparable municipalities and are not acting as an effective deterrent. The updated bylaw will also introduce a new offence of a $1,000 fine for carrying or setting up fireworks for use in a public place. This will allow enforcement officers to intervene when people are preparing to set up fireworks in parks, streets or other public spaces before they are discharged, helping prevent unsafe activity. The amendments come in response to ongoing concerns about unauthorized fireworks activity in Calgary. Between 2023 and 2025, The City received 183 fireworks-related service requests through 311. “These changes are about protecting public safety while supporting safe and responsible celebrations,” shares Glenn Baxter, Fire Marshal, Calgary Fire Department. “These bylaw amendments give enforcement partners stronger tools to address unauthorized fireworks activity and reduce risks to residents, property and public spaces.” Ryan Pleckaitis, Chief, Community Standards, added “by increasing penalties and introducing a new offence for the open display of fireworks in public places, we are reinforcing a simple message: public safety comes first.” The City is also recommending a community-led, City-supported approach to celebrations that use fireworks. Through collaborative efforts, The City is committed to helping organizations access grants, permits, logistical support and event-planning assistance while providing safe opportunities for Calgarians to come together and celebrate cultural traditions. Over the past few months, The City has developed a coordinated operational plan involving Emergency Management & Community Safety (EMCS), the Calgary Fire Department (CFD) and the Calgary Police Service (CPS) to improve planning, education and enforcement during peak periods such as Diwali, Stampede and New Years Eve. Implementation of these plans will begin in Q4 2026. By strengthening enforcement and improving education to support safe celebrations, Calgary is building a future where cultural traditions can thrive while keeping communities safe, welcoming and vibrant for all. For more information visit: www.calgary.ca/fireworks -30-

title: The City releases findings of internal review into 911 calls related to Parker Wells
summary: CALGARY - The tragic death of Parker Wells continues to have a profound impact on his family and loved ones, the broader Calgary community, and the many residents, emergency professionals and first responders who were impacted by the events surrounding his disappearance and the subsequent search efforts. In the aftermath of these events, and to ensure The City followed applicable policies and procedures, 9-1-1 undertook a comprehensive internal review of the calls received on the day Parker was reported missing from his day home. That review has now been completed, and a summary of the outcomes are being shared as part of The City's commitment to accountability, continuous improvement and maintaining public trust. The internal review examined dispatch actions and decision-making, as well as adherence to operational policies. “The outcome of this review is difficult,” says Iain Bushell, Director of Emergency Management and Community Safety with The City of Calgary, “as it identified instances where established procedures were not followed, resulting in a delay in how certain information was acted on. That delay did not meet the standard of service we expect.” The review found gaps in adherence to procedures, rather than gaps in the procedures themselves. As a result, appropriate disciplinary action has been taken. Due to confidentiality obligations related to personnel matters, no further details regarding individual employment actions will be provided. In addition to the immediate corrective actions taken, a number of measures have been implemented to strengthen accountability and reinforce the consistent application of procedures and protocols, including enhanced training and operational oversight. “We are committed to strengthening our processes and ensuring our employees have the support, training and tools they need to serve Calgarians effectively,” says Bushell. “Calgary 911 employees are deeply committed to public safety, and when an event has a tragic outcome such as this, they feel the weight of that responsibility. “Our thoughts remain with Parker's family, loved ones and all those affected by this tragic loss. We will ensure the lessons from this tragedy lead to meaningful improvements in how we serve the community.” - 30 - BACKGROUNDER 9-1-1 INTERNAL REVIEW: KEY FINDINGS Dispatch actions and decision-making Two calls were made from the day home to 9-1-1 on July 16, 2026. A Priority 1 police event was not created during the first call, received at 10:53 a.m., as the caller confirmed they did not wish to file a missing person report at that time and would call back if Parker was not found shortly. The internal review, however, found that sufficient information was provided to identify the situation as an “endangered missing child” and a Priority 1 police event should have been actioned according to policy. The supervisor reviewed the call that was entered as an advised event but did not reopen, escalate or reassess the event after reviewing it. The internal review found that the supervisor should have more fully considered the totality of available information, specifically the child's age and the inability of day home staff to locate the child. At 11:24 a.m. the original caller phoned 9-1-1 back to officially report Parker missing and a Priority 1 Missing Person event was created at 11:41 a.m. The internal review found that the delay in entering the event represented a potential opportunity to dispatch police earlier. Adherence to operational policies and procedures The review found that sufficient information was shared to recognize the occurrence as an endangered missing child event and that the established procedures related to missing persons, event prioritization, dispatch requirements and event management were not followed. The review highlighted gaps in applying existing policies rather than gaps in the policies themselves. It further determined that departures from established procedures contributed to delayed police notification and response. Identified opportunities for improvement and actions taken in response Strengthen oversight and quality assurance Actions taken in response All advised events (calls entered as not requiring police assistance) are now reviewed every 15-30 minutes by two supervisors, rather than one, providing an additional layer of oversight to support consistent decision-making and application of operational procedures. (completed) A program of spot checks and periodic call reviews is being implemented by coaching mentors and the coaching pool to reinforce operational standards and support continuous learning. (in progress) Additional workplace supports have been implemented by positioning employees closer to senior staff to facilitate real-time guidance, mentorship and operational oversight. (completed) Reinforce policy compliance Actions taken in response All employees completed a mandatory review of missing persons policies, including reinforcement of key procedures and expectations . (completed) Focused team briefings were conducted to reinforce policy adherence, accuracy, timeliness, critical thinking and decision-making, including the operational impacts of dispatch decisions . (completed) A broader review of policies and standard operating procedures is underway to strengthen clarity, reduce ambiguity and support consistent operational decision-making. (in progress) Enhance training and professional development Actions taken in response New recruit training is being extended by one week, bringing the program to a total of 11 weeks. (in progress) Additional training focused on critical thinking, emotional intelligence, and problem solving is being developed for delivery to future new-hire classes and all existing employees. (in progress) Enhanced training for supervisors, including strengthened guidance on event review and escalation responsibilities, is being developed and implemented . (in progress)

title: Man charged with several firearms offences
summary: We have charged a man after police seized a loaded, high-velocity weapon, along with ammunition, magazines, and a suppressor following a traffic stop outside of a local hotel. On Friday, Sept. 18, 2026, at approximately 11 p.m., officers conducted a traffic stop on an occupied truck parked outside of the Red Carpet Inn, located at 4635 16 Ave. N.W. The license plate was not registered to the vehicle and the driver did not have a valid licence. Officers determined the vehicle was stolen and arrested the driver. They subsequently searched his hotel room and recovered a loaded AR-15 – style rifle, with the serial number removed, along with several magazines, a suppressor, ammunition and cell phones. A picture of the rifle and some of the recovered items is available on The City of Calgary Newsroom. Matthew Randel Lynden SMITH, 35, is charged with: · Nine possession of firearms-related offences, including unsafe storage and possession when prohibited · One count of possession of stolen property over $5,000 · Five counts of failing to comply with conditions SMITH remains in custody and is scheduled to appear in court on Monday, Sept. 28, 2026. Anyone with information related to this case is asked to call the police non-emergency line at 403-266-1234. title: ECCO Landfill Fire Update- Sept 21
summary: The Calgary Fire Department (CFD) continues suppression and containment operations at the ECCO Recycling facility fire in southeast Calgary. Crews remain focused on identifying and treating areas of elevated heat within the landfill pile. Ground assessments, thermal imaging and aerial observations are being used to locate remaining hotspots and guide suppression efforts. Additional clean fill material continues to be brought to the site and staged for ongoing operations. Crews are placing and compacting soil over targeted areas of the landfill pile to help smother deep-seated hotspots, reduce the amount of oxygen reaching heated areas and limit smoke production. To support this work, additional heavy equipment is being brought to the site, including an excavator equipped with a specialized tamping attachment. The equipment will be used to compress soil in selected areas of the pile, helping eliminate pockets and gaps where heat, smoke and air can move. This compaction is expected to improve the effectiveness of suppression efforts and support longer-term containment of remaining hotspots. While progress is being made, crews continue to monitor isolated areas of concern within the landfill pile that have experienced intermittent flare-ups. Residents may continue to observe periods of smoke, steam or localized fire activity as crews expose, assess and suppress remaining heat sources. These conditions are expected during landfill-fire suppression operations and do not necessarily indicate a deterioration in conditions. The Calgary Police Service is supporting operations through aerial drone assessments of the site. Information gathered during these flights will assist incident commanders in identifying areas of elevated heat and tracking suppression progress across the landfill pile. Air quality monitoring continues by Alberta Environment and Protected Areas, in and around the incident area. The ECCO landfill fire remains a complex, long-duration incident. Extinguishing deep-seated hotspots within the landfill pile will require continued suppression, monitoring and soil-placement operations in the days ahead. Residents can find the latest information, frequently asked questions and previous updates at Calgary.ca/landfillfire .

title: ECCO Landfill Fire Update- Sept 20
summary: Operations continue at the ECCO Recycling facility landfill fire in southeast Calgary as crews work to contain and suppress isolated hotspots within the landfill. Fire suppression resources remain on site and continue to monitor areas of elevated heat within the landfill pile. Crews are conducting ongoing assessments in the area of an underground utility access point where elevated temperatures have previously been observed. This work is helping guide suppression and containment efforts. The fire remains contained to the landfill site, with crews focused on managing hotspots and preventing fire spread within the affected area. Crews continue staging significant volumes of soil and cover material to support the next phase of suppression and containment operations. More than 800 cubic metres of materials were delivered to the site yesterday, with similar volumes expected throughout the coming week as protective cover continues to be built over affected areas. Air quality monitoring continues on and around the site and continues to indicate no immediate public safety concerns beyond the landfill property. Residents in southeast Calgary may continue to notice smoke or odours as weather and wind conditions change. Individuals sensitive to smoke should consider limiting outdoor activities and taking appropriate precautions. For the latest updates and information, visit Calgary.ca Landfill Fire Updates . -30-

title: Police investigate serious-injury motorcycle collision in the city's southwest
