title: ECCO Landfill Fire Update- Sept 19
summary: ECCO landfill fire remains under control as crews continue targeted suppression efforts The Calgary Fire Department (CFD) continues suppression operations at the ECCO Recycling facility landfill fire in southeast Calgary. The fire remains under control, and crews are focused on accessing, isolating and extinguishing buried burning material while maintaining environmental and public safety monitoring. Heavy equipment operators continue building and reinforcing access routes throughout the affected area to safely reach remaining hot spots and areas requiring additional soil cover. Overnight, water application was intentionally limited in some locations to allow newly constructed routes to stabilize. These routes are essential for supporting heavy equipment and maintaining access to isolated portions of the site. Excessive water can soften road surfaces, increase erosion and hinder ongoing suppression efforts. Operational crews observed some improvement in smoke conditions overnight; however, residents may continue to experience localized smoke and odours as suppression activities progress. Smoke conditions can change as crews excavate and extinguish buried hot spots and as weather conditions shift. Additional truckloads of soil and clay continue to arrive on site to support suppression efforts. Soil placement remains a critical component of landfill fire suppression, helping crews isolate burning material, reduce oxygen flow and minimize the potential for re-ignition. As operations continue, new soil is also being placed in areas where cover material has been disturbed during excavation and hot spot removal. Crews continue making progress in the southern portion of the affected area, where operations are focused on accessing, isolating and extinguishing buried hot spots. During operations near an underground utility access structure, workers reported an unusual odour. As a precaution, the Calgary Fire Department Hazardous Materials Team assessed conditions within the structure and surrounding work area. The assessment confirmed conditions were safe and operations continued as planned. Residents may continue to see smoke, odours and occasional visible flames as crews expose and extinguish buried burning material. These flare-ups are an expected part of landfill fire suppression operations and do not indicate worsening conditions. Alberta Environment and Protected Areas continue air quality monitoring in and around the affected area and surrounding communities. Monitoring equipment remains deployed near the incident to track air quality conditions and help inform public health guidance. Please visit Air Quality Health Index | Alberta.ca for more information from the province. CFD reminds residents that unauthorized drone activity near emergency operations creates significant safety risks and may interfere with response efforts. Drone operators should stay clear of the incident area and comply with all applicable Transport Canada regulations. Please visit calgary.ca/landfillfire for more information regarding the incident and links to additional resources and information. -30-

title: ECCO landfill fire update-Sept 18
summary: The Calgary Fire Department (CFD) continues suppression operations at the ECCO Recycling facility landfill fire in southeast Calgary. The fire remains under control , with activity confined to the landfill site as crews continue working toward full extinguishment. During the last operational period, crews identified several underground utility access points buried beneath landfill material. These openings are believed to be contributing to re-ignition by allowing oxygen to travel through underground pipes and culvert systems, feeding hidden hot spots below the surface. Crews are capping accessible openings to restrict airflow; however, some access points are elevated above the surrounding ground area or located in difficult-to-reach areas, requiring additional soil placement before they can be safely accessed and sealed. Fire suppression efforts remain focused on locating and extinguishing hot spots, reducing smoke impacts and preventing re-ignition. Water application is being used strategically to knock down active hot spots and support earth-moving operations. City of Calgary Water Services continues to manage contaminated runoff associated with suppression activities. Residents may observe vacuum trucks operating near the site and hear generators running as crews extract contaminated water from stormwater infrastructure and redirect it to appropriate treatment systems. CFD continues to use drone and thermal imaging technology to identify hot spots, monitor fire behaviour and support suppression planning. CFD crews are seeing unauthorized drones flying over the ECCO incident site. Residents are reminded that unauthorized drone activity near emergency operations creates significant safety risks and can interfere with response efforts. Transport Canada prohibits drone use within the perimeter of a first responder emergency operation. Breaking these rules under Transport Canada regulations can result in steep Administrative Monetary Penalties up to $3,000 for individuals. Drone operators are therefore asked to stay clear of the incident area. For the latest information, visit calgary.ca/landfillfire -30-

title: Police investigate pedestrian collision in Somerset
summary: UPDATE: Sadly, the victim in this incident has succumbed to her injuries. The investigation is ongoing. Our Traffic Section is investigating a serious, life-threatening collision involving a school bus and a pedestrian that occurred yesterday afternoon in the southwest community of Somerset. At approximately 3 p.m. on Thursday, Sept. 17, 2026, a collision involving a school bus and a pedestrian occurred near the intersection of 162 Avenue and Sixth Street S.W. The pedestrian, a woman in her 60s, was transported to hospital as a precaution with what were initially believed to be non-life-threatening injuries. However, her condition has since deteriorated, and she is now in serious, life-threatening condition. Our Traffic Section continues to investigate. At this time, it is too early to determine whether impairment, speed or distraction contributed to the collision. All possible factors remain under investigation. Anyone with information about this incident is asked to contact police by calling 403-266-1234. Tips can also be submitted anonymously to Crime Stoppers through any of the following methods: TALK: 1-800-222-8477 TYPE: www.calgarycrimestoppers.org APP: P3 Tips Case #: CA26426231

title: Calgary Fire Department provides update on ECCO landfill fire response
summary: The Calgary Fire Department (CFD) continues to lead a large-scale, multi-agency response to the ongoing landfill fire at the ECCO Recycling facility in southeast Calgary. While crews have made significant progress reducing visible flames, the fire remains active beneath the surface of the waste pile. Thermal imaging continues to identify extensive underground hot spots, and smoke conditions may change quickly as winds shift, and suppression operations continue. 24-hour operations remain focused on cooling, containing and smothering the fire. Crews are applying soil over active areas of the landfill while using targeted water application to control hot spots and limit further fire spread. Significant improvements to site access have allowed additional heavy equipment and haul trucks to accelerate containment efforts. Crews strategically position firefighting equipment during daylight hours for nighttime operations as movement of heavy and firefighting equipment overnight is reduced due to low light conditions for the safety of the crews. As a result, residents in southeast Calgary may continue to see small fires or smell smoke, particularly during overnight and early morning hours. Equipment is repositioned as quickly and safely as possible to knockdown hot spots. Smoke movement remains heavily influenced by changing weather conditions and wind direction. Environmental monitoring continues throughout the affected area. Alberta Environment and Protected Areas continue to monitor air quality, while City of Calgary Water Services and environmental contractors remain on site managing runoff and conducting water quality monitoring. To help residents access the latest information, the Calgary Fire Department has launched a dedicated landfill fire information page at calgary.ca/landfillfire . The webpage provides current incident updates including photos and video, links to resources and information, and answers to frequently asked questions. The Calgary Fire Department will continue to provide updates as significant developments occur. -30-

title: Seeking dashcam footage in serious collision investigation
summary: We are investigating a single-vehicle collision that occurred earlier this month and are asking the public for help determining the vehicle's movements before the collision. At approximately 12:05 a.m. on Saturday, Sept. 5, 2026, a blue Subaru WRX was travelling north on Deerfoot Trail, approaching an unrelated collision scene that had temporarily closed the road. The driver attempted to exit onto 17 Avenue S to avoid the closure, lost control and rolled several times. The vehicle narrowly missed first responders and road crews at the scene who were responding to the earlier collision. Two passengers were ejected. Two passengers, a 14-year-old girl and a 19-year-old woman, were transported to hospital with serious, life-altering injuries. A third passenger, a 23-year-old man, was also transported to hospital with serious injuries. The driver, a 21-year-old man, was taken into custody and transported to hospital with minor injuries. The two men and the 14-year-old girl have since been released from hospital. The 19-year-old woman remains in hospital in serious but stable condition. Speed and alcohol are believed to be factors in the collision. After speaking with witnesses, investigators believe several vehicles may have been racing before the collision. Police are asking anyone with dashcam footage from northbound Deerfoot Trail in the moments leading up to the collision to come forward. The investigation is ongoing and charges are pending. Anyone with information about this incident is asked to contact police by calling 403-266-1234. Tips can also be submitted anonymously to Crime Stoppers through any of the following methods: TALK: 1-800-222-8477 TYPE: www.calgarycrimestoppers.org APP: P3 Tips Case #: CA26405048/5646

title: Calgary Housing starts work to breathe new life into Bridgeland Place
summary: Calgary Housing is bringing new life to Bridgeland Place Tower. When completed, the highrise tower in the historic Bridgeland/Riverside neighbourhood will include 203 homes with 1-, 2-, and 3-bedrooms. Bridgeland Place will operate under Calgary Housing's mixed-income model. This means families of all sizes and a wide range of incomes will live in the completely renovated tower at 736 McDougall Court N.E. “Bridgeland Place has been home to countless Calgarians in its 52 years of operations, and we're proud to get the work underway to extend the life of the structure for decades more,” Bo Jiang, Calgary Housing interim President and CEO said. “I'm excited to see the new life this work will bring to the building and the neighbourhood.” Originally constructed in 1971, Bridgeland Place was decommissioned in 2023 due to significant concerns over aging systems like heating and water. One year later, Calgary Housing was brought on by The City of Calgary to lead redevelopment of the 17-storey building, with a nine-month interior demolition and abatement being the first step. Design and permitting processes followed, which included rearranging floorplans to include more family-friendly homes and refurbishment of amenities. “Redevelopment of Bridgeland Place is a fiscally responsible way to improve the existing housing stock we have as a city, while also minimizing impacts on the surrounding community. I'm glad to have Calgary Housing at the helm of this redevelopment,” Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas said. Redevelopment of Bridgeland Place will involve rehabilitating the exterior envelope – including replacing windows and siding – to make it more energy efficient. Crews will then focus on a thorough retrofit of the interior, which has been taken down to the cast concrete structure. Exterior work includes landscaping and family-friendly, safety-oriented environmental design. “Alberta's government is proud to invest in the renewal of Bridgeland Place, helping ensure more than 500 Calgarians have a safe and affordable place to call home. Strategic investments like this are a smart use of existing infrastructure, stretching taxpayer dollars further and delivering more homes for Albertans,” said Minister of Assisted Living and Social Services Nathan Neudorf. The retrofit focuses on improving efficiency, reducing emissions and utility costs, improving indoor air quality, and extending the lifespan of the building at a cost less than that of a similar new build. After an anticipated completion in 2028, more than 500 Calgarians will call Bridgeland Place home once again. "Calgary Housing's Bridgeland Place retrofit is one of many projects we're proud to support in Calgary. Maintaining existing housing stock is crucial to extend the life of affordable and community housing. We'll continue our work alongside our partners at all levels of government to continue to make homes like these a reality for Calgarians," said Corey Hogan, Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy and Natural Resources and Member of Parliament for Calgary Confederation, on behalf of the Honourable Gregor Robertson, Minister of Housing and Infrastructure and Minister responsible for Pacific Economic Development Canada. “Bridgeland is a wonderful place for Calgarians to call home, and the new residents at the renovated Bridgeland Place will find it to be a walkable and vibrant neighbourhood that supports a rich community life,” said Ward 9 Councillor Harrison Clark. “I look forward to welcoming you all!” Under Calgary Housing's mixed-income model, rents at the renovated Bridgeland Place will fit the incomes of the households, and the rents range from deeply affordable to near-market in a mix that meets the operating funding needs of the entire building. That mix means government funding is not required for ongoing operations, only for the construction. -30-

title: New slide to carry the Thunder Slide's legacy into the future at Village Square Leisure Centre
summary: Generations of Calgarians have climbed the tower, braved the cold walk to the top and raced through the twists and turns of the Thunder Slide. Now, after more than 30 years of memories, a new slide will carry that legacy into the future at Village Square Leisure Centre. Today, we're unveiling the design for the Thunder Slide's replacement, giving Calgarians a first look at one of the facility's most anticipated new features. The new slide will replace the Thunder Slide, which served Calgarians from 1994 to 2026, when it had reached the end of its service life. As part of the Village Square Leisure Centre repairs and upgrades project, the replacement slide has been designed to deliver a new generation of thrills while building on the experience Calgarians know and love. Unlike the current open-air corkscrew design, the new slide will be fully enclosed, helping protect it from Calgary's weather and supporting more reliable operation throughout the year. The ride will feature a dynamic path, taking riders through a series of changing twists and turns before reaching the runout below. The design also incorporates translucent sections that create changing colours and light effects throughout the experience. A vibrant gradient colour scheme featuring reds, pinks, purples, oranges and yellows will make the slide a striking new addition to the Village Square Leisure Centre pool area. “We've heard from countless Calgarians about what the Thunder Slide has meant to them over the years," said Mayor Jeromy Farkas. “The incredible turnout for the slide's final weekend showed just how much people care about places like this and that recreation facilities create memories that last a lifetime. Replacing the Thunder Slide means future generations will have the chance to create memories of their own and enjoy this beloved recreation experience for decades to come." The replacement slide forms part of The City's broader work to renew aging recreation infrastructure and respond to increasing demand for recreation opportunities across Calgary. Through GamePLAN, The City's public recreation strategy, Calgary is taking a long-term approach to investing in existing community facilities where it makes sense and planning new recreation spaces for a growing city. Work is underway on repairs and upgrades at Village Square Leisure Centre, with the facility and new slide expected to reopen near the end of 2027. Updates can be found at calgary.ca/VillageSquareRepairs Quick facts - The Thunder Slide opened in 1994 and has served generations of Calgarians. - The existing slide and support structure were more than 30 years old and reached the point where replacement was a more practical long-term solution than continued repairs. - The new slide will be fully enclosed to improve reliability and help protect it from Calgary's weather. - Village Square Leisure Centre is expected to reopen by the end of 2027. -30-

title: Fire Chief: ECCO landfill fire status improved but poses continued challenges
summary: Fire Chief Steve Dongworth updated Calgarians today regarding the historic ECCO landfill fire that began September 6, 2026. When this incident began on September 6th, firefighters immediately encountered challenging conditions, including limited site access, difficult ground conditions and fire burning deep within landfill materials. With an estimated volume of one million cubic metres, the impacted are of the fire equals about 7 or 8 CFL football fields. “As you'll be able to see in the overhead drone footage that we've provided, this is literally a mountain of garbage with deep pockets of active fire,” said Chief Dongworth. “The steep, mountainous face of this fire makes access for crews and trucks particularly challenging.” Crews will continue to work with contractors and partner agencies to fully extinguish the fire using specialized landfill fire suppression techniques. The strategic goal is to cap and smother the remaining fire with dirt. This approach follows industry best practices for control of smoke and extinguishing deep-seated landfill fires and preventing re-ignition. Additional technologies, such as carbon dioxide injection, may be required. “We are prioritizing actions that will reduce smoke impact on neighbouring communities. However, unlike a structure fire, landfill fires can burn for extended periods beneath the surface, making them difficult to locate and extinguish,” said Chief Dongworth. “Although we should be able to control smoke from the fire in the next few days, this incident could last weeks or even months until onsite fire risk is fully mitigated.” Even after fire smoke becomes better controled, Chief Dongworth advised there may be occasional instances of increased smoke and visible flame. “While these flare-ups may appear concerning, they are an expected part of the suppression process. As these flare ups occur we will suppress the flames and cover up the area to control the smoke as soon as possible. To those residents in impacted communities, we appreciate your resilience and patience.” The list of communities impacted by smoke is significant and include: East Shepard, Remington, Copperfield, New Brighton, McKenzie Towne, Quarry Park, Mahogany, McKenzie Lake, Douglasdale, Seton, Cranston, Chaparral, Lake Bonavista, Riverbend, Parkland, Legacy, Deer Run and Altadore. “Again, our immediate efforts remain focused on actions that reduce smoke impact on communities,” said Chief Dongorth. “This includes identifying hot spots, applying water where required and using soil to cap and smother remaining areas of fire.” Earlier this week, air monitoring at the province's Mobile Air Monitoring Laboratory identified one fine particulate matter concentration exceeding the Alberta ambient air quality guideline. While no other exceptions were measured, air quality can change significantly over short distances due to wind patterns, terrain, and local conditions. Therefore, monitoring results may not reflect individual exposures at all locations. Residents affected by smoke are encouraged to limit outdoor activity, keep windows and doors closed when smoke is present, and contact Health Link by dialing 811 if they have concerns about smoke-related health impacts. Residents can also check current conditions through Alberta's Air Quality Health Index: https://www.alberta.ca/air-quality-health-index The Calgary Fire Department will continue to provide updates on this incident. Thank you to Alberta Environment and Protected Areas, Calgary Police Services, Alberta Health Services, City of Calgary Waste & Recycling Services, contracted suppression specialists and neighbouring businesses for their continued support during this prolonged and complex incident. For more information about the ECCO landfill fire, including current status, FAQs and other resources, please visit: www.calgary.ca/landfillfire -30-

title: Construction progress celebrated at Symons Valley Centre Library
summary: The City of Calgary, Calgary Public Library and project partners gathered today to celebrate construction progress at Symons Valley Library, a community hub taking shape in the community of Sage Hill. Construction is underway on Phase 2 of the project, which includes a new 15,000-square-foot public library, a multi-modal street, and parking facilities, will help address a service gap in northwest Calgary and provide spaces for learning, programs and community gathering. Phase 2 also includes an outdoor community commons where people can meet, relax and play. Today's celebration recognizes significant progress made since construction began on the new library and marks an important milestone in the transformation of the seven-acre site into a vibrant community destination for northwest Calgary. Construction is expected to continue through 2028. "Symons Valley Library is an investment in the people and communities of northwest Calgary. This project will bring together important amenities, including a new library, public gathering spaces, and future community services such as a Calgary Transit Terminal, helping create a vibrant destination where residents can connect, learn and thrive,” says Mayor Jeromy Farkas. When complete, Symons Valley Library will welcome residents to a new community space designed to support the needs of one of Calgary's fastest-growing areas. Future planned phases for this site include the development of adjoining land parcels dedicated for non-market housing and mixed-use development, as well as a Calgary Transit terminal. By co-locating public amenities within a walkable, community-focused environment, the project will create opportunities for connection, recreation and learning close to home. "After years of advocacy, I'm proud to see this project moving forward and becoming a reality for our growing community. This new purpose-built library will provide a modern, welcoming space designed to meet local needs," says Jennifer Wyness, Councillor for Ward 2. "A growing city needs more libraries, and the welcoming, accessible, community spaces they provide. Calgary Public Library is a vital part of our city's core civic infrastructure, and the Symons Valley Library creates more connection, learning, and discovery, for our community,” says Sarah Meilleur, CEO, Calgary Public Library. “This new Library will expand our collections, increase access to early learning opportunities, and bring people together around new ideas and perspectives. Together, we are supporting the community of today, and building the future of our great city.” Phase 2 of the project includes: · A new 15,000-square-foot public library · Community commons green space · Underground and surface parking to support the site · A street designed to improve access throughout the site, whether you walk, drive, bike or wheel. · Supporting infrastructure to service future phases of development and community amenities About Symons Valley Library Symons Valley Library is a new public library and community space currently under development at 251 Sage Hill Boulevard N.W. Located within the larger Symons Valley Centre project, the library will serve as a welcoming hub for learning, connection and community life. Future planned phases for this site include the development of adjoining land parcels dedicated for non-market housing and mixed-use development, as well a Calgary Transit terminal. The development will primarily serve residents of Sage Hill, Kincora, Sherwood, Nolan Hill and Evanston.

title: ECCO landfill fire under control while hotspots and air quality concerns persist
summary: The Calgary Fire Department (CFD) advises that the fire at the ECCO Recycling facility in Calgary's Shepard Industrial is under control. This does not mean that the fire is out, but that the strategies, tactics and resources assigned continue to make a positive progress. Crews continue to work with contractors and partner agencies to fully extinguish the fire using specialized landfill fire suppression techniques. The affected area covers approximately 43,000 square metres, or the equivalent of eight Canadian Football League football fields or around six soccer pitches, making this a large and complex fire suppression operation. The strategic goal is to cap and smoother the remaining fire with dirt. Current estimates indicate approximately 6,000 cubic metres of soil will be required to cap and smother the fire, enough material to cover two football fields with a 60-centimetre layer of earth. This approach follows industry best practices for extinguishing deep-seated landfill fires and preventing re-ignition. Fire crews are applying water to hot spots and spot fires as required to allow heavy equipment operators to safely move dirt into necessary areas. Water runoff is being monitored and collected to keep our storm waters systems safe. Heavy application of water can negatively impact the road access and erode areas where dirt has already been spread. The incident began on September 6, when CFD crews responded to reports of smoke and fire at the private landfill. Firefighters encountered challenging conditions from the outset, including limited site access, difficult ground conditions and fire burning deep within landfill materials. These factors required a specialized, long-term suppression strategy involving heavy equipment, dedicated fire suppression contractors and continuous monitoring. Unlike a structure fire, landfill fires can burn for extended periods beneath the surface, making them difficult to locate and extinguish. As crews expose buried hot spots and burning material, periods of increased smoke and visible flame can occur. While these flare-ups may appear concerning, they are an expected part of the suppression process and indicate crews are accessing and extinguishing hidden fire. Fire activity remains confined to the landfill site and significant progress has been made over the past week. Current efforts remain focused on identifying hot spots, applying water where required and using soil and clean fill to cap and smother remaining areas of fire. Air quality monitoring continues Alberta Environment and Protected Areas continue to monitor air quality in communities surrounding the fire. Monitoring indicates that smoke-related fine particulate matter (PM2.5) remains the primary air quality concern associated with the incident. Air quality conditions can change quickly depending on weather and wind direction. Current assessments indicate the overall health risk for most Calgarians remains low. However, individuals in areas affected by smoke may experience temporary symptoms such as eye, nose or throat irritation, coughing, headaches or worsening of existing respiratory conditions. People with heart or lung conditions, older adults, young children and pregnant individuals may be more sensitive to smoke exposure. Residents affected by smoke are encouraged to limit outdoor activity, keep windows and doors closed when smoke is present, and contact Health Link by dialing 811 if they have concerns about smoke-related health impacts. Residents can also check current conditions through Alberta's Air Quality Health Index: https://www.alberta.ca/air-quality-health-index CFD thanks Alberta Environment and Protected Areas, Calgary Police Services, Alberta Health Services, City of Calgary Waste & Recycling Services, contracted suppression specialists and neighbouring businesses for their continued support during this prolonged and complex incident. -30-

title: Seeking public assistance to locate man wanted on warrants
summary: We are looking for the public's help to locate a man who is wanted on a warrant in relation to a historic sexual interference investigation. Chaz Damien Paul LAVALLEE, who is also known as Cage LALIBERTE, 37, is wanted on a warrant for sexual interference with a child under 16 years old. LAVALLEE is described as 5'10” tall, 215 pounds, with brown eyes and black hair. It is believed that LAVALLEE may be travelling through cabs or rideshares and may be in the Calgary or Airdrie areas. Tips can also be submitted anonymously to Crime Stoppers through any of the following methods: TALK: 1-800-222-8477 TYPE: www.calgarycrimestoppers.org APP: P3 Tips Case # CA26377670

title: Submissions for The City of Calgary 2027 W.O. Mitchell Book Prize now open
summary: The City of Calgary is now accepting submissions from local authors for the 2027 W.O. Mitchell Book Prize, recognizing literary works published in 2026. This prize is awarded in honour of acclaimed Calgary writer and broadcaster W.O. Mitchell (1914–1998), whose best-loved novel Who Has Seen the Wind (1947) portrayed Prairie life through the eyes of a child and sold almost a million copies in Canada. Established in 1996, the W.O. Mitchell Book Prize is coordinated through a partnership between The City of Calgary and the Writers' Guild of Alberta, which administers the award as part of the Alberta Literary Competitions. Since its creation, 30 Calgary writers have received this prestigious award. The winning author receives a $5,000 cash prize, presented at the Calgary Awards in June 2027. Submissions are being accepted until Dec. 1, 2026. Full award criteria and the entry form can be found at calgary.ca/calgaryawards . Eligibility details: Eligible books must have been published anywhere in the world between Jan. 1 and Dec. 1, 2026. The author must have lived (permanent address) in Calgary for a minimum of two years, as of Dec. 31, 2026. Eligible categories include fiction, poetry, non-fiction, children's literature, or drama. Self-published books with an ISBN are eligible. Entries are judged by an independent jury recruited by the Writers' Guild of Alberta. Shortlisted authors will have the opportunity to participate in a public reading event. The 2026 recipient of the W.O. Mitchell Book Prize was Calgary writer Marcello Di Cintio for his book Precarious: The Lives of Migrant Workers . Previous recipients include: Julie Sedivy ( Linguaphile: A Life of Language Love, 2025) Clem Martini (Cantata and The Extinction Therapist, 2024) Suzette Mayr ( The Sleeping Car Porter , 2023) Jaspreet Singh (My Mother, My Translator, 2022) A complete list of previous winners can be found at calgary.ca/calgaryawards . For more information, visit calgary.ca/calgaryawards or writersguild.ca .

title: Calgary Fire Department crews continue to work around the clock alongside industrial firefighters and heavy-equipment operators to manage the ongoing fire at a southeast Calgary landfill
summary: Crews are applying water, smothering burning material with soil and using heavy equipment to reach fires buried deep within the landfill. Heavy equipment was also used yesterday and overnight to improve road access and site conditions, allowing crews to move equipment more effectively and to reach affected areas. Landfill fires are complex and can take considerable time to fully extinguish because of the volume and variety of materials involved. We appreciate the patience of Calgarians as crews work to safely resolve this incident. The Government of Alberta continues to monitor air quality. Anyone with health-related concerns should contact Health Link at 811.

title: The Calgary Fire Department (CFD) remains on scene at the landfill fire in southeast Calgary
summary: The Calgary Fire Department (CFD) remains on scene at the landfill fire in southeast Calgary. Crews kept the fire contained overnight, and established firebreaks and ongoing suppression efforts are helping reduce fire activity. We understand Calgarians have questions about how long it is taking to extinguish the fire. Landfill fires are particularly complex and can require prolonged operational timelines due to the volume and variety of materials involved and because fire can burn deep within debris piles. Heavy equipment is needed to uncover burning material so crews can apply water before covering it with clean soil or gravel to cool the material and smother the fire. Contractors are bringing in large volumes of dirt which heavy equipment operators will use in conjunction with firefighting crews to cover and smother impacted areas of the site. This process has proved to be effective, and efforts are underway to speed up this process. This support will continue until the fire is fully extinguished. Protecting the health of Calgarians remains a priority. Please contact Health Link at 811 to speak with a registered nurse if you have questions or concerns related to smoke exposure or air quality. In a medical emergency, including severe difficulty breathing, call 9-1-1 or seek immediate medical attention. We appreciate Calgarians' patience as crews manage this complex incident.

title: Smoke from southeast landfill fire prompts health advisory
summary: The Calgary Fire Department (CFD) is advising residents in areas downwind of the ongoing fire at the ECCO Recycling landfill in southeast Calgary to take precautions as smoke conditions have worsened. Vulnerable groups such as children, youth, seniors, pregnant women, and those with asthma, heart disease or other underlying health conditions should limit outdoor activities and move indoors if they see or smell smoke. Residents with existing respiratory or cardiovascular conditions should monitor their symptoms, continue taking prescribed medications and follow the advice provided by their healthcare professionals. Alberta Environment and Protected Areas (AB-EPA) has deployed portable and mobile equipment to monitor air quality near the fire since September 9. Air monitoring data is collected and reviewed by Alberta Health Services. There were hourly average readings above Alberta's ambient air quality guidelines identified in the monitoring and residents in areas directly downwind of the fire may still experience smoke and related health effects. The greatest potential for smoke exposure remains in areas directly downwind of the fire, including Douglasdale, Quarry Park, East Shepard, McKenzie Town, New Brighton, Copperfield, and other neighbouring communities. People in areas affected by smoke may experience symptoms such as eye, nose and throat irritation, increased mucus production, coughing or headaches. Residents who experience these symptoms should reduce their exposure to smoke where possible. CFD recommends residents in affected areas: keep windows and doors closed, including attached garage doors reduce physical activity indoors and outdoors, as needed turn furnace thermostats down and furnace fans to the minimum setting. If you have a forced air system to heat or cool your home, upgrade your furnace filters to the highest efficiency filter your system can handle. avoid using ventilation systems or whole-house fans that bring outdoor air into the home keep air conditioner fresh-air intakes closed and filters clean close fireplace dampers on wood-burning fireplaces use a high-quality air filter or air cleaner/purifier, if available check on family members, neighbours and others who may be more vulnerable to smoke call Health Link at 811 if they have health concerns related to smoke exposure seek immediate medical attention for severe difficulty breathing, chest pain or other medical emergencies Residents should remain aware of changing conditions where they are located. Exposure can vary based on distance from the fire, wind direction and speed, time spent outdoors, and proximity to visible smoke or odours. Please contact Health Link at 811 to speak with a registered nurse if you have questions or concerns related to smoke exposure or air quality. In a medical emergency, including chest pain or severe difficulty breathing, call 9-1-1 or seek immediate medical attention. Fire suppression and air quality monitoring continue at the site. -30-

title: Outdoor water restrictions not anticipated during planned electrical work at water treatment plant
summary: Essential electrical work at the Bearspaw Water Treatment Plant required for the construction of a pump station for the North Calgary Water Servicing Project is planned for next week. This electrical work will temporarily reduce the amount of water that can be supplied to Calgary and regional water customers. Based on current weather forecasts and projected water demand during this period, outdoor water restrictions are not anticipated at this time. Forecasted cooler temperatures and lower seasonal water use are expected to help keep overall water demand below the available system capacity while the work is underway. Residents and businesses are encouraged to continue using water wisely, particularly outdoors, while the work is underway by continuing to follow Calgary's regular Lawn and Landscaping Watering Schedule. While restrictions are not anticipated, weather conditions will continue to be monitored, and plans may be adjusted if circumstances change. If conditions change significantly, The City will provide an update. This work is separate from the planned connection of the new Bearspaw South Feeder Main to the existing water system in mid- to late-October, which will require temporary Stage 4 water restrictions and indoor water conservation for an approximately four-week period. About the North Calgary Water Servicing Project The North Calgary Water Servicing Project includes the construction of a 22-kilometre feeder main, complemented by 10 support facilities, including pump stations and underground storage reservoirs. This project will support Calgary's growing population and strengthen system resilience by adding redundancy to our existing water distribution system.

title: Large Fire at Southeast Private Landfill UPDATE#3
summary: During the afternoon on Wednesday September 9, Calgary Fire Department (CFD) re-established fire operations at the private landfill between 24 Street SE and Barlow Trail SE. While contractor heavy equipment and fire suppression resources were beginning to arrive on scene, the fire was actively spreading and creating a large plume of smoke. Multiple fire engines and around a half kilometer of supply hose line was used to establish the water supply as firefighters deployed large volume portable master streams. Fire crews worked with heavy equipment crews to apply water to fire that was hidden beneath layers of waste and recycling materials and debris. Contractors set up several fire pumps and crews gradually cycled out Calgary Fire equipment while maintain the fire firefighting efforts throughout the evening and night. At around 4:00am, on Thursday September 10, contractor fire suppression equipment was fully operational and CFD continued to provide support. The fire remains contained to the landfill of origin however smoke continues to spread over neighbouring businesses and communities. Alberta Environment and Protected Areas (AB-EPA) have relocated some air monitoring instruments to adjust to the smoke direction of travel. Air monitoring data is collected and reviewed by Alberta Health Services. Firefighting efforts have continued throughout the day as cycles of effective knock down and ignition of fire in different areas occur as smouldering fires are under covered. A fire break was established on one end the fire which has helped reduced the spread of the fire. With each cycle of ignition, there is a corresponding increase in volume of smoke. The public can expect to observe this continued cycle as fire operation continues. Please contact 811 Health Link with any questions or concerns regarding air quality or smoke exposure. -30-

title: Declutter and discover! The city-wide curbside treasure hunt is back
summary: Ahoy treasure hunters! The City of Calgary is pleased to announce that the Curbside Treasure Hunt is set to return September 12 and 13, 2026. On those days, residents are invited to set out gently used, reusable items they no longer need on their curb for neighbours to take and enjoy. Think of it as a giant, free garage sale for the whole city! Members of the public are also welcome to explore their neighbourhoods to find unique and unwanted items that would otherwise end up in landfills. “Over the past few years, this has become one of our most beloved events, and by taking part, residents can make a big impact in helping reduce waste,” says Natalia Gonzalez, Waste Diversion Specialist. “We invite all members of the public to take part, whether decluttering their home or searching for that next great find.” New this year To help make it easier for prospective treasure hunters to see what's out there, declutterers can now add items they plan to set out for the event to a new online map simply by filling out this form . How to participate Gather: identify items in your home that you no longer need but could be valuable to someone else. Post : add your items to our online map by filling out this form . Label: mark these items with a “Free” label. Place: set the items out at the curb on September 12 and 13. Discover: residents and treasure hunters can explore different neighborhoods, picking up items they find interesting or useful. Clean up: remove left over items from the curbside by 5 p.m. on September 13. Visit calgary.ca/whatgoeswhere to find out where to recycle, donate or dispose of any remaining items. For safety reasons, please don't put out items that could be hazardous or not safe to reuse, such as: Mattresses Toilets Unsafe or recalled items Baby gear or safety equipment that may not meet current standards For more information on permitted items and other event details, visit calgary.ca/treasurehunt .

title: Large Fire at Southeast Private Landfill UPDATE#2
summary: The Calgary Fire Department has been on scene at a private landfill fire that started on Sunday September 6. After initial operations concluded and the fire was brought under control by CFD in the evening of Monday September 7th, responsibility to monitor and maintain the site was transferred back to the business. After receiving several calls regarding smoke and fire, the Calgary Fire Department dispatched crews in the morning of Tuesday September 8 to monitor fire conditions and suppression efforts by the business. Fire watch crews were assigned throughout the day and overnight. Calgary Fire Hazardous Materials crews worked with Alberta Environment teams to set up air monitoring equipment in the area and develop pre-plans if conditions did not improve. This morning at around 6:00am, fires ignited in several spots and fire began to actively spread throughout the piles resulting in heavy smoke conditions in the area. Calgary Fire has contacted contractors to bring in heavy equipment that will be able to safely move the piles of debris, and additionally, contracted dedicated fire suppression equipment and personnel. While the spread of fire is limited to the landfill, the smoke conditions and continual reignition of fires require dedicated resources to properly extinguish this type of fire. Operations are currently being set up. Calgarians do not need to call 9-1-1 unless they observe fire spreading to other structures or areas. There are dedicated fire suppression teams on site, and an active response is in progress. -30-

title: Calgary Transit launches naming rights sponsorship opportunity for Free Fare Zone
summary: Calgary Transit has launched an opportunity for organizations to explore naming rights sponsorship of the downtown Free Fare Zone. The Free Fare Zone is an important part of downtown mobility, connecting customers, visitors and workers between Downtown West/Kerby and City Hall/Bow Valley College stations. Currently, customers can travel within the zone without paying a transit fare. This initiative will help Calgary Transit assess market interest in a naming rights partnership that could generate non-fare revenue while providing a sponsor with a prominent presence along the 7 Avenue transit corridor. The sponsorship would not affect the availability of fare-free service within the Free Fare Zone. "Calgary Transit is exploring whether there is interest in a naming rights partnership that creates value for both Calgary Transit and a future sponsor," says Sharon Fleming, Director of Calgary Transit. "This process will help us better understand what opportunities may exist while continuing to support the important role the Free Fare Zone plays in downtown mobility." The initiative follows direction from Council to explore sponsorship opportunities for the Free Fare Zone as part of broader efforts to identify potential non-fare revenue sources. "I heard from residents and businesses that the downtown Free Fare Zone is a service that Calgarians want to see maintained. I advocated for continuing the search for a corporate sponsor to secure its long-term viability, offering local businesses a direct way to invest in Calgary's growth, tourism and event economy," said Ward 1 Councillor Kim Tyers. Interested organizations can learn more about the opportunity beginning Sept. 3 through mid-October 2026. The results will help determine whether a naming rights sponsorship is viable and the value it could provide for both Calgary Transit and Calgarians. Learn more about the opportunity here.

title: Three Calgary firefighters added to list of fallen at annual memorial service
summary: In its annual Fallen Firefighter Memorial ceremony, the Calgary Fire Department (CFD) added three names to Police Officers and Firefighters Tribute Plaza in front of Calgary's Municipal Building today. Since its inception in 1885, Calgary has lost 84 firefighters in the line of duty, nine during active firefighting, 71 due to illnesses related to firefighting, and four who served in World War I. Together, these firefighters gave a combined 2,331 years of service to Calgary, reflecting generations of firefighters who dedicated their lives to protecting Calgary and its residents. To honour our city's fallen firefighters, Mayor Jeromy Farkas, members of City Council, the Calgary Fire Fighters Association (Local 255) and others joined the Calgary Fire Department and families of the fallen in remembering the Calgary firefighters who have given their lives in service to their community. Each year, the names of those who have made the ultimate sacrifice are read aloud during the public ceremony. As each name is read, the Memorial Bell is sounded in their honour, followed by the Firefighters' Invocation and Bell Ceremony. Sadly, the Calgary Fire Department Honour Guard added the names of Captain Lorn Howes, Lieutenant Ronald A. Randen, and Deputy Chief Alton G. Mathers to the Walls of Memory/Lantern of Light monument in the plaza. All three firefighters died due to cancers acquired through occupational exposure. “Today, we remember not only how our fallen firefighters died, but how they lived, served and cared for this community,” said Calgary Fire Department Chief Steve Dongworth. “We gather with heavy hearts, along with profound gratitude.” Of the 84 firefighter deaths in Calgary, nine are considered “traumatic.” Four others died while fighting in World War I. The remaining 71 deaths are considered “presumptive” — the result of illnesses such as cancer that can manifest years later. Having not seen a traumatic workplace fatality since 1992, the Calgary Fire Department is committed to continued improvements and protections against firefighter illness and injury. In addition to annual cancer screening for all firefighters, Calgary Fire has made many changes to improving supports for mental health, wellness and safety, and continues to modify its practices and improve its equipment and duty gear. “Our fire service continues to adapt to new risks, such as highly toxic lithium-ion battery fires,” says Chief Dongworth. “Even residential house fires that we routinely attend produce significantly more toxic smoke and heat than in the past. Newer synthetic and petrochemical-based materials release lethal volatile organic compounds, benzene, styrene, hydrogen cyanide, and dioxins.” In response, Calgary Fire is currently investigating emerging technologies that could, for example, result in significant improvements in decontamination of firefighter duty gear, using enhanced carbon dioxide cleaning that would also increase the lifespan of front-line clothing and equipment. “The greatest way we honour those we have lost is by carrying their lessons forward and making this profession safer for the firefighters who serve today,” said Chief Dongworth. “We learn. We improve. We adapt. And we do everything we can to help future firefighters live longer, healthier lives.” As always, the memorial concluded with the laying of wreaths and a closing opportunity for reflection. For more information on the Calgary Fire Department and our fallen firefighters, please visit our website . -30-

title: Large Fire at Southeast Private Landfill UPDATE
summary: On September 6 th , 2026, the Calgary Fire Department (CFD) began fire operations at the ECCO Recycling site in southeast Calgary. Crews maintained continuous suppression operations at the site with the assistance of City of Calgary Waste and Recycling (CoCWR), contractors from CoCWR, Alberta Environment and employees of ECCO. In the evening of September 7 th , 2026, the CFD was able to bring the incident under control and release the scene back to ECCO for continued monitoring and work maintaining the site. The smoke from the site has been reduced significantly and there is no longer a plume drifting into adjacent communities. The cooperation of citizens has been pivotal during this operation and conditions should return to normal. Through the night, CFD crews will be demobilizing in the area and returning to regular service. Please be aware of fire crews working in the Shepard area this evening as conditions return to normal. -30-

title: Large Fire at Southeast Private Landfill
summary: On September 6 th , 2026, at approximately 6:00 PM the Calgary Fire Department received calls for smoke and flames sighted near Barlow Trail and Shepard Road SE. On arrival at the site, crews found a large fire on the east side of the “ECCO Recycling” private landfill. Access to the landfill was extremely limited due to poor roads in the site, wet conditions and general lack of access. The initial arriving fire crews proceeded to another business site east of the landfill and set up defensive operations to attempt holding the fire to the area of origin. This operation continues today and is being supported by landfill staff. The City of Calgary Waste and Recycling Services is also providing equipment and expertise to the site to bring the fire under control and eventually extinguish the fire. Plumes of smoke from the site are rising and drifting to the southeast. The Calgary Fire Department Hazardous Materials team is sampling the air and modeling the path of the smoke being emitted. The smoke will likely cause some irritation if breathed in and people in the communities of Douglasdale, Quarry Park, East Shepard, McKenzie Town, New Brighton and Copperfield should keep windows closed and remain indoors when possible until the fire is out. Should you smell smoke in your area of business or residence, keep windows closed and stay indoors if possible. The Calgary Fire Department will continue to contain the situation and work with Alberta Environment to ensure that the released smoke is continually monitored. This will likely be a long duration incident, and updates will be added when available. -30-

title: Traffic Safety Team wraps up Operation Silent Night, shifts focus to school zone safety
summary: The City of Calgary's Traffic Safety Team has concluded Operation Silent Night, an enforcement and education initiative focused on excessive vehicle noise and safe driving along 17 Avenue S.W. The operation resulted in over 200 enforcement actions and increased awareness of traffic safety and vehicle noise regulations. Excessive noise is defined as any noise that is emitted or produced that is beyond the regular operation of the motor vehicle. Under the Traffic Bylaw, excessive noise refers to a motor vehicle that is capable of emitting any sound exceeding 92 dB(A) while the engine is at idle or emitting any sound exceeding 96 dB(A) while the engine is at any speed greater than idle. Throughout the operation, conducted in partnership with the Calgary Police Service (CPS), peace officers issued 240 tickets including 41 noise-related violations, and provided 40 warnings to drivers. The initiative targeted ongoing concerns from residents, businesses and City Council about excessive vehicle noise and safety along the corridor. “Operation Silent Night demonstrated the value of combining officer presence, education, and enforcement to address issues that matter to Calgarians,” said Brad Johnson, Inspector and head of the Traffic Safety Team. “The results show that when drivers understand the rules and see a visible enforcement presence, we can make a meaningful difference in reducing excessive vehicle noise and improving the quality of life for residents and businesses.” The enforcement initiative focused on overall driver behaviour down along 17 Ave. Some of the violations that officers came across were noisy exhaust systems, excessive engine revving, squealing tires and other unnecessary vehicle noise along with speeding, illegal U-turns, and no registration / or insurance. "Driver behaviour can disrupt communities and impact livability," said Johnson. "Drivers are responsible for their behaviour and the noise generated by their vehicles at all times." Team shifts focus to playground zone safety With the completion of Operation Silent Night, the Traffic Safety Team has resumed playground zone enforcement as students return to classrooms across Calgary. Officers will be rotating through communities across the city, beginning in northwest Calgary, with a focus on speeding and improving safety around schools and playgrounds. Playground zones are in effect daily from 7:30 a.m. to 9 p.m., year-round. Drivers must obey the posted speed limit and remain alert for children, pedestrians and other vulnerable road users. Speeding fines in playground zones are based on how far a driver exceeds the posted speed limit. Drivers travelling 15 km/h over the limit can face a fine of $249, while those travelling 30 km/h over the limit can face fines of $543, not including victim surcharges and demerit points. “Back-to-school season is one of the busiest times of year around schools and playgrounds,” said Johnson. “Slowing down in playground zones is one of the simplest and most effective ways drivers can help keep children safe. A few extra seconds behind the wheel can prevent a serious collision and make our communities safer for everyone.” The City reminds motorists to reduce their speed, eliminate distractions and watch for children who may enter roadways unexpectedly. About the Traffic Safety Team The Traffic Safety Team was established by City Council in November 2023 with $1.69 million in funding to address growing concerns about road safety and vehicle noise. The team includes eight peace officers, two sergeants and one inspector, and works closely with CPS and other partners to support coordinated, city-wide traffic safety enforcement. Residents wishing to submit a complaint about traffic issues can do so by visiting the Calgary Police Service Traffic Reporting page and selecting the Traffic Service Request (TSR) form. -30- .

title: Stephen Stanley named Chair of Calgary's Water Utility Oversight Board
summary: Stephen Stanley has been named the inaugural Chair of the Water Utility Oversight Board (WUOB), a new independent body being formed to strengthen oversight of Calgary's water utility. The appointment marks an important step in implementing recommendations from the Bearspaw Independent Review Panel, which identified the need for independent oversight and the Chair position as a critical leadership role. Stanley's appointment follows a competitive recruitment and selection process created specifically for selecting the WUOB Chair. Stanley is a retired utility executive with more than 25 years of experience at EPCOR Utilities Inc., including 11 years as Senior Vice President of EPCOR Water Canada, where he was responsible for providing water and wastewater services to more than 85 communities, including over 1.5 million people in the Edmonton region. He also served on the boards of the Canadian Water Network and Global Water Futures Observatories. Most recently, Stanley sat on the Bearspaw Feeder Main Independent Review Panel and Advisory Group, where he gained direct insight into Calgary's water utility and the challenges facing the system. "Stephen has an impressive background in utility operations, governance and risk management gained over a long career in the sector," said Councillor Rob Ward, Chair of the WUOB Chair Selection Committee. "The Selection Committee was looking for a candidate with proven leadership, deep utility expertise and the ability to help establish this board from the ground up. Stephen's experience makes him exceptionally well-suited for that role." As Chair, his immediate priorities will be recruiting additional board members and developing the WUOB's initial work plan. The full WUOB is expected to be in place by the end of 2026. “Reliable water service depends on informed, risk-based decision making and a focus on long-term system performance," said Stanley. "I look forward to helping establish the Board and working with future members, Council and Administration to help shape the future of Calgary's water utility.” Background The establishment of the Water Utility Oversight Board (WUOB) was directed by Council in response to recommendations from the Independent Review Panel, following the Bearspaw Feeder Main failures. The WUOB will provide Council with independent oversight, expertise and advice on utility performance, finances, long-term planning, risk management and compliance with regulations and policies. The WUOB will consist of one Chair and four members and will serve as an independent committee of Council. The WUOB's role is advisory and will not make operational decisions. Appointments to the WUOB are made by Council through the Nominations Committee. For the inaugural Chair position, Council approved a dedicated recruitment and selection process that included support from an independent search firm and a Council-appointed Selection Committee. Stephen Stanley, Ph.D, P.Eng Stephen Stanley is a retired executive with over 25 years of experience at EPCOR Utilities Inc. This included roles such as Senior Vice President Commercial Service where he was responsible for EPCOR's business development activities as well as EPCOR's operations of water, natural gas and electricity utilities in Ontario. He also spent 11 years as the Senior Vice President of EPCOR Water Canada, responsible for providing water and wastewater treatment services to more than 85 communities, including over 1.5 million people in the Edmonton region. Stephen was a member of the Independent Review Panel for the City of Calgary Water Utility, member of the Board for the Canadian Water Network and Chair of the Board for Global Water Futures Observatories. Stephen holds a B.Sc. in Civil Engineering, a M.Sc. in Water Resources Engineering, and a Ph.D. in Environmental Engineering, all from the University of Alberta. He is also a graduate of the Executive Program at Queen's University. Prior to joining EPCOR, Stephen was a Professor in the Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering at the University of Alberta.

title: Building trust through action: How Council's Strategic Priorities will shape Calgary's next chapter
summary: CALGARY – As Calgary prepares for the 2027–2030 budget and continues to grow toward a city of two million residents, the choices made today will help shape Calgary's next chapter. In a new episode of Calgary Conversations , Mayor Jeromy Farkas joins host Jose Rodriguez for a timely conversation about how Council's Priorities will shape the city's next four years, and what it takes to move from aspirations to measurable action. From trust, transparency and accountability to affordability, public safety and essential infrastructure, the conversation explores how Council's Strategic Priorities will help guide decisions, investments and trade-offs as The City develops its 2027–2030 business plans and budgets. “Trust isn't something government gets to declare; it's something we earn,” said Mayor Jeromy Farkas. “Calgarians want to know their concerns are being heard, their tax dollars are being spent wisely and decisions are being made responsibly. These priorities help us stay focused on what matters most and, ultimately, Calgarians should be able to see and feel the results.” Council established six priorities to provide focus and direction for the next four years: Reliable & Sustainable Infrastructure Safe City Functional Transportation Network Community Livability & Well-being Balanced Growth & Evolving Neighbourhoods Trusted & Collaborative Government Using Trusted & Collaborative Government as a lens, the episode explores how all six priorities connect to the services and issues Calgarians experience every day. Mayor Farkas reflects on lessons from the Bearspaw South Feeder Main break and how the experience reinforced the importance of reliable infrastructure, planning for the future and communicating openly with Calgarians. The conversation also looks ahead to the 2027–2030 budget and how Council will balance affordability with the investments needed to support a growing city. “Budgets are ultimately about choices. We can't do everything at once,” said Mayor Farkas. “Council's priorities give us a framework for those decisions and help us focus investments where they can have the greatest impact for Calgarians.” The episode also explores how Calgarians will know whether progress is being made. Council's Strategic Priorities will help guide The City's business plans, budgets and decision-making over the next four years, with progress measured through reporting, public dashboards and performance measures. For Mayor Farkas, accountability means being clear about what success looks like, showing progress and being open about where more work is needed. “The measure of success isn't the plan itself; it's what gets delivered,” said Farkas. “People shouldn't have to take our word for it. They should be able to see and feel the results.” As Calgary grows, public input will continue to help inform the choices ahead and how The City balances service expectations, infrastructure needs, affordability and long-term growth. Join the conversation. Watch or listen to Episode 23: Building trust through action: how Council's Priorities will shape Calgary's next chapter at Calgary.ca/CalgaryConversations , YouTube or Spotify. Learn more about Council's Priorities on calgary.ca . - 30 -

title: Calgary parks earn international recognition for a second year
summary: Reader Rock Garden and Confederation Park have once again been recognized with a prestigious Green Flag Award, marking the second consecutive year both parks have received the international designation. The Green Flag Award is one of the world's most respected benchmarks for parks and green spaces, celebrating excellence in management, maintenance and visitor experience. “Calgary's parks are some of the spaces that makes our city so special,” said Mayor Farkas. “This international recognition is something all Calgarians can be proud of. For Reader Rock Garden and Confederation Park to earn the Green Flag Award for a second year in a row speaks to the incredible work of our City staff, volunteers and community partners who care for these spaces every day. As the first parks in Canada to receive this recognition, they're also showing the world the standard Calgary sets for our amazing parks and open spaces.” Following a rigorous evaluation process, the two Calgary parks successfully retained their Green Flag status, reinforcing Calgary's reputation for providing exceptional public spaces. “ It's fantastic to see the parks team in Calgary being recognised with two Green Flag Awards for another consecutive year. Achieving and retaining the international certification shows they are committed to providing top quality parks and green spaces for their communities,” said Carl McClean, International Development Manager for the Green Flag Award. “Congratulations to everyone involved.” Receiving this award highlights The City's ongoing commitment to creating welcoming, high-quality parks for residents and visitors alike. " Our staff, partners and volunteers are passionate about these park spaces and it shows,” said Jeffrey Martin, Zone Superintendent, Parks & Open Spaces. "This recognition demonstrates our commitment to ensuring Calgary's parks continue to be vibrant, accessible and enjoyable places for people to gather, explore and connect." About the Green Flag Award Originating in 1996, the Green Flag Award has recognized over 2,000 parks and green spaces in over 15 countries around the world, rewarding well managed parks and green spaces and setting the benchmark standard for the management of recreational outdoor spaces across the United Kingdom and around the world. Parks are judged across a broad spectrum of criteria with a purpose: To ensure that everybody has access to quality green and other open spaces, irrespective of where they live. To ensure that these spaces are appropriately managed and meet the needs of the communities that they serve. To establish standards of good management. To promote and share good practice amongst the green space sector. To recognise and reward the hard work of managers, staff and volunteers. About our winning parks Reader Rock Garden Historic Park is one of the city's most unique cultural landscapes hosting thousands of different plant species and located in Calgary's established community of Erlton. First created in 1913, its restoration has earned it an official designation as both a provincial and national historic resource. Confederation Park was created in 1967 to mark the centennial of Canadian Confederation. This crescent shaped park of more than 160 hectares was once known as "the North Hill Coulee" and includes a wetland section and home to a host of aquatic wildlife and plant species.

title: Calgary Culture Days returns with a month of arts, culture and community
summary: This September, Calgary Culture Days returns for its 12th year, bringing together artists, organizations and communities for a month-long celebration of arts and culture. Through a diverse range of events, many of which are free, the locally driven initiative showcases the creativity and cultural experiences that shape Calgary. From festivals to film screenings, art exhibitions to dance performances and live music to workshops, there are new opportunities every week to connect, learn and experience Calgary through arts and culture. "One of the things that makes Calgary Culture Days so special is the element of serendipity," said Olivia Rocskar, Arts & Cultural Development Coordinator with The City of Calgary. "You might come across an event and leave with a new perspective, a new connection or a deeper appreciation for a community, culture or art form. Those moments of curiosity and connection stay with people long after the event is over." Calgary Culture Days also highlights the important role arts and culture play in Calgary's growth and quality of life. "Arts and culture are no longer a nice-to-have. They're a need to have," said Mayor Jeromy Farkas. "They connect us to our history, help tell the stories of Indigenous Peoples and the many communities that have shaped Calgary, and reflect who we are today. They are also essential social, civic and economic infrastructure. Arts and culture create connection, foster belonging and help make Calgary the best place to make a life." Helping share the spirit of the celebration are this year's Calgary Culture Days Cultural Ambassadors. Representing different corners of Calgary's arts and culture sector, ambassadors lend their voices to the celebration while highlighting the value of arts and culture in building a vibrant city. This year's ambassadors include Mayor Jeromy Farkas; Evelyne Kemajou, Executive Director of Portail de l'Immigrant Association and organizer of Franco Festival Calgary; Marc Stevens, President and CEO of the Calgary Philharmonic Orchestra; and Kristy North Peigan, member of the Piikani First Nation and artist and designer. “People may move to Calgary for a job, but they stay because of the curiosity, creativity, connections and community they discover through arts and culture,” said Marc Stevens. “That can take many forms, from a busker on the street or the wonderful murals across the city, to seeing your favourite artist in concert, going to the theatre or taking a dance lesson. There are countless ways to engage with the arts, and that's what helps turn a city into a place people want to call home." For the second year, The City of Calgary is supporting community-led programming through the Calgary Culture Days Microgrant, aimed at activating Calgary's greater downtown with local arts and cultural programming during September. This year, funding was awarded to 20 recipients to help bring new and expanded arts and culture experiences to life throughout September. Calgary Culture Days takes place Sept. 1-30. Explore events happening across Calgary at calgary.ca/CultureDays . #YYCCultureDays -30-

title: Calgary Transit introduces new 500-series express routes
summary: Calgarians have a new way to travel across the city with the launch of Calgary Transit's new 500-series express routes, a modernized approach to express service designed to provide faster connections, better integration with the transit network and more value for customers. The first route in the series, Route 503 Symons Valley Express, begins service today, connecting Sage Hill and surrounding communities with downtown through a direct, limited-stop service. Calgary Transit is also renaming Route 300 Airport/City Centre to Route 500 Airport Express, creating the foundation for a new family of express routes that will expand over time. "Calgary is growing, and the way people travel is changing," says Sharon Fleming, Director of Calgary Transit. "The new 500-series gives customers the fast, direct service they value while better connecting them to the rest of our transit network. It is a smarter, more flexible approach that helps us serve more people, more efficiently." The 500-series is part of Calgary Transit's ongoing work to build a more connected, reliable network in line with RouteAhead, Calgary Transit's 30-year strategic plan. Unlike traditional express routes, which primarily operated during peak periods and in one direction, the new 500-series model provides two-way service throughout the day, allowing customers to travel to a wider range of destinations when it works for them. The new express network has been designed to: Provide fast, direct travel with limited stops Offer more consistent service throughout the day Better connect customers to transit hubs and local routes Support travel to a wider variety of destinations across Calgary Make more effective use of available transit resources The launch of Route 503 also supports broader improvements made through Calgary Transit's North Central Transit Service Review. The route creates a direct connection between Sage Hill and downtown while complementing existing services such as MAX Green and local community routes. It also helps maximize previous investments in transit infrastructure along key corridors including Centre Street North. The 500-series is part of Calgary Transit's strategy to ensure investments made by Council deliver the greatest benefit for customers. "This is about making the best use of every transit dollar," says Fleming. "The 500-series allows us to deliver the speed and convenience customers want while supporting a network that is more reliable, connected and sustainable for the future." The performance of Route 503 will help inform future 500-series routes planned for other areas of Calgary as the city continues to grow and travel patterns evolve. For route information, schedules and trip planning tools, visit calgarytransit.com.

title: Investing in new community spaces that bring people together
summary: Infrastructure projects in 2026 are creating new park, sport and library spaces for Calgarians to enjoy Life is about more than just work and sleep. Having places people can go to relax, socialize, learn and play is a big part of what makes a good city great. As Calgary grows, we're creating more places where people can connect with community, nature, recreation and learning. "Calgary is growing quickly, and we're investing in both new and improved spaces that respond to that growth," says Ryan Atkinson, Director of Public Spaces Delivery with The City. "Whether it's a park, library, athletic field or community hub, these investments mean more ways for people to connect with each other and their communities." More places to play and stay active Calgarians will soon have more opportunities to get active, join local sports leagues and enjoy recreation close to home. This fall, we're finishing construction on Rocky Ridge Athletic Park with two new outdoor artificial turf fields. Artificial turf allows the fields to be available earlier and later in the season, while new lighting helps people play later into the evening. Future plans for the site include an indoor fieldhouse. We're also beginning work on the Northeast Athletic Complex : a new sport space which will boast four outdoor multisport fields, an indoor fieldhouse, and Calgary's first cricket pitch designed to host competition at the local, regional and national level. Looking forward, GamePLAN has identified more investments in new and renewed recreation infrastructure to help meet Calgary's long-term recreation needs. Funding for these investments will be considered as part of Council's budget process this fall. We're building new places to learn and connect. Libraries and community hubs help bring people together. They create welcoming spaces where residents can learn, access services, spend time with neighbours and build community. Construction began this year on the Symons Valley Centre Library , a new 15,000 square foot facility including parking and a green space. The new library is part of a larger community hub that will eventually include a transit terminal, housing and shops, bringing a growing community together. Construction also continues on the Belmont Fieldhouse and Library : a new community hub featuring a 10,000 square foot public library paired with fieldhouse for year-round sport. When it opens in 2027, it will be a focal point for community activity, where Calgarians in the southwest can meet, read a book, train and play all year round. Future plans include a new recreation facility that will add even more ways for residents to gather and connect. More places to relax and enjoy nature Parks give people room to breathe, explore and spend time outdoors. We're upgrading Munro Park with new features like a natural play zone, community plaza, a 3-on-3 basketball court, and rainwater-powered gardens that clean water and create habitats for birds, bugs and butterflies. Finally, we've moved the Centennial Grove public art and the Richardson Ground Squirrel sculptures from the old Olympic Plaza here, where they can continue to be enjoyed. The upgraded park will reopen in late Fall 2026. We're also creating a new feature section – the Chinese Market Gardens – to the Inglewood Bird Sanctuary that honours the Chinese families who once farmed the land and helped feed Calgary's growing population. New pathways, native plants and interpretive features will help visitors connect with local history while enjoying one of Calgary's most loved natural spaces. When complete, this will be a new and beautiful area for people to relax, birdwatch and experience nature.

title: Calgary Fire Responds to Riverbend Garage Fire
summary: At around 8:40am fire crews responded to the 100 block of Riverview Close SE for a structure fire. On approach, crews observed a large column of dark smoke and declared a working fire. Crews arrived at a two-story residential home with a front attached garage with heavy smoke and visible flames coming from the garage. Firefighters stretched multiple hose lines and began knocking down the fire from the driveway while other firefighters completed searches of the home and confirmed there was no one inside. The occupants had all self-exited and stated that they were alerted by a neighbour/passerby of the fire. There were no injuries reported. A vehicle was inside the garage at the time and also on fire. Crews checked for extension into the roof of the garage and the majority of the fire damage was confined to the garage. A fan was set up to ventilate the rest of the home from smoke. Fire investigators attended the scene and have started their investigation into the origin and cause of the fire. Emergency Health Services Alberta, Calgary Police Services, ATCO Gas and Enmax all attended the scene. Utilities to the home were isolated and a fire watch crew remains on scene. The cause of the fire is still under investigation; however, the Calgary Fire Department would like to remind all Calgarians on some important safety tips around garages: Avoid clutter and storage of household waste such as old paints and aerosol cans. Routinely clean up and safely dispose of these items at an appropriate City of Calgary Facility in Household Hazardous Waste (HHW) Program . Practice safe charging of any electrical batteries Never store propane inside Please visit www.calgary.ca/fire for more fire safety and prevention information -30-

title: Stage A Microtunneling Complete as Bearspaw South Feeder Main Advances on Schedule
