summary: The Bearspaw South Feeder Main Replacement Project continues to advance on schedule, and Stage A microtunneling and installation of the concrete carrier pipe is now complete. "The completion of Stage A microtunneling is a significant step forward for the project," said Darren Finney, Manager, Major Projects. "This complex work involved tunneling beneath major infrastructure, minimizing impacts on the community. With the concrete carrier pipe now in place, we will continue installing the new steel feeder main, preparing for the critical system connection work planned for the Fall." Stage A construction update Construction on Stage A of the new Bearspaw South Feeder Main began in January using microtunnelling. This method allows the new feeder main to be installed beneath existing infrastructure with minimal surface disruption. First, a concrete carrier pipe is installed underground and then the new steel feeder main is placed inside it. Stage A construction has now completed approximately 3.7 kilometres of microtunnelling and the full installation of the concrete carrier pipe between the Shaganappi Pump Station and 73 Street N.W. Installation of the new steel feeder main remains on schedule, with more than two kilometres of pipe now installed inside the carrier pipe. Stage B construction update Stage B open-cut construction along 34 Avenue N.W. in Bowness began in June and remains on schedule. More than 1 km of the new steel feeder main has now been installed, with 40% of Stage B feeder main installation now complete. Construction is currently active on three blocks, and four blocks where feeder main installation has been completed have reopened to traffic. Two additional blocks are expected to reopen next week. Construction is being completed in sections, and roadways, sidewalks and property access are being restored as work advances. Looking ahead In mid-October the Bearspaw South Feeder Main will need to be shut down to connect the new feeder main to the existing water system. Work on improving Calgary's drinking water system will begin in September with three phases. Work at the Shaganappi pump station to connect it to the new feeder main is estimated to begin in September. In addition, unrelated work for the new North Calgary Water Servicing feeder main will mean the Bearspaw Water Treatment Plant will need to be temporarily shut down in mid-September. There may be a need for temporary outdoor water restrictions, but it will depend on the weather and water demand at that time. Teams are continuing to assess conditions and will make a final decision on restrictions closer to the start of work. Pipe tie-in connections are estimated to begin in mid-October at various locations along the new feeder main pipe and include open-cut construction similar to ongoing Stage B construction. Stage 4 outdoor water restrictions and indoor water conservation will be required during this time. Feeder main commissioning is estimated to begin in mid-November. This will include disinfecting the pipe, filling it with water and taking the existing feeder main out of service. No restrictions are anticipated during this time. These estimated date ranges are subject to change based on construction timelines and project logistics. Parkdale Boulevard Repairs While the feeder main is shut down, The City will complete six additional repairs on the feeder main between the Shaganappi Pump Station and the Memorial Pump Station along Parkdale Boulevard and Memorial Drive N.W. Recent condition assessments identified six locations on the 1500 mm section of the Bearspaw South Feeder main that require proactive repairs. While the 1500 mm and the 1950 mm pipe, which is currently being replaced, are both part of the same feeder main, they are separate sections with different condition profiles. Assessments of the 1500 mm section show it remains in good overall condition and does not require replacement. Instead, targeted repairs at specific locations will help maintain the pipe's long-term reliability. Completing this work while the feeder main is already out of service for planned connection work is the most efficient approach and helps reduce future risk and disruption. The repairs will involve 24/7 construction, excavating six locations, removing sections of pipe and replacing them with new steel segments. Community support We continue to work directly with residents, businesses and property owners affected by construction and encourage anyone with questions or concerns to reach out. Community members can visit the project's Community Resource Centre at the Bowness Community Association. Office hours are Monday and Wednesday: 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., Tuesday and Thursday: 10 a.m. to 7 p.m. The Bearspaw South Feeder Main Construction Liaisons are available at the Community Resource Centre on Wednesdays from 10 a.m. to 12 p.m. For project information and construction updates, visit calgary.ca/bearspawfeedermain

title: City acknowledges community tributes honouring Parker Wells
summary: Our thoughts remain with the family and all those impacted by the tragic death of Parker Wells. The City of Calgary recognizes the many ways community members continue to honour and remember Parker. The tributes that have been created in the days and weeks since Parker's passing reflect the care, compassion and sense of community that many have felt in response to this tragedy. "We understand the desire to remember Parker and the importance these tributes hold for many people," said Doug Morgan, Chief Operating Officer – City Services. "We recognize that everyone grieves differently and that these memorials were created with heartfelt intentions." The City manages memorials in accordance with its internal processes and any applicable bylaws. Temporary memorial items such as flowers, cards and stuffed animals left in parks are typically maintained for a short period before being respectfully removed and, where appropriate, offered to the family. Because these items are exposed to weather and environmental conditions, they can deteriorate over time and create maintenance and safety concerns. Other tributes, if defined as graffiti under The City's bylaws, are removed in accordance with established processes. Although Administration understands the intent behind the Parker tributes, they have been removed in accordance with established operating practices. Their removal does not diminish the significance of his memory or the community's desire to honour him. As stewards of public spaces across Calgary, The City has a responsibility to approach these situations consistently and fairly, while ensuring that everyone affected by this tragedy is treated with compassion, dignity and respect. Prior to the removal, those most directly affected were notified and expressed no concerns. While temporary memorials can provide an important outlet for community grief in the immediate aftermath of a loss, permanent memorials offer an enduring way to honour and remember someone over time. For community members interested in exploring a lasting tribute to Parker, Administration can provide guidance on the appropriate processes and requirements for permanent memorials. "While the methods used to honour Parker may vary, the compassion and care behind them are clear," said Morgan. "We will continue to approach this situation with respect for those grieving while applying our responsibilities fairly and consistently." The grief associated with Parker's death continues to be felt across our community. We recognize that reminders of this tragedy may affect people in different ways and encourage anyone who is experiencing emotional distress to seek support. The Calgary Distress Centre provides confidential 24-hour support by phone or text at 403-266-HELP ( 403-266-4357 ). - 30 -

title: New bus screens deliver information where and when customers need it
summary: Calgary Transit is making it easier for customers to navigate their trips on the road, with new onboard display screens on buses and community shuttles. Passengers can view real-time route detail, route number, requested stops, upcoming stops, and estimated arrival times, as well as service announcements. “Customers want accurate, consistent and timely information to help them make decisions during their trip,” said Dennis Uvbiama, Manager, Service Vehicles, Calgary Transit. “They also want to know about service changes or disruptions that may affect their journey. These new screens deliver useful information to customers where and when they need it.” As part of a pilot project, Calgary Transit has installed new 21- or 29-inch screens on 100 service vehicles. Starting in October 2026, we plan to roll out passenger screens broadly across our 1,000-plus fixed route bus and shuttle fleet, with installation expected to be completed by early 2027. This enhancement is possible because we've modernized the CAD/AVL/APIS (Computer-Aided Dispatch/Automatic Vehicle Location/Advanced Passenger Information) system we use to share real-time vehicle tracking and manage our bus fleet operations. The system integrates dispatching, safety, emergency response, and communication with our Transit Control Centre, helping improve service reliability and trim passenger waiting times. The upgraded system has also improved bus tracking accuracy in all our customer tools, including Transit , our trip planning app, trip planner on calgarytransit.com, and our older phone-based Teleride and Teletext services. New CAD/AVL/APIS system features for operators include simplified employee login, turn-by-turn navigation, detailed information about incidents and up-to-date construction detours, and live videos in case of emergencies.

title: Safer routes help students start school year with confidence
summary: With students heading back to classes and school loading zones about to get busier, The City of Calgary has completed safety upgrades at 50 schools in 2026 across the city to help make daily commutes safer for children and families. The upgrades include new pedestrian crossings, curb extensions, speed cushions and other traffic-calming measures designed to slow vehicles, improve visibility and reduce risk in areas where students are walking, wheeling and crossing the street. “These improvements are about creating safer, more comfortable routes for students and their families,” said Traffic Engineer Surendra Mishra. “Whether children are walking to school, riding a bike or arriving with their parents, every improvement helps reduce risk and increases awareness for everyone using the road.” The work includes proven safety improvement measures such as curb extensions and Rectangular Rapid Flashing Beacons (RRFB) at schools across Calgary. Curb extensions shorten crossing distances and make pedestrians more visible to approaching drivers. Studies have shown that curb extensions help to reduce collisions by 30-45 per cent. RRFBs improve drivers' yielding compliance to pedestrians resulting in 30-40 per cent collision reduction. When these treatments are combined, safety at an intersection improves dramatically, resulting in 70-80 per cent collision reduction. In addition to pedestrian-focused improvements, traffic-calming measures have been added near dozens of schools. New speed cushions and speed humps were installed at 17 schools in 2026 to help slow traffic in playground zones and residential areas, encouraging safer driving behaviour where children are most likely to be present. Results have indicated that speed cushions result in an average of 7 km/h speed reduction on a 50 km/h roadway. This work supports Vision Zero and reflects The City's continued partnership with the Calgary Police Service to make streets safer and save lives. Together, education, enforcement and street improvements help reduce vehicle speeds, increase driver awareness and create a more predictable environment for everyone. “With more traffic on the roads this time of year, there is an increase in risk especially to young pedestrians, cyclists, and other vulnerable road users,” said Calgary Police Service Insp. Robbie Patterson. “Drivers need to be especially vigilant around schools and playground zones. Not only does that mean slowing down, but it also means paying attention to the task at hand and avoiding all distractions including phones or anything else that could take your eyes of the road.” Parking behaviour is also a key part of playground zone safety. Through the School Patrol Program, Parking Safety and Compliance officers support safer drop-off and pick-up times by educating drivers, encouraging voluntary compliance and addressing unsafe parking behaviours that can reduce visibility or create risk for children and other road users. “Playground zones are busiest when families are under pressure and that is when safe parking choices matter most,” said Todd Sullivan, Coordinator, Parking Safety and Compliance, Mobility, The City of Calgary. “Through our School Patrol program, our officers are there to educate drivers, answer questions and reinforce the behaviours that keep children visible, including keeping crosswalks, corners, bus zones and no-stopping areas clear. Education comes first, but when unsafe parking puts people at risk, enforcement is one of the ways we help protect students and keep school zones safer for everyone.” As the school year begins, drivers are reminded to slow down, stay alert and watch for children near schools, playgrounds and residential streets. Parents and caregivers can also help by reviewing safe travel routes with their children and allowing extra time for trips during the busy first weeks of school. "Back to school means our streets are busier, with more children walking, wheeling and crossing roads every day,” said Jacquelyn Oriold, Safety Education Programs Manager. “The City has made significant investments to improve safety around schools, but infrastructure is only part of the solution. The simple choices we make behind the wheel, such as slowing down, staying focused, parking safely and keeping crossings clear, make a real difference. Kids deserve to get to and from school safely, and their lives are in your hands.”

title: The City of Calgary launches Beyond the Badge program for Grade 9 students
summary: The City of Calgary is launching Beyond the Badge, a new educational program that brings Community Peace Officers into Grade 9 classrooms to help students explore citizenship, community safety and career opportunities in public service. The free program combines curriculum-connected lessons with real-world learning experiences designed to build confidence, teamwork and civic responsibility. Through interactive lessons in Social Studies, English and Health, students will engage in discussions and activities that connect classroom learning to real community issues. The program helps students better understand the role Community Peace Officers play in supporting safe communities while encouraging students to consider how they can contribute positively to the city around them. Teachers participating in the program receive a ready-to-use manual developed by certified educators and Community Peace Officers. The manual includes lesson plans, classroom activities and supporting resources to help teachers deliver the program and prepare students for a culminating classroom visit and mock interview experience with Community Peace Officers. “Beyond the Badge gives students a unique opportunity to connect what they are learning in the classroom to the communities they live in every day,” said Lucy Roy, Community Liaison Officer with Community Standards. “By exploring citizenship, civic responsibility and community safety in an engaging way, students gain a deeper understanding of how they can make a positive contribution to their communities.” The program was designed to help students build practical skills, collaborate with their peers and develop an understanding of local government and community services. By participating in the program, students learn about citizenship, rights and responsibilities, teamwork and career pathways in public service. “We want students to see that community safety is a shared responsibility and that everyone has a role to play in creating strong, vibrant neighbourhoods,” said Rajdeep Gill, Community Liaison Officer with Community Standards. “Beyond the Badge provides hands-on learning experiences that encourage students to think critically, work together and explore future career possibilities.” Beyond the Badge is offered free of charge to Grade 9 classrooms and supports outcomes related to citizenship, life learning choices and collaborative learning. The program helps students understand local bylaws, explore community partnerships and develop skills that support future educational and career transitions. Teachers can access program resources and learn more about participation through the Beyond the Badge webpage. Teachers will have access to the teacher manual online, allowing them to review lesson plans and program materials before booking the culminating officer visit. -30-

title: The City is enhancing safety at 15 Storm Ponds Across Calgary
summary: In an ongoing commitment to improving safety around storm ponds, The City of Calgary will be installing additional safety measures at 15 city storm ponds this year beginning in mid-August. Th rough a review of ponds across The City, the se locations were identified as the highest priority for safety enhancements. Storm ponds are part of The City of Calgary's stormwater infrastructure and are in many communities across the city. They are marked by caution signs following the perimeter of the pond, reminding people that going into or onto storm ponds is strictly prohibited. Safety enhancements will include replacing old caution signage with new signage, installing new interpretive signage to increase awareness of risks, and increasing thorny and dense vegetation to create a barrier to the storm pond. Permanent partial fencing and temporary seasonal fencing will also aid in creating a physical barrier to public access. Storm ponds have been assessed to determine what safety measures will be applied at each pond. Ongoing field assessments will continue to identify additional storm ponds that require safety enhancements. Current storm pond safety work can be viewed on the storm pond map available on calgary.ca/stormponds . Storm pond safety is a priority for The City of Calgary with a focus on educating the public and creating awareness that recreational activities on storm ponds year-round are prohibited in accordance with the City Stormwater Bylaw . It is important to remember that where there's water, there's risk; the importance of safety around storm ponds or any bodies of water cannot be understated. Stormwater ponds are working stormwater facilities, not recreational areas. Stay safe, stay off storm ponds. For more information on safety around storm ponds, visit calgary.ca/stormpondsafety . What to do if you see someone in trouble in the water Call for help and call 911. Throw them something to hang onto that floats. Reach out to them with something they can grip and pull them back to the edge, if you can do so safely. If you cannot reach them, keep them in your sights and memorize the location and a description of their clothing. Make sure that they receive medical attention for injuries, even if there are no apparent wounds. DO NOT enter the water unless you are trained in water rescue. – 30 –

title: Suite success: how homeowners created thousands of homes through Incentive Program
summary: Thousands of Calgarians now have safer, legal housing options through The City of Calgary's Secondary Suite Incentive Program , which committed $45 million in federal and municipal investments so far to help homeowners build, improve and legalize secondary suites. “This is an achievement owned by Calgarians who stepped up, utilizing incentives that resulted in thousands of new housing options in our city,” says Josh Howes, Suites Manager, Development, Business and Building Services. “Giving renters confidence that their home has been reviewed and approved by The City is an important outcome, as all Calgarians deserve to feel safe in their home.” The incentive program, which provided qualified homeowners up to $10,000 to cover a portion of construction costs, significantly contributed to the expansion of safe housing in Calgary, doubling the number of suites on the Secondary Suite Registry from 13,000 in 2024 to 26,000 today. “We started with just 431 registered suites in 2015. Today, new registered secondary suites represent a quarter of all new units added in Calgary over the past three years. That growth shows homeowners are choosing to meet safety standards, complete inspections and provide renters with a suite that is legal and safe,” says Cliff De Jong, Manager of Programs and Services, Development, Business and Building Services. The Secondary Suite Incentive Program is part of Home is Here, The City of Calgary's Housing Strategy. “At less than $10,000 per door, this program has been the most efficient and cost-effective way to create thousands of new homes across Calgary,” says Reid Hendry, Chief Housing Officer. “By helping homeowners add safe, legal secondary suites, we've vastly increased the supply of market-affordable rental homes in established communities where people already have access to services and amenities." Corey Hogan, Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy and Natural Resources and Member of Parliament for Calgary Confederation, says: “Canadians need more housing options and secondary suites are a way communities can add homes more quickly while making better use of existing neighbourhood infrastructure. Through the Housing Accelerator Fund, the federal government is supporting initiatives that help increase housing supply. The results of Calgary's Secondary Suite Incentive Program demonstrate the role these local solutions can play in addressing housing needs.” While the Secondary Suite Incentive Program applications are wrapping up, homeowners under review are still in line to receive funding. The waitlist remains open until applications are reviewed, and all funding is disbursed. The Amnesty Program remains open until December 2026. Owners of suites constructed prior to March 2018 must ensure their existing suites meet the minimum life safety requirements. Renters searching for a safe, legal suite can look for The City's official Registered Secondary Suite sticker in the window and visit the Secondary Suite Registry . Background: 50 per cent of suites added to the Secondary Suite Registry in Calgary were incentivized through this program. Approximately 7,000 secondary suites will have benefited directly from the incentive program (once all contracts are fulfilled and money handed out in mid-to-late 2027). The Secondary Suite Registry will grow to 30,000 suites by 2027.

title: City of Calgary, Rocky View County and Canada Infrastructure Bank sign MOU to advance Prairie Economic Gateway
summary: The City of Calgary, Rocky View County and the Canada Infrastructure Bank (CIB) have signed a project acceleration Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) to advance the next stage of work on Prairie Economic Gateway (Gateway). The project acceleration MOU will help speed up the transition from engineering design to construction activities at the proposed landmark trade and logistics hub in the Calgary region. The project acceleration MOU establishes a framework for the three organizations to jointly assess the commercial, technical, and financial feasibility of the public off-site infrastructure required to enable future development. Today's MOU builds upon an early-stage project development MOU signed by the same three parties in early 2025, which set out to explore the CIB's potential participation in the Gateway project. The new agreement moves the work into a more detailed due diligence phase focused on the infrastructure, financing and delivery considerations needed before construction decisions can be made. For residents of the Calgary region, the agreement represents another step toward building the infrastructure needed to support future jobs, attract private investment and reinforce the region's role as a connected, competitive, resilient economic hub. By helping address transportation and servicing constraints around a proposed rail-anchored inland port east of Calgary in Rocky View County, Gateway is intended to support new industrial growth while strengthening the regional supply chains that businesses and households rely on every day. Prairie Economic Gateway is envisioned as a rail-anchored inland port and multimodal logistics hub located east of Calgary in Rocky View County, Alberta, within Canada's Prairie Core Trade Corridor on the CPKC mainline. Led by The City of Calgary and Rocky View County in partnership with private-sector rail and development partners, Gateway is intended to expand trade-enabling infrastructure capacity, address first-mile and last-mile constraints, increase economic benefit through trade, improve the reliability and resilience of supply chains and support increased trade diversification. Quotes “This agreement with the Canada Infrastructure Bank is an important step toward finalizing the infrastructure investments needed to unlock new trade, logistics and industrial development, create jobs and strengthen Calgary's competitiveness. By working with our regional partners and the Canada Infrastructure Bank, we are building the foundation for sustainable long-term growth that benefits residents, businesses and the broader regional economy.” – Mayor Jeromy Farkas, City of Calgary “Prairie Economic Gateway is a generational opportunity to attract investment, create jobs and strengthen Rocky View County's position as a trade and transportation hub. This MOU reflects our strong partnership with The City of Calgary and our shared commitment to responsible planning and investment. The Canada Infrastructure Bank's expertise will help us assess the infrastructure needs and financing options required to bring this vision to life.” – Reeve Sunny Samra, Rocky View County -30- About Prairie Economic Gateway Prairie Economic Gateway is a regionally approved, shovel-ready collaboration between The City of Calgary and Rocky View County to enable rail-served industrial development and economic diversification in the Calgary region. Gateway is envisioned as the centre of a future inland port supported by private sector investment. By extending trade infrastructure capacity beyond Canada's congested seaports and into the Prairies, the project is intended to strengthen national supply chains, open new opportunities for industrial development, and support long-term economic growth in Alberta and across Canada. About the Canada Infrastructure Bank The Canada Infrastructure Bank (CIB) is an impact investor developing the next generation of infrastructure Canadians need. The goal of CIB's investments is to use public capital to accelerate projects which are in the public interest, attract private investment and deliver measurable economic and social outcomes for Canadians. Media Contacts Rocky View County Janine Workman jworkman@rockyview.ca 403-371-8606 Canada Infrastructure Bank media@cib-bic.ca

title: Calgary Fire Department Responds to Multiple Lithium-Ion Battery Fires
summary: The Calgary Fire Department responded to three separate fires incidents over the past 24 hours involving lithium-ion batteries. At around 9:25am on Thursday August 6, fire crews responded to 0-100 block of Covercreek Mews NE for a structure fire. Crews arrived at two story residential home with a front attached garage. Firefighters noticed smoke staining along the garage door and were met by occupants outside. Crews were shown inside the home and lead to the interior access door to the garage where crews found heavy smoke conditions. On entry to the garage, crews observed thick dark smoke but no visible flames. A fan was set up at the front door to ventilate. There was no fire damage inside the home. One occupant was assessed for smoke inhalation by Emergency Health Services Alberta. No other injuries were reported. A fire investigator attended the scene and removed three electric scooters and determined the fire originated from one of the scooters as all three were being charged. At around 3:35am on Friday August 7, fire crews were dispatched to the 6600 block of 106 Avenue SE for a fire at a large commercial warehouse. Crews arrived and all staff had self-exited the building and the alarm system was active. Firefighters completed a size up and located a fire in an exterior compactor. A fire extinguisher was used to knock down the fire. A fire investigator attended and spoke with staff members who reported seeing a glow from the boxes immediately before the fire. They also reported having fires in the compactors due to lithium-ion batteries being inadvertently left in boxes going through the compactor. The fire investigator determined this was the most likely cause of this fire. Shortly after, at around 3:50am, fire crews responded to the 0-100 block of Saddlemont Close NE for a structure fire. Crews arrived at a two-story residential home with smoke coming from a side basement door. All the occupants had self-exited and there were no injuries reported. Firefighters stretched a hose line to the basement and encountered low visibility due to the smoke and did a quick knock down the fire. A cat was rescued during the search in another part of the home and reunited with the owners on scene. The fire was contained to the basement suite. A fire investigator attended the scene and determined that the fire had originated from an electric scooter that had been plugged in. The Calgary Fire Department would like to remind Calgarians to follow safe charging practices to reduce the risk of lithium-ion battery fires: Once a battery has charged to 100%, unplug the device to prevent overcharging the Lithium Battery Avoid l eaving batteries unattended while charging Avoid charging batteries that show signs of damage, swelling, overheating, or physical deterioration Follow manufacturer charging instructions and use compatible charging equipment Learn how to safely dispose of batteries and keep them out of blue, black, or green carts Please visit www.calgary.ca/fire for more fire safety and prevention information. -30-

title: Calgarians asked to consider urban wildfire risk and take action in new prevention campaign
summary: From Vernon BC to Spokane WA, wildfires are encroaching communities at unprecedented rates this summer, causing significant property damage, displacement and, sometimes, injury and death. Wildfire, along with other outdoor fire types, have on average seen increased activity in Calgary since 2020, similar to other municipalities in western Canada. While Calgary is not adjacent to large boreal forests, its natural areas inevitably see fires and with increased densification and population growth in our City, more residents than ever are living near urban wildland areas, grasslands and other natural areas. “Seasonal risk of wildfire, grass fires and other outdoor fires is a growing reality across Canada, especially where residential neighbourhoods join up with wildlands,” says Fire Chief Steve Dongworth. “While The City of Calgary provides some of Canada's most effective fire response, planning and emergency preparedness, we also rely on residents and communities to reduce our shared fire risk, both at home and in City parks and natural areas. Hotter, dryer summers mean that we all play a role in keeping our homes and communities safe.” In response to this shared risk, the Calgary Fire Department (CFD) has developed Calgary's first dedicated wildfire resilience and prevention campaign, which runs August 3 to September 6 and is supported through funding from the Forest Resource Improvement Association of Alberta (FRIAA) FireSmart Program. Wildfire awareness campaigns are now common in rural and forested areas of Canada, often through provincial and federal FireSmart programs, and are increasingly common in municipalities across Canada. Like any municipality, Calgary has unique topography and natural areas with a number of “wildland-urban interfaces” where residential development is adjacent to natural vegetation. These areas are detailed in maps at calgary.ca/wildfire where Calgarians can determine their proximity to our City's major natural and wildland areas, including a community-specific map . Wildland-urban interface areas exist across Calgary, and they can be found in both established and growing communities. Living in these areas increases exposure to wildfire risk, especially during hot, dry, and windy conditions that are currently being observed across southern Alberta and British Columbia. On July 30, CFD issued a fire advisory for Calgary , asking Calgarians to use extra caution when using open flames or any solid-fueled appliance such as fire pits, barbeques and campfires. “If nature is next door, wildfire is a risk. Learn about outdoor fire risk specific to where you live – and then take any number of our recommended big and small actions that will make a difference to reduce wildfire, grass and bush fire risk in and around your home and community,” says Chief Dongworth. Reflecting on his own experience touring the aftermath of the deadly Los Angeles fires in 2025, Chief Dongworth says a little goes a long way in terms of adapting to warming summers and emergency preparedness. “Becoming more resilient in the face of increasing wildfire risk is a multi-year process,” he says. “We don't expect everyone to replace their roofing and siding however there is a lot that Calgarians can do today, whether you rent or own your home – or while visiting our City's parks and natural areas.” Calgary Fire has specialized equipment to combat wildland fires, and trains regularly to be ready for major incidents. CFD and other City business units also collaborate with wildland-adjacent communities like Discovery Ridge to identify risks and opportunities related to potential wildfire activity. The City is also developing a wildfire threat assessment program to better understand wildfire conditions in natural areas across Calgary. “Discovery Ridge is a community where we need to balance the beauty of the natural landscape with the risk of wildfires,” says Dana Fleury, Vice President, Discovery Ridge Community Association. “We encourage our community members here and in other areas of Calgary to learn more about how we can all mitigate the risk of wildfire in our city while preserving our environment.” Calgarians are asked to: 1. Create a safe perimeter around your home and property. Take steps to remove combustibles. Limit the amount of flammable vegetation in any potential ignition zone close to your residence. 2. Manage fuels and flammable materials. Store propane tanks, firewood and yard waste away from your home. Do not store propane tanks inside. 3. Upgrade when renovating. Choose ignition resistant building materials and construction techniques. 4. Practice outdoor fire safety everywhere. Improper disposal of smoking materials remains one of Calgary's leading causes of outdoor fires. Extreme caution should be used in the city's natural areas and green spaces during fire bans and periods of high temperatures. 5. Prepare and know what to do. Learn how to become more resilient during periods of wildfire smoke and maintain an emergency kit with wildfire-specific items such as N95 masks. Always call 9-1-1 in an emergency. Please visit calgary.ca/wildfire for more information. -30- Calgary Fire Department – wildland fire fast facts Wildfire in Calgary, along with other outdoor fire types, have on average seen increased activity in Calgary since 2020, similar to other municipalities in western Canada. Calgary Fire has responded to an average of 23 wildland fires (wildfire, grass and brush fires) per month annually since 2016. Peak activity usually occurs in May, which on average sees an average of 42 wildland fires. Seasonal conditions continue to be variable despite long-term trends. From January to June 2026, for example, wildland fires in Calgary declined by 17 per cent, primarily due to fewer brush, or brush and grass mixture fires, compared to the same period in 2025. This was strongly influenced by persistent cold temperatures and heavy snow accumulation during January to April 2026, which reduced several ignition risk factors, including construction activity, outdoor smoking near entrances and balconies, and the use of outdoor heating or open-flame devices. While spring 2026 wildland fires decreased in frequency compared to Calgary's historical average due to wet conditions, it is expected that outdoor fire activity will continue to trend upwards this summer and increase, on average, in the coming years. As of July 2026, Calgary Fire had responded to more wildland fire incidents in the first half of 2026 than recorded for entire individual years between 2017 to 2020.

title: Calgary Fire Department Responds to Fatal Three-Vehicle Collision
summary: The Calgary Fire Department (CFD) responded to a tragic three-vehicle motor vehicle collision on Tsuut'ina Trail SW just before 11:00pm that claimed the lives of four people and left four others injured. Multiple CFD crews were dispatched to the scene following reports of a serious collision. Upon arrival, firefighters encountered two of the three vehicles fully engulfed in flames. Crews immediately initiated an aggressive fire attack while simultaneously conducting rapid searches of the involved vehicles and providing emergency care to those who could be reached. Once the fire was brought under control, firefighters continued to work in coordination with Alberta Emergency Health Services (EHS) to assess and treat those involved. Despite the rapid actions of first responders, four people were pronounced deceased at the scene. Four additional patients were transported to hospital by EHS for further assessment and treatment. The Calgary Fire Department extends its deepest condolences to the families, friends, and loved ones of those who lost their lives, and our thoughts are with those who were injured and everyone affected by this tragic incident. Following the completion of firefighting and rescue operations, the scene was turned over to the Calgary Police Service, which is leading the investigation into the circumstances surrounding the collision. The Calgary Fire Department urges all motorists to drive attentively, obey posted speed limits, avoid distractions, and always wear a seatbelt. Safe driving practices remain one of the most effective ways to prevent serious and fatal collisions. -30-

title: Calgary Fire Department Responds to Three Significant Fires During Busy Sunday Afternoon
summary: Calgary Fire Department (CFD) crews responded to three significant fires across the city during the afternoon on Sunday August 2, which challenged the department's ability to manage multiple complex emergencies while maintaining emergency response coverage for Calgary residents. At approximately 12:20 p.m., a structure fire was reported in the 400 block of MacLeod Trail SE. Responding crews encountered a substantial fire with multiple occupants requiring immediate rescue. Firefighters promptly initiated rescue operations and executed an aggressive interior attack. A second alarm was requested to provide additional resources. Several individuals were safely extricated, and the fire was contained to the room of origin, although smoke damage affected the remainder of the structure. Numerous patients were assessed on scene, with six transported to hospital by Alberta Emergency Health Services. Given the extent of the damage and approximately fifty displaced residents, the Calgary Emergency Management Agency (CEMA) attended and provided on-site support. While operations were ongoing at the initial incident, CFD was dispatched to a second major fire at approximately 1:54 p.m. in the 100 block of 16 Street NW. Upon arrival, firefighters found two detached garages fully involved. Crews established command, deployed multiple hose lines, and successfully contained the fire to the affected garages, thereby preventing extension to adjacent properties. No injuries were reported in this incident. At approximately 3:00 p.m., CFD responded to a third major incident at the Shepard Landfill. Due to the magnitude and complexity of the situation, CFD personnel collaborated with landfill staff, employing specialized tactics and heavy equipment to contain the fire. Operations continued into the evening to achieve full mitigation and minimize the incident's impact. Despite responding to three major fires over the course of less than three hours, the Calgary Fire Department maintained emergency response capabilities across the city through coordinated resource deployment and support from crews at multiple stations. The causes of all three fires remain under investigation by the Calgary Fire Department Fire Investigation Team. Damage estimates are not available at this time. The Calgary Fire Department extends its appreciation to the Calgary Police Service, Alberta Emergency Health Services, the Calgary Emergency Management Agency, City of Calgary partners, and landfill personnel for their collaboration and support during these incidents. Early detection played a critical role in protecting lives and property during today's events. The Calgary Fire Department reminds all residents to ensure smoke alarms are installed on every level of their home, outside all sleeping areas, and are tested monthly to ensure they are functioning properly. With current hot, dry, and windy conditions increasing the risk of fire across southern Alberta, residents are also encouraged to use extra caution with any outdoor activities that could create a fire and to report fires immediately by calling 9-1-1. Anyone with photos, video, or information especially prior to the arrival of fire crews is encouraged to email piofire@calgary.ca -30-

title: Housefire in Hawkwood
summary: At approximately 1030PM on Sunday July 26 th , 2026, the Calgary Fire Department (CFD) responded to a possible house fire in the northwest community of Hawkwood. On arrival at the 200 block of Hawkstone Drive, crews encountered light smoke in the air and one person with injuries. On investigation, firefighters found a working fire in the rear of the single family detached home and a fire on the rear deck. Fire crews also found another person with injuries at the rear of the home. The fire was quickly brought under control and extinguished by crews on scene and the injured people were assessed and transported by EHS ambulances. The Calgary Police Service were quickly on scene and worked with crews to assess the cause of the fire. At this time the incident has been turned over to CPS for further investigation. Nine fire apparatus and over 20 firefighters were on scene. The cause of the fire is still under investigation. -30-

title: Patient in critical condition following paddleboard incident near Bowness Park
summary: At around 1:10 PM on July 23, 2026, fire crews responded to reports of a paddleboard user colliding with an abutment on the 85th Street N.W. Bridge by Bowness Park. Crews arrived and an adult male victim was located face down in the water and attached to his paddleboard leash near the bridge abutment. The patient's location was shared with responding boat crews and Calgary Police Service HAWKS was requested to provide aerial support. CFD's aquatic rescue boat arrived from downstream, reached the victim, who was brought to shore while crews performed CPR. Once on shore, CPR continued until the patient was transferred to Emergency Health Services-Alberta. Crews assisted with ongoing CPR before the patient was transported to Foothills Medical Centre in critical condition. There was initial uncertainty about whether there was a second individual involved in the incident and CFD crews worked to confirm that all people had been accounted for. The second individual was identified as the 11-year-old son of the patient, who had floated downriver following the collision with the bridge abutment and was brought to shore by a bystander. EMS assessed the child and did not have any medical concerns. "The patient did have a personal floatation device on, but with the power of the river and the current itself, the person was pulled under the water and was attached to the paddleboard by an ankle leash,” said Battalion Chief Bruce Barrs. Standup paddleboards are increasingly popular on Calgary's waterways and are trending within this year's aquatic rescue incidents, including three paddleboarders rescued on the Bow River during the June 2026 high water event and river safety advisory. The Calgary Fire Department reminds Calgarians that paddleboard ankle leashes are not safe for use on moving water. Paddleboard leash usage has resulted in at least two aquatic fatalities and other serious incidents in recent years. Please remember: There is a high risk of being pulled under water or getting the leash entangled, which can trap someone under water as the force of the river may make it impossible to detach the leash during an emergency. Do not use the ankle leash while paddleboarding on the river. If you're worried about losing your board if you fall off, consider putting your phone number on the board. Using anchors on moving water poses a similar risk. Visit calgary.ca/watersafety for more information as well as calgary.ca/flood for the latest information on river conditions. -30-

title: Calgary Fire Responds to Two Afternoon Fires
summary: At around 1:45pm, fire crews responded to the 3000 block of Dover Ridge Drive SE for a structure fire. Crews arrived at a single-story residential home with light smoke showing. Firefighters stretched a hose line and located a fire in the basement. The crew quickly identified the fire as being lithium-ion batteries and used a large dry chemical extinguisher to knock down the fire. A fire investigator attended the scene and confirmed the fire originated in the basement where renovation work was in progress and was caused by lithium-ion batteries that were left charging. There were no injuries reported. A youth was home at the time of the incident and quickly evacuated when alerted by the working smoke alarms and went to a neighbours home to call 9-1-1. Due to the toxic smoke from the lithium-ion battery, the occupants will be temporarily displaced and staying with family members At around 3:30pm, fire crews responded to the 1700 block of 26 Avenue SW for a structure fire. Crews arrived at a low-rise residential complex with smoke showing and called a working fire. Firefighters saw smoke throughout the top floor and assisted residents with exiting the building, along with their pets, while continuing to search for the fire. Two ladder trucks were set up to access the roof, and additional fire engines were called to attend the scene. Fire was located in the walls and ceiling of the top floor of the building and was extending through void spaces. Firefighters checked for extension of fire from both the roof top and interior ceiling and confirmed the fire is extinguished. A total of five people, from two different units, will be displaced as their units have extensive damage. No injuries were reported and all pets are accounted for. A fire investigator is on scene and has started the investigation into the origin and cause of the fire. Calgary Police Services, Emergency Health Services Alberta, ATCO and Enmax all attended the scene. The Calgary Fire Department would like to remind all Calgarians that: Working smoke alarms save lives Install smoke alarms in every bedroom, outside each sleeping area and on every level of your home, including the basement. Test all smoke alarms, including 10-year lithium-ion battery powered alarms, at least once a month by pushing the test button and replace batteries at least once per year. Replace smoke alarms when they are 10 years old or don't respond when tested. Practice safe charging Once a battery has charged to 100%, unplug the device. Don't overcharge the Lithium Battery . Don't charge a device under your pillow, on your bed or on a couch. Place the device on a hard surface to allow airflow around the device. Don't charge your batteries overnight. Please visit www.calgary.ca/fire for more fire safety and prevention information. -30-

title: Calgary Fire Responds to Sunday Drowning Incident in Legacy
summary: At around 1:15pm on Sunday July 12, 2026, fire crews responded to the 200 block of Legacy Main Street SE for a possible drowning. The district fire crew arrived on scene at a community feature storm pond and found an adult, who was later confirmed to be a family member, had entered the water and brought a child to shore where bystanders began CPR. Firefighters took over CPR on the child as Emergency Health Service (EHS) Alberta paramedics and Calgary Police Services arrived on scene. Patient care was transferred to EHS-AB paramedics and firefighters continued to assist with resuscitation efforts as the child was in critical and life-threatening condition. It is estimated that the child may have been in under water for around 20 minutes. STARS ambulance was called to attend and CFD cleared a landing zone however, sadly, the child was pronounced deceased on scene and not transported. CFD Aquatic rescuers completed a surface and sonar search of the pond and confirmed that there were no other patients in the water. -30-

title: Calgary Fire Department lifts June 29 River safety advisory for Bow and Elbow Rivers
summary: Due to improved conditions on the Bow and Elbow Rivers, the Calgary Fire Department is lifting the river safety advisory issued on Monday, June 29, 2026, effective immediately. Flow rates on both the Bow and Elbow rivers have decreased to below advisory levels. While there may still be some reduced visibility and debris, conditions are expected to gradually improve to typical summer conditions however, and the water temperature remains cold. The public can resume normal activities on and around our City's rivers but are encouraged to continue to use caution and practice safety. Calgary's rivers are closely monitored by several City departments. During the annual runoff season, melting snow and floating debris can create dangerous conditions for people on the river, prompting these types of advisories. A lifted advisory does not remove the need for caution on Calgary's waterways. Conditions are unpredictable and can change without warning, such as when we experience sudden thunderstorms that result in rapid, short duration increases in flow. The Calgary Fire Department Aquatic Rescue Team will continue to monitor and patrol Calgary's waterways. As always, Calgarians are reminded to use caution and plan ahead to be prepared for anything on the water. Calgary Fire Department reminds all Calgarians and their guests to: Actively supervise any children and stay within arm's reach of any young children in the water Select the proper watercraft for the waterway and have a boat safety kit Avoid tying watercrafts together while on the river Avoid wearing ankle leashes while on the river All watercraft users must wear their own properly fitting lifejackets Find out more about how to float and boat safely at calgary.ca/watersafety as well as calgary.ca/flood for information on river conditions. -30-

title: Calgary Fire Responds to Two House Fires in Sundance
summary: At around 5:05 pm fire crews responded to a structure fire in the 0-100 block of Sunmount Close SE. Fire crews arrived to find a fire at the back of a two storey residential house. Firefighters stretched hose lines from the alley into the back yard and started knocking back the fire when they discovered the gas line was damaged and further fueling the fire. Firefighters used a fog pattern to hold back the fire while they attempted to clamp the gas line. A clamp was applied which reduced the gas flow and ATCO gas attended to fully clamp and repair the gas line. No occupants were inside at the time of the incident, and the fire damage was limited to the exterior of the home. At around the same time fire crews were dispatched to a second house fire across the alley in the 0-100 block of Sunvalley Drive SE. Fire crews saw smoke coming from a second story window as two occupants self-exited from the home. Firefighters stretched a hose line into the home and knocked down a fire in a second-floor bedroom. Crews checked for extension and found fire in the walls and attic space. A ladder tower was set up to access the roof and upper exterior of the home. The fire was extinguished and a fire watch crew remains on scene. ATCO gas, Enmax, Emergency Health Services-Alberta all attended the scene. No injuries were reported. Neighbours reported hearing extremely loud thunder and a bright flash immediately before the fires. Two fire investigators attended the scenes. -30-

title: Calgary Fire Department Responds to Bow River Rescue
summary: At around 11:55am fire crews responded to the Bow River in an area downstream of Edworthy park for a water rescue. The first arriving fire crew located three people in the water holding onto a cluster of trees. Two Fire Department aquatic rescue jet boats were deployed and able to safely get the three people, one adult and two youths back to shore. Aquatic rescuers were also able to recover their paddleboards and personal belongings. While all three people were wearing lifejackets and were not injured, this was a close call incident, and the current conditions are not suitable for recreational activities. The flow rate of the Bow River has increased to over 500 cubic meters per second, which is almost double the threshold for when a river safety advisory is issued. The very fast flow rate, along with debris in the water and other hidden hazards beneath the surface make it very challenging to paddle. This increases the risk of getting pushed into hazards such as trees and bridge pillars and being pinned by the rush of cold water. The Calgary Fire Department would like to remind all Calgarians and any visitors to Calgary to: Reschedule any recreational activities on Bow and Elbow Rivers until the advisory is lifted. Cyclists and pedestrians should watch for low-lying areas where the river can submerge the pathways. Please help us share these safety messages with your friends and family Visit calgary.ca/watersafety for more information as well as calgary.ca/flood for the latest information on river conditions. Visit calgary.ca/pathwayclosures for up-to-date information on pathway closures. -30-

title: Calgary Fire Department issues river safety advisory for Bow and Elbow Rivers
summary: With continued rainfall and rising waters levels, the Calgary Fire Department (CFD) advises against boating and all other water activities on the Bow and Elbow Rivers, effective immediately. The Bow and Elbow Rivers have exceeded safe recommended flow rates for boating, floating or swimming, and it is expected these levels will sustain through Canada Day and potentially into the end of the week. While The City's Environmental Risk and Resilience team has advised that widespread overbank flooding is not anticipated, localized flooding remains possible, and high flow rates may continue, making conditions on and near the river dangerous. Water temperature remains cold and with the higher flow rates water turbidity is increased, making hazards difficult to see. Strong winds have also increased the number of debris, such as trees and branches in the rivers. The higher speed of the water increases the risks of being swept away for anyone that falls into the water, and there is a higher risk of being pinned against obstacles such as bridge pillars. “While the school year has ended and everyone is excited for summer, the Calgary Fire Department advises everyone to stay off the Bow and the Elbow Rivers, until safer conditions return and the river safety advisory is lifted,” says Alex Kwan, CFD's Public Information Officer. “We know that Calgarians love their rivers, and as we head into the Stampede, we welcome lots of visitors, so we want to remind everyone that when our waterways flow this high and fast, there's significant risk, regardless of your watercraft or skill level. Those walking near our City's rivers, including people with pets, should be careful as well.” Along with turbidity and debris, conditions for a CFD River usage advisory include Bow River flow rates exceeding 280 cubic meters per second and flow rates in Elbow River exceeding 50 cubic meters per second. Calgary Fire and its Aquatics Team will continue to monitor Calgary's waterways while the advisory is in place and will notify Calgarians when the advisory is lifted. It is important for Calgarians near the river to be careful due to high flow levels. Calgarians are urged to: Reschedule any recreational activities on Bow and Elbow Rivers until the advisory is lifted. Warn their children about the dangers of fast-moving water, particularly those residents who live near the rivers. Cyclists and pedestrians should watch for low-lying areas where the river can submerge the pathways. Keep pets away from fast-moving water. Visit calgary.ca/watersafety for more information as well as calgary.ca/flood for the latest information on river conditions. Visit calgary.ca/pathwayclosures for up-to-date information on pathway closures. Note to media and water safety partners: today and going forward, the Calgary Fire Department will be issuing a “River Safety Advisory” for unsafe river conditions instead of “Boating Advisory” as Calgarians at risk include pathway users, pet owners and others who do not own conventional watercraft. The scope and criteria of the advisory itself remains unchanged. -30-

title: Calgarians celebrate community connection on Neighbour Day
summary: Calgarians came together across the city to celebrate another Neighbour Day, an annual tradition that encourages people to celebrate our community spirit and come together for a quick chat, a barbeque, or outdoor activity that helps build strong and lasting connections. “This is an incredible legacy that we've made to last. After more than 10 years now as a tradition, it's very clear that Neighbour Day is part of Calgary's bones – it's a day about Calgary, and being the best neighbours in the world,” said Mayor Jeromy Farkas. Despite periods of rain and windy weather, this past weekend, on Saturday, June 20, neighbours across our city carried out their Neighbour Day events. One of this year's featured celebrations took place at the Millican Ogden Community Association, where residents marked MOCA's 70th anniversary with a parade, historical tours, interactive activity stations, cultural performances, food, and celebrations. Mayor Jeromy Farkas joined residents, volunteers and community leaders to recognize the role community associations play in creating welcoming, connected neighbourhoods. “Neighbour Day is about showing up for one another and taking pride in the places we live,” said Mayor Jeromy Farkas. “Across Calgary, neighbours came together through block parties, community concerts, barbecues, crafts, gardening and more — simple ways to spend time together and strengthen local connections. Thank you to everyone who hosted, volunteered, and took part in this year's celebrations.” Neighbour Day events included arts and crafts, community markets, live music, family games, garden gatherings, cultural activities and neighbourhood picnics in communities such as Sherwood, Kensington, Highland Park, Triwood, Edgemont, West Hillhurst, Dalhousie, Acadia, Auburn Bay, Chaparral, Maple Ridge and more, giving residents many ways to connect close to home. Willow Ridge hosted a community picnic with neighbours' invited to paint tiles to be added at the Greener Grounds Grand Opening of a mural mosaic. In Tuxedo Park, a free outdoor art station was offered, and the Capitol Hill Community Association hosted cool experiences to celebrate the end of the school year, the day before. In Acadia, the Osten & Victor Alberta Tennis Centre celebrated its 10th anniversary with tennis activities, face painting, a barbecue, and opportunities to gather. The Hidden Valley Community Association celebrated a Neighbour Day carnival with fire dances, stilt walkers, carnival games, and an outdoor movie. Neighbour Day also connected with Sport Calgary's All Sport One Day, giving children and youth a free opportunity to try new sports, while Tourism Calgary's Come Together, Colour Calgary initiative invited participants at select events to help colour collaborative canvas murals celebrating Calgary's people, places and diversity. For the second year in a row, the #YYCNeighbourDay microgrant helped bring celebrations to life. This year, 54 microgrants of up to $2,000 supported community associations, business improvement areas, and non-profit organizations in hosting free, community-led events across Calgary. -30-

title: Young Calgarian Discovers Rare Fossil at Local Playground
summary: Calgary playgrounds are designed to spark adventure and curiosity for thousands of children each year. For one seven-year-old girl, this sense of adventure led to an extraordinary discovery. After playing on the equipment of a local playground, Alyssa decided to examine some of the medium-sized stacked boulders surrounding the perimeter of the park. As Alyssa looked for bugs and collected rocks, she spotted a dark shape embedded in the top of one of the boulders. Fascinated by all things dinosaur, Alyssa immediately knew what she had found and amazingly knew exactly what to do about it. She urged her parents to contact experts at the Royal Tyrrell Museum who confirmed the validity of the discovery. Alyssa had found a rare 250 to 400-million-year-old sea star fossil measuring around five centimeters in size. Dr. Don Henderson, the Curator of Dinosaurs at the Royal Tyrrell Museum, said sea stars require extremely specific conditions to fossilize, making specimens of this age very rare and limited to only a handful of sites worldwide. The boulder that holds the sea star was placed there during the playground's construction in 2005 leading us to believe the fossil has remained there for over 20 years. Dr. Henderson says he has inquired where the boulders were sourced from, but the exact location has not been confirmed. Sitting at the playground where the fossil was found, Alyssa crouched down studying her discovery further. When asked what her favorite thing about the fossil was, she replied, “I love how preserved it is”. Even at the age of seven, Alyssa is thinking beyond this moment, recognizing the importance of preserving a piece of Alberta's history. Speaking with Alyssa's parents, it was clear this was a special moment for their family filled with pride, excitement and a touch of disbelief. They described their daughter's passion for palaeontology and the thoughtful questions she brought to the Tyrrell team, including “how do sea stars fossilize if they don't have bones?” a question that left many adults saying, “I had never thought of that.” Dr. Henderson explained that “Tyrrell's mandate is to preserve the fossil heritage of the province” meaning the fossil must be carefully removed from the park and stored in a controlled environment for research and conservation. The Tyrrell team used a diamond saw to diagonally cut into the stone, removing the section of rock containing the fossil, leaving the remaining boulder in place. City crews are working to smooth out the area and will be pouring new concrete to reconstruct the remaining rock. The fossil was taken back to the Tyrrell Museum where it will be cleaned, cataloged, and may eventually go on display. Alyssa watched from a distance as the fossil was removed, climbing to the highest point of the playground for a better view. Once the rock was lifted, she had a chance to hold her discovery — a small but meaningful moment after her curiosity set everything in motion. Laureen Bryant, an Archaeologist from The City of Calgary's Cultural Landscapes group, says in Alberta fossils are protected under the Historical Resources Act. It is very important to report suspected fossil finds directly to the Royal Tyrrell Museum. This includes noting the location, photographing the find, and most importantly leaving it undisturbed, making sure not to damage any fossils you encounter. For more information about reporting fossil finds, visit the Royal Tyrrell Museum website . The City of Calgary Parks & Open Spaces team was amazed by Alyssa's commitment to conservation and recognized her unbound potential and enthusiasm for science. As a thank-you, Parks & Open Spaces presented her with some small tokens of appreciation. These included swimming passes from The City of Calgary's Recreation and Social Programs group, admission from Calgary Civic partners at the Calgary Zoo, TELUS Spark Center and Heritage Park along with a tree to plant in memory of the day she uncovered a remarkable piece of history. -30- Media contacts Royal Tyrrell Museum Ashley Makohoniuk, Head of Marketing and Public Relations Ashley.Makohoniuk@gov.ab.ca

title: Autonomous mowers bring increased efficiency and innovation to select recreation locations
summary: The City of Calgary is testing autonomous grass mowers at two sites this season as part of a pilot focused on supporting the operations and maintenance of athletic fields. The pilot, led by Recreation & Social Programs, is taking place at Glenmore and Frank McCool Athletic Parks. The goal is to better understand how the technology performs in real-world conditions and where it may be appropriate to use in the future. “This is a small, controlled trial that allows us to explore how new technology can support our crews and day-to-day operations,” says Marc Sackman, Team Lead, Recreation & Social Programs. “We're focused on learning what works well and where it makes sense to use tools like this.” Supporting crews and improving field conditions The autonomous mowers are designed to handle routine grass cutting in open areas, operating along pre-programmed routes. By taking on some of this routine work, the pilot allows staff to focus more time on detailed maintenance and site upkeep. The technology can also support more consistent mowing throughout the week, helping maintain healthier and more even playing surfaces. In addition, flexible scheduling allows mowing to take place overnight or between bookings, which can be difficult to achieve with traditional equipment and competing site demands. In addition, the units operate at a low noise level of up to 52 dB, similar to a conversation, helping minimize noise impacts to nearby users and communities. Focused on learning The pilot will continue through the 2026 season, with a focus on safety, reliability and overall performance. The City will use what it learns to assess where this technology adds value and where it does not. There are no current plans to expand beyond the two pilot sites. Any future decisions will be made after results have been fully reviewed. -30-

title: Partners in Aquatic Safety ask Calgarians to stay safe on our rivers and lakes this summer
summary: With the first day of summer approaching, The City of Calgary's Partners in Aquatic Safety are urging Calgarians to prioritize safety while enjoying water activities. Partners in Aquatic Safety is a collaborative effort across The City's emergency rescue, enforcement and recreation business units. The group officially launched the water recreation season today with a strong message emphasizing the importance of being cautious and prepared when venturing onto Calgary's waterways. With more Calgarians than ever expected to be enjoying our City's lakes and rivers, the Calgary Fire Department emphasized that “where there's water, there's risk,” and that good safety practices can prevent trouble not only on fast-moving water like the Bow River, but also on calm waters like community lakes. “Our City's waterways are wild places that are seeing a growing number of preventable incidents,” says Alex Kwan, Calgary Fire Department Public Information Officer. “Last week, Calgary Fire rescued seven indviduals who became pinned on a bridge abutment on the Bow River, including one person who was pulled from the water.” “Water incidents, including drownings, can happen very quickly yet are avoidable if you follow simple guidelines, such as knowing your route, current river conditions and ensuring that your plan and boating equipment is appropriate to conditions and the skill level of your group,” says Kwan. “And on all lakes and rivers, lifejackets and proper supervision are critical for children and inexperienced swimmers.” Throughout the summer, Calgary Fire Department's aquatic crews patrol the Bow and Elbow rivers and respond to incidents on all bodies of water within Calgary. Law enforcement officials from CPS and CCS will also patrol Calgary's waterways, pathways and riverbanks to enforce municipal bylaws and provincial statutes. “If you're on a boat, you need to wear a life jacket,” says Staff Sgt. Andy Woodward, with the CPS Traffic Unit. “If you're steering that boat, you need to wear a life jacket and you need to be sober. Being impaired by drugs or alcohol while operating a boat is no different than being impaired by drugs or alcohol while driving a car. It's dangerous, and it's illegal.” Calgarians are reminded that not wearing a life jacket or personal flotation device (PFD) on Calgary's waterways can result in a fine up to $500 and a mandatory court appearance. “Wearing a lifejacket or personal flotation device is not just a choice; it's the law,” says Inspector Susan Wall, City of Calgary Community Safety. “Bylaw and CPS officers are dedicated to enforcing water safety bylaws, so let's protect ourselves and avoid fines while enjoying Calgary rivers and lakes.” In addition to practicing water safety and following water safety bylaws, Calgarians are reminded of the importance of swimming lessons and encouraged to build their knowledge of staying safe around the water. “Learning to swim is one of the most important steps Calgarians can take to stay safe around the water,” explains Team Lead of Thornhill Aquatic & Recreation Centre, Kadyn Morris. “Too often, incidents happen when people don't expect them. Knowing how to swim and how to stay calm can save your life. It's never too late to start. No matter your age or experience, everyone deserves to feel confident in the water.” To help more Calgarians build these life-saving skills, The City of Calgary is offering free-swimming lessons on June 25 at Thornhill Aquatic & Recreation Centre, Sir Winston Churchill Aquatic & Recreation Centre, Acadia Aquatic & Fitness Centre and Bob Bahan Aquatic & Fitness Centre. These free lessons are a part of a global initiative called “The World's Largest Swimming Lesson” focused on water safety education and drowning prevention. “We're proud to be part of this global effort,” adds Morris. “It's an opportunity for Calgarians of all ages to take that first step. Register, learn the skills and help keep yourself and others safe.” And finally, when calling 9-1-1 in a water emergency, knowing your location is critical. You may not know exactly where you are, but sharing what you can see around you - such as outfall numbers along shorelines, pathway markers, nearby addresses, bridge names, or other landmarks - can help 9-1-1 Emergency Communications Officers pinpoint your location and dispatch emergency crews quickly. “One of the most important things people can do in a water emergency is to call 9-1-1 immediately and provide as much location information as possible,” says Dan Heyde, Deputy Chief of Operations, Calgary 9-1-1. “If you see someone in distress, don't hesitate to call for help.” Visit calgary.ca/watersafety for more information on how to stay safe this summer on the water as well as calgary.ca/WorldSwim to register for the June 25 free event. Calgary Fire Department -- aquatic safety fast facts Source: Calgary Fire Department Current incident tracking and modelling from the Calgary Fire Department (CFD) project a potential all-time peak in water rescues for 2026. The greatest number of water rescues occur in July, averaging 50 rescues that month since 2016. Geographically, Calgary Fire sees the greatest number of water rescues on the Bow River between the Shouldice Boat Ramp downstream to Harvie Passage. The communities of Montgomery and Inglewood, at either end of this float, see the greatest number of aquatic rescues in the waters adjacent to their communities. Lakes and ponds across Calgary also see notable aquatic rescue incidents, including popular locations around the Glenmore Reservoir, community lakes and smaller bodies of water, including the Saddle Ridge storm water pond. In 2024, the second greatest number of rescues were recorded at Harvie Passage since 2016, a popular white-water destination that requires appropriate water craft, skill and water safety equipment. These incidents are considered serious, considering the flow and difficulty of the Bow River in that area. Calgary Fire has recorded seven aquatic rescue incidents involving paddleboards and individuals falling off them. One of these incidents involved a person being tied to a paddleboard and subsequently dragged downriver. Calgary Fire has attended a total of 30 fatalities related to aquatic rescue calls since 2016, including five in 2017 and four in 2021. Last year, in 2025, three Calgarians drowned and 2026 has already seen one drowning fatality. Source: Calgary Fire Department -30-

title: Calgary Fire Department lifts boating advisory for Bow and Elbow Rivers
summary: Due to improved conditions on the Bow River, the Calgary Fire Department is lifting the boating advisory issued on Friday, May 29, effective immediately. Flow rates on both the Bow and Elbow rivers have decreased and river conditions have improved, however there is still reduced visibility, and the water temperature remains cold. At these levels, people can resume normal activities on and around our City's rivers but are encouraged to use caution. Calgary's rivers are closely monitored by several City departments. During the annual runoff season, melting snow and floating debris can create dangerous conditions for people on the river, prompting these types of advisories. Along with turbidity and debris, conditions for a Calgary Fire Department boating advisory include Bow River flow rates exceeding 280 cubic metres per second above the Elbow River confluence. A lifted advisory does not remove the need for caution on Calgary's waterways. Conditions are unpredictable this time of year and can change without warning, such as when we experience sudden thunderstorms that result in rapid, short duration increases in flow. Calgary Fire and its Aquatics Rescue Team will continue to monitor and patrol Calgary's waterways. As always, Calgarians are reminded to use caution and be prepared for anything on the water. All watercraft users must wear lifejackets, ensure they have the required safety equipment for boating, and must avoid consuming alcohol and other intoxicants on Calgary's waterways. Find out more about how to float and boat safely at calgary.ca/watersafety as well as calgary.ca/flood for information on river conditions. -30-

title: Calgary Fire Department Launches 100+ Birthday Visit Program
summary: As we celebrate the 40 th anniversary of Seniors' Week in Alberta, the Calgary Fire Department (CFD) is launching a new program to celebrate Calgarians who are turning 100+ years old. If you, a friend or a relative is turning 100 years old or more, you can submit a request for firefighters to help you celebrate. A crew of firefighters will pull up to your door in a fire truck and will pop in to help you party with your friends and loved ones. “As first responders, it is important for us to stay connected with the community and the people we serve. This program allows us to recognize the value and experience of older adults in Calgary, while celebrating their lives and achievements with them,” said Calgary Fire Chief, Steve Dongworth. “We have already visited several Calgarians who turned 100+ years old and had great conversations with the celebrants and their guests. I hope this program allows us to visit more Calgarians who are celebrating a big birthday and show them our appreciation”. Please visit calgary.ca/100birthday to find out who is eligible and how to apply. This program is for people who are turning 100 years old or more within Calgary City limits and is not for any other celebrations. -30-

title: Calgary Fire Responds to Morning Portable Trailer Unit Fire
summary: At around 6:20 am fire crews responded to the 60 block of Peacekeepers DR SW for a structure fire. As crews arrived at a commercial warehouse yard, they were met by workers on site, who led them to a portable washroom unit next to a large warehouse. There was moderate smoke showing and they located a fire in between the unit and warehouse. Fire crews stretched hose lines and began protecting the main warehouse. Firefighters knocked back the fire, which appears to have originated from the smaller washroom unit. Crews ventilated smoke from the main warehouse and are rotating crews on scene to knock down hot spots in the walls of the portable washroom unit. No injuries were reported and utilities to the unit has been isolated. A fire investigator attended the scene and is working to determine the cause of the fire. Firefighters are working with the business to move the trailer unit away from the building as smouldering fires and hot spots continue to re-ignite within the walls of the washroom unit. Fire crews will remain on scene until the fire is confirmed to be extinguished. A number of fire trucks left the scene at shift change and returned to scene with new crews, making it seem that more fire trucks responded to this incident when the response was a first alarm response to an industrial warehouse. -30-

title: Calgary Fire Responds to Beltline High Rise Fire
summary: At around 4:20 pm, fire crews responded to the 1000 block of 13 AV SW for a high-rise structure fire. Crews arrived at visible flames and heavy smoke from the top of a 15-story residential building . Firefighters began evacuating residents and located a fire in the ceiling area of a top floor apartment unit and roof top area. Crews conducted an internal fire attack while other firefighters evacuated nearby units. A ladder truck was set up to access balconies and units from the exterior, but no one needed to be evacuated using the ladder truck. The building is reported to have 75 units; the majority of residents were evacuated while some residents were sheltered in place in unaffected areas. One person was transported with minor injuries sustained during the evacuation; one firefighter was assessed for minor injuries sustained during routine on scene activities. No other injuries reported. Fire investigators are on scene and have begun an investigation. A fire watch crew will be rotating throughout the evening and night.
