All residents, with the exception of two top floor units, have been able to re-occupy the building and reunite with their pets that were sheltered in place during the incident. Calgary Police Services, Alta Paramedic Health, Enmax and ATCO Gas all supported on scene. Anyone with any information, photos or video prior to the arrival of fire crews are asked to please contact the PIO via email piofire@calgary.ca We are interested in any photos or video taken from higher vantages points. -30-

title: Calgary Fire Department Issues Boating Advisory for the Bow and Elbow Rivers
summary: With continued snowmelt and rising waters, the Calgary Fire Department (CFD) advises against boating and all other water activities on the Bow and Elbow Rivers, effective immediately. The Bow River has exceeded safe recommended flow rates for boating, floating or swimming and it expected that the Elbow River will continue to rise over the weekend with an incoming rain event. While The City's Environmental Risk and Resilience team has advised that widespread overbank flooding is not anticipated, localized flooding remains possible and high flow rates may continue, making conditions on and near the river dangerous. Pathways near the river may continue to be affected. Water temperature remains cold and with the higher flow rates water turbidity is increased, making hazards difficult to see. “For the safety of river users and emergency responders, the Calgary Fire Department advises everyone to stay off the Bow and the Elbow Rivers until safer conditions return and the boating advisory is lifted,” says Alex Kwan, CFD's Public Information Officer. “We know that Calgarians love their rivers, yet we also know that when our waterways flow this high and fast, there's significant risk to anyone, regardless of your watercraft or skill level. Those walking near our City's rivers, including people with pets, should exercise caution as well.” Along with turbidity and debris, conditions for a Calgary Fire Department boating advisory include Bow River flow rates exceeding 280 cubic metres per second above the Elbow River confluence. Calgary Fire and its Aquatics Team will continue to monitor Calgary's waterways while the advisory is in place and will notify Calgarians when the boating advisory is removed. It is important for Calgarians near the river to be careful due to high flow levels. Calgarians are urged to: -Exercise caution around riverbanks as fast-moving water can cause erosion and destabilization. -Warn their children about the dangers of fast-moving water, particularly those residents who live near the rivers. -Cyclists and pedestrians should watch for low-lying areas where the river can submerge the pathways. -Keep pets away from fast moving water. Visit calgary.ca/watersafety for more information as well as calgary.ca/flood for the latest information on river conditions. Visit calgary.ca/pathwayclosures for up-to-date information on pathway closures.

title: Serving on the Front Line—City of Calgary Emergency Services Career Fair happening this weekend
summary: Calgarians interested in a career in public service are invited to attend the City of Calgary Emergency Services Career Fair, taking place this weekend on May 30 and 31, at the Calgary Multi-Agency Training Centre (MAT, 5705 23 Avenue SE) from 10:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. This two-day event is hosted by the Calgary Fire Department, Calgary Police Service, ALTA Paramedic Health (previously Emergency Medical Services), Calgary Transit Public Safety, Community Safety (Bylaw), and Calgary 911. All those interested in learning more are encouraged to attend on May 30, while May 31 is dedicated specifically to women who want to pursue a career in emergency services. “This event gives people the opportunity to connect directly with our teams, ask questions, and gain a clear understanding of what a career in emergency services looks like,” said Tania Tyson, Recruitment Officer with The Calgary Fire Department. “The Women on the Front Line day on May 31, is an important part of this. It's about creating space for women to explore these careers, connect with those already doing the work, and see themselves reflected in frontline roles as we continue building a diverse workforce that represents the communities we serve.” Now in its third year, this career fair continues to grow as a collaborative effort across Calgary's emergency services, reflecting the strong partnerships between agencies and a shared commitment to serving the community. Multiple agencies are currently accepting new recruits, and this is an opportunity for attendees to get a behind-the-scenes look at what it takes to be on the front line. There will be opportunities to connect with recruitment teams, experience interactive displays, see demonstrations, and gain insight into the day-to-day life of a responder. Participants will also learn more about hiring timelines, intake processes, and the qualifications required to apply. Discover how you can serve your community and register today! https://www.eventbrite.ca/e/city-of-calgary-emergency-services-career-fair-tickets-1987015055520?aff=ebdssbdestsearch https://www.eventbrite.ca/e/city-of-calgary-women-on-the-front-line-emergency-services-career-fair-tickets-1987016090616?aff=ebdssbdestsearch -30-

title: Calgary Fire Early Morning Response to Sherwood House Fire
summary: At around 12:15 am fire crews responded to the 100 block of Sherwood Crescent NW for a structure fire. Crews arrived at heavy flames and smoke coming for the rear of a two-story residential home with front attached garage. Firefighters stretched high volume fire hoses between the homes and began knocking back the fire. Crews also set up high-flow ground monitors to contain the fire and limit spread to other homes. The fire had extended up the backside of the home and into the roof. A ladder truck was set up to help protect neighbouring homes and access the roof. A fire crew made entry into the home with a hose line to extinguish hot spots in the ceiling of the second floor while other crews completed searches to confirm all occupants were out. Wind gust of over 40km/hr were reported and firefighters noted the wind shifted during this incident however crews were able to limit the spread of the fire and the response was kept at a first alarm response. A total of 17 occupants had self-exited from three homes and no injuries were reported. The exterior of two neighbouring homes sustained damaged to the exterior, but all occupants were able to reoccupy. Seven people have been displaced from the source home. A fire investigator attended the scene and fire watch crews rotated throughout the morning to ensure no reignition. While the cause of this fire is still under investigation, improper disposal of smoking materials continues to be the leading cause of outdoor fires in Calgary. To help reduce outdoor fire risks, Calgarians should make an effort to properly dispose of smoking materials. It is recommended to: Never put out cigarettes or smoking material in flower planters, peat moss, your lawn or garden. Use a deep, wide, sturdy metal container with a lid, filled part way with sand or water that should be emptied regularly. Ensure all butts and ash are out by soaking them with water prior to putting in the trash. Never discard your butts by throwing them off of your balcony, or out of your vehicle window. For more information on general fire safety and fire prevention, please visit calgary.ca/fire . -30-

title: Find your purpose: the Calgary Fire Department seeks qualified, community-minded applicants for its annual recruitment intake
summary: The Calgary Fire Department (CFD) is opening its annual application process for firefighter recruits. Anyone who meets the minimum requirements, is ready for a life of service to the community and is committed to fitness and teamwork, is encouraged to apply online from June 1-30, 2026. “Calgary firefighters are highly motivated and compassionate people who have a passion for public safety and helping others when they need it most,” says Kristin Boisjoli, Recruitment Coordinator. “We serve a fast-growing and diverse city, and we're searching for recruits who represent our values of Pride, Professionalism, Teamwork and Respect.” Calgary firefighters respond to a variety of calls, including fires, emergency medical incidents, motor vehicle collisions, and other emergencies. They also are very present in the community and can be seen at many public events, building community connections and promoting fire safety. As part of their career development, firefighters can specialize in technical rescue, aquatic rescue and hazardous materials. The CFD anticipates hiring 120-150 probationary firefighters from this posting. Last year, the Calgary Fire Department received over 2700 recruit applications while graduating 119 new probationary firefighters. With nearly 1700 firefighters on staff by the end of 2026, CFD expects to grow significantly during the next four years to keep up with one of Canada's fastest-growing municipalities. In 1999, CFD became the first Canadian fire service to receive accreditation status with the Commission on Fire Accreditation International, making them part of one per cent of fire agencies in North America to have achieved this status so far. “CFD firefighters are held to a high standard by the organization and the citizens of Calgary. They are community members themselves reflecting the city we serve, adding value to the service to the citizens of Calgary through varied backgrounds, experiences and skills,” says Fire Chief Steve Dongworth. “In many ways, firefighters are ordinary people who are trained to do extra-ordinary things,” says Chief Dongworth. “If you are considering a career in the fire service, know that it's not always easy but it's certainly rewarding and full of purpose.” The CFD is committed to supporting a safe and healthy work environment. This includes a respectful and inclusive workplace dedicated to serving Calgarians. Candidates don't need to live in Calgary to participate in the recruitment process either. On May 26, CFD is hosting a virtual information session at 6pm -8pm. Find out more about this and other upcoming Recruitment events at calgary.ca/CFDYYC . -30-

title: Calgary Fire Crews Respond to Thorncliffe Basement Fire
summary: Shortly before 3:00 a.m. on Monday, May 11th, Calgary 9-1-1 received a call from the residents of a home in the 5400 block of Centre Street NE where a basement fire was quickly growing. Calgary Fire Department crews responded immediately and, upon arrival, found smoke and flames visible from the back of the house. Crews started a quick fire attack immediately searching for any occupants. The residents of the house were alerted to the fire by one of the occupants and all evacuated. Four occupants were assessed by EHS paramedics for injuries with one of these being transported to hospital with minor burns and smoke inhalation. Fire crews rescued numerous pets from the structure. Unfortunately, one dog and two cats died as a result of the fire. Three other dogs and two cats were rescued alive and survived. Enmax and ATCO assisted at the scene with ensuring that the power and gas utilities were made safe for responders and the public. A Calgary Fire Department Fire Investigator attended the scene to determine the exact origin and cause of this fire and fire crews remained at the scene overnight to ensure full extinguishment. Working smoke alarms save lives and can reduce your risk of dying in a house fire. For more information on smoke alarms and general fire safety and fire prevention, please visit calgary.ca/fire . In a typical home fire, you may have as little as two minutes to escape from the time the smoke alarm sounds. These three important actions will help make sure your smoke alarms are an effective first line of defence: · Install smoke alarms in every bedroom, outside each sleeping area and on every level of your home, including the basement. · Test all smoke alarms, including 10-year lithium-ion battery powered alarms, at least once a month by pushing the test button and replace batteries at least once per year. · Replace smoke alarms when they are 10 years old or don't respond when tested. -30-

title: Northwest House Fire
summary: At approximately 9:25 a.m., the Calgary Fire Department (CFD) responded to reports of a house fire in the 1500 block of 23 Avenue NW. Upon arrival, crews observed smoke coming from windows on the main floor, and a working fire was declared. Firefighters initiated an interior fire attack, deploying multiple hose lines to bring the situation under control. A thorough search of the residence was conducted, and no occupants or pets were located. The structure is currently under redevelopment. CFD crews remain on scene and are actively engaged in firefighting operations at this time. There have been no injuries reported. The cause of the fire is currently under investigation. Due to ongoing firefighting activities, traffic disruptions are expected in the area, particularly along 14 Street NW and 23 Avenue NW. The public is advised to avoid the area if possible. -30-

title: Calgary Fire Responds to SE Community Lake Drowning Incident
summary: At around 7:20pm on Sunday May 3, 2026, fire crews responded to a drowning incident at a community lake in the 0-100 block of Masters Park SE. The first arriving fire crew was met by staff and directed to witnesses on the shore. It was reported that a youth had been playing basketball before deciding to jump off the dock and into the lake. Witnesses attempted to assist but the youth went below the surface of the water. The Calgary Fire Department Aquatic Rescue Team arrived, and rescuers entered the water to begin searching the last scene point. Crews reported poor visibility and cold temperatures conditions. A rescue boat was launched, and multiple rescuers conducted a systematic surface search dive while Calgary Police Services (CPS) worked with lake staff to review security camera footage and CPS' Helicopter Air Watch for Community Safety (HAWCS) provided additional aerial view support. The additional information allowed rescuers to focus the search area, and the youth was pulled from the water by rescuers from a depth of just over 6m (20 feet). Rescuers assisted with moving the patient to a waiting Emergency Health Services Alberta ambulance (EHS-AB) and two firefighters assisted with patient care at the patient was transported to hospital. Calgary Fire Department would like to thank our partners at Calgary Police Services and Emergency Health Services Alberta, along with staff at the lake and witnesses, for their assistance. Their efforts and collaboration were instrumental in locating the youth. -30-

title: National Public Safety Telecommunicators Week (NPSTW) recognizes Calgary 9-1-1 Emergency Communications Officers as call volume and complexity rise
summary: The City of Calgary proudly joins municipalities across Canada in recognizing the critical work of 9-1-1 emergency communications professionals during National Public Safety Telecommunicators Week (NPSTW), April 12–18. As the first point of contact in an emergency, Emergency Communications Officers (ECOs) play a vital role in keeping both the public and first responders safe. Before emergency crews arrive at the scene, it's the Calgary 9-1-1 ECO who is there, gathering critical information, reassuring the caller, providing life‑saving instructions, coordinating complex multi‑unit responses, and relaying critical information to help emergency crews respond quickly and safely. In addition to supporting the Calgary Police Service, Calgary Fire Department, and Community Safety Peace Officers, Calgary 9‑1‑1 serves as the fire dispatch centre for 11 regional fire departments. As Calgary continues to grow, demand for 9‑1‑1 services is increasing, with more than one million emergency and non‑emergency calls answered by Calgary 9-1-1 each year. In 2025, Calgary 9‑1‑1 saw a four per cent increase in overall call volume compared to the previous year, accompanied by growth in events created and supported across multiple public safety partners. Calgary Police Service and Calgary Fire Department events each increased by five per cent in 2025, while regional fire events rose by 14 per cent. Calgary 9‑1‑1 also supported more than 18,000 Community Peace Officer events and redirected more than 2,000 calls to 2‑1‑1, helping ensure callers were connected to the most appropriate services while reducing pressure on emergency response resources. Beyond higher call volumes, the complexity of calls has also increased. Over the past two years, the time spent on each call has risen by 10 per cent. Contributing factors include a growing number of calls requiring language services, which typically take three times longer to process and add significant complexity to emergency response. Between 2024 and 2025, calls requiring language support increased by 10 per cent. At the same time, dispatchers may manage up to 2,000 radio transmissions in a single shift, while maintaining constant awareness of responder safety and providing critical scene support. Requests from public safety partners for dispatch support at large public events and demonstrations have also increased, rising by approximately five per cent annually over the past five years. Dispatchers assigned to these events require additional, specialized training to manage heightened public safety risks. One of the largest examples is the Calgary Stampede, which continues to grow in both size and attendance, resulting in additional incident command posts and expanded monitoring needs across the city. As a result, requested dispatch support has increased from three dispatchers per day in 2023 to five per day in 2025. “Year after year, our Emergency Communications Officers and Dispatchers are handling more calls and increasingly complex situations - all while continuing to do their work with professionalism and compassion,” says Lori Bailey, Chief of Calgary 9‑1‑1. “Their work is often unseen, but its impact is felt across our community every day. National Public Safety Telecommunicators Week is an opportunity to recognize these dedicated professionals and the vital difference they make in our community every day.” -30-

title: Camp Courage Calgary applications close on March 20
summary: You have what it takes! Join the fifth Camp Courage Calgary Applications are closing on March 20, 2026, for Camp Courage Calgary – a camp for young women and gender-diverse youth, aged 15 to 18, that are interested in pursuing a career as a First Responder. Camp Courage was originally founded by Andréa Speranza in Halifax in 2006 and we are excited to offer Camp Courage for the fifth year in Calgary. Camp Courage Calgary is a free week-long camp for young women and gender-diverse youth, aged 15 to 18, who are interested in pursuing a career in fire services, policing, and/or paramedicine. The camp provides participants with the opportunity to gain firsthand knowledge of what it is like to work in emergency services, while empowering them to reach their full potential through challenging activities, leadership opportunities, and team building. “I really love being able to encourage others, especially youth who are considering a career as a first responder. Mentoring campers at the fire stations has always been a highlight for me watching them learn, grow, and accomplish new things alongside their peers is incredibly rewarding. It can be so hard for teens to figure out what they're passionate about, and choosing a career can feel overwhelming. Camp Courage helps bridge that gap by connecting them with inspiring mentors and showing them that a career like this is possible,” said Calgary Fire Recruitment Officer and Camp Courage Calgary Spokesperson, Tania Tyson. This camp is only possible through the collaborative initiative delivered by women in Calgary Police Service, The Calgary Fire Department, and Emergency Health Services. It is funded by the Calgary Police Youth Foundation and the Bridges to Brighter Futures Program, which is proudly supported by the Shaw Family Foundation. Applications Close: March 20, 2026 (Open Jan. 1 - March 20, 2026) Successful Applicants Receive Notice: May 1, 2026 Camp Dates: July 13-19, 2026 Website to Apply: https://campcourage.ca/apply/how-to-apply/ -30-

title: Devonian Gardens, the forever home for wood carvings created by beloved Calgarian Tom Ward
summary: For over 40 years, more than 30 wood carvings created by local craftsperson, Tom Ward, have been on display at Devonian Gardens . They are hard to miss when you visit the park, with their striking, watchful faces carved into knots nestled among the lush foliage of this unique indoor green space. They were loaned to The City on a handshake and a smile back in 1986. A prolific craftsperson, Tom never sold any of his creations but instead loaned it to organizations that displayed them. From the late 1960s until his death in 1984, Tom carved approximately 200 masks out of pine and spruce burls harvested from the Jumping Pound Area of Alberta. On March 6, The City and Tom Ward's family are honouring the Calgarian and his creations by signing a formal agreement ensuring the wood carvings stay on display at Devonian Gardens. “It's extremely important to our family that these carvings remain in a public place where they can be appreciated by park visitors,” said Tim Ward, Tom's son. Carving was just one of Tom's hobbies that helped him unwind after a day working in The City's planning department and later as lead for The City's first bylaw enforcement office. “My father was a prolific craftsperson,” said Tim. “While he was recovering in England following the Second World War, someone showed him how to do needlepoint. From there he started also creating rugs and then taught himself wood carving.” Tom, along with his family and neighbours, built an outdoor studio and community gathering place in his backyard. There, he would work in front of an enormous fireplace for 10 to 20 hours per week. The family also made numerous trips outside Calgary to collect logs to fuel his passion. “He got a permit from the Head of Forestry in those days to harvest dead and diseased trees that had knots,” said Tim. “We would go out in the dead of winter because the trees grew in areas with moist muskeg that were only accessible when it was really cold. So, we would trek in, cut down these logs with knots in them, carry them out then attach them to our 1950s four-door sedan and drive home.” Tom was known as a generous force of nature that was always open to sharing his time, including teaching others how to carve and shared many conversations in front of the fire. “He would look at a piece of wood and already see the creation he was going to make,” said Tim. “When he carved you could watch him take the face out of that piece of wood; that unto itself was unique.” The family feels that there really is no better place than in a park for Tom's unique wood carvings as he deeply loved the outdoors and the company of trees. “Having his carvings in Devonian Gardens is really perfect, quite serendipitous; we actually couldn't imagine them anywhere else,” said Tim, adding that he has heard this from many family members.

title: Designing a winter that welcomes everyone
summary: As Chinook Blast heads into its final weekend, festival‑goers may notice something new: practical, people‑first features designed to make winter fun more accessible to everyone – even as Calgary enjoys an unseasonably warm stretch that feels more like spring than February. A festival built for everyone Now in its sixth year, Chinook Blast brings Eau Claire Plaza and Princes Island Park Lagoon to life with art, music and winter experiences. For many Calgarians, the festival has become a bright spot in the season, and this year it's even easier to enjoy. A calm Chill Out Zone, easy‑to‑ride Ice Bikes and on‑site All‑Terrain Wheelchairs are helping more people take part in the way that works best for them, whether they're locals embracing the season, newcomers getting to know the city or families planning their long weekend outing. These features are supported by The City of Calgary's Winter City Strategy , which aims to reduce social isolation and improve access to outdoor activities and cultural experiences during the typically colder months. Even in this unusually warm stretch, the Strategy's goal remains the same: creating opportunities for people to get outside, connect and enjoy winter – whatever form it decides to take. “Winter can feel long for many people – we want to make it easier to step outside and feel part of something,” says Mary Quinlan, Project Manager with Arts & Culture at The City of Calgary. “When people can move through the festival comfortably and enjoy it on their own terms, you can see what the Winter City Strategy is meant to do. Small changes create real moments of connection.” What's new Chill Out Zone – A quiet, low‑stimulus space where people can reset, warm up or take a breather. The tent is wheelchair accessible and has already become a welcome stop for families, sensory‑sensitive visitors and anyone who needs a moment away from the hustle and bustle of the festival. Ice Bikes (Prince's Island Park Lagoon) – With skates and a wide base, Ice Bikes offer a way to enjoy the ice without needing skating experience. They are designed for a range of ages and have been constant conversation starters on the lagoon. With warmer‑than‑usual weather, availability may vary. Please check chinookblast.ca for updates and calgary.ca/rinks for ice status. All‑Terrain Wheelchairs (Eau Claire Plaza pathways) – These adaptive wheelchairs allow people who benefit from the use of a mobility device to safely explore snowy or uneven pathways around the festival. Check out The City's new Winter All-Terrain Wheelchair pilot project , which is providing the chairs available at the festival and can also be booked for use at select parks. “The Chill Out Zone shows how low-stimulation spaces can support cultural participation by giving people a place to pause, decompress and choose how and when to re-engage with the festival,” says Michelle Brandenburg, Director of Relationships at Inside Out Theatre and facilitators of the Chill Out Zone. “While it was developed with neurodivergent audiences in mind, it's been embraced by families, seniors and anyone needing a break from noise, crowds and sensory intensity – reinforcing that when access is built in, cultural experiences become more welcoming for everyone.” More than a strategy The Winter City Strategy is not just a policy document. It's a lens used by The City and its partners to design winter experiences that feel welcoming to more people. At Chinook Blast, that work includes providing these new features at no cost to the festival and attendees. Placing these options in a busy, central space gives thousands of visitors the chance to see, experience and learn about them. Celebrate the season this long weekend Chinook Blast was created to bring people downtown and energize Calgary's winter economy – a goal that continues to shine through its installations, performances and community partnerships. That spirit continues into the final weekend, which also includes The GOOD Games – Winter Edition at the BMO Centre, a celebration of inclusivity in sport that adds an extra spark of movement and connection. Discover what makes winter in Calgary vibrant, active and full of possibilities. Learn more at calgary.ca/lovewinter . -30-

title: Explore parks in a new way this winter with an All-Terrain Wheelchair
summary: When Candice McLellan visits a Calgary park with her family in the winter, she has a lot more to consider than remembering to bring mitts, hats and hot chocolate. “Having a child who is a wheelchair user makes it very difficult to get out and enjoy many parks due to how wheelchairs are built,” said McLellan. “The front caster wheels are small and easily get stuck when not on well paved surfaces. When it comes to winter, these issues are exacerbated due to snow and slush and all the uneven surfaces.” The City of Calgary's Winter All-Terrain Wheelchair (ATW) pilot project aims to make it easier for families like Candice's to enjoy our beautiful winter park spaces. Between now and early March, Calgarians can reserve an ATW to explore two parks — North Glenmore Park and Prairie Winds Park. There is no cost to book an ATW, you just need to login or create an Live and Play account. An ATW is a rugged chair designed to allow users to visit places and landscapes that would otherwise be inaccessible. These wheelchairs have extra-wide tires to increase stability on uneven or unsteady terrain and skis to help navigate snow. “We are very focused on making it easier for everyone to enjoy our parks and we recognize that for some people winter presents unique challenges,” said Mark Murias, Superintendent, Parks & Open Spaces. “Now Calgarians can borrow an ATW to explore these two parks freely, including using the wheeled version on our skating rinks and ice trails.” Executive Director of Cerebral Palsy Kids and Families Sheralee Stelter said winter creates uneven terrain and slippery conditions for their clients that can turn a simple outing into something unsafe or even impossible. This pilot is an example of inclusive programming that supports a healthy, active lifestyle year-round for individuals needing a mobility device. “Winterized All-Terrain Wheelchairs (ATW) are life-changing, but they're simply too expensive for many families who are already carrying the cost of caring for someone with a disability,” said Sheralee. “By offering them for free, the City is removing a major barrier and creating more equitable access to outdoor play and recreation for people with disabilities. “Access to outdoor spaces brings immense joy and improves both physical and mental well-being for our clients. Through our accessible equipment programs , we see increased confidence, social connection, and happiness when individuals and families can fully participate in outdoor experiences.” Once the pilot wraps up in March, Parks & Open Spaces will review the results and determine if they will extend the pilot. “We are super thankful for projects like this so that we can get out as a family in all seasons,” said Candice. “Having tried the ATW with skis in deep and hard packed snow, I was surprised with how easy it was to push. With Kanen being a teenager now, who is taller than me, I was able to run and push him with ease! I'm really excited for the chance to get out and try these chairs throughout our city.” Users can choose from an ATW with wheels to travel pathways, snowy areas and skating rinks or an ATW with skis to traverse the snow. ATWs can be used by anyone who would benefit from using a mobility device, however, there are weight restrictions and height guidelines. To find out more about the program, how to book an ATW and additional guidelines for use, visit calgary.ca/atw This is another example about how The City helps more Calgarians stay active, connected and included through the winter months. For more ideas about how to enjoy our Winter City, visit calgary.ca/lovewinter . -30-

title: Calgary's About To Get Much Hotter: Chinook Blast Unveils Full Three-Weekend Lineup To Calgary's Winter Festival
summary: Chinook Blast returns to downtown Calgary with an electrifying celebration from January 30 to February 16, transforming our coldest months into the hottest winter experience of the year. Across three action-packed weekends, Chinook Blast will fuse music, performance, sport, art, and community into a bold, FREE, all-ages winter festival at the newly renovated Eau Claire Plaza (101 Barclay Parade SW). This year, guest curators, Paul Magnuson , Victoria Bucholtz (aka Karla Marx ), and Kayla Bigras (aka Smokey Waters/B.Sassidy ) bring their creativity and experience to the festival hub, filling it with new installations, dynamic entertainment, and the kind of winter magic you can only find at Chinook Blast. From larger-than-life light installations, a drag show on ice and electronic music showcases to artist markets and live performances, Chinook Blast proves that winter in Calgary is meant to be embraced. “Chinook Blast is an event that has been building from strength to strength over the past six years, providing amazing experiences for visitors from far and wide,” says Alisha Reynolds, President and CEO of Tourism Calgary. “We are very lucky to be living in one of Canada's fastest-growing major cities, and in many ways, our winter season is just as vibrant as our summer. Chinook Blast kicks off a busy year with a sport or cultural event almost every week in the first few months of 2026, so we encourage everyone to get out and have a “cool-cation” in Calgary!” Alisha Reynolds, President & CEO, Tourism Calgary (Part of Chinook Blast's Executive Committee) WEEKEND 1 – Electrifying performances ignite Eau Claire Plaza ● Friday, January 30 - High Performance Rodeo kicks off Chinook Blast at the RISE UP Outdoor Community Stage with the dynamic duo Cedric Lightning and Kris Demeanor . Calgary Folk Music Festival's Block Heater returns with performances from L'omelette and Tribe Artist Society . ● Saturday, January 31 - Drag on Ice 4 returns with a full-on Frozen Disco Extravaganza featuring, for the first time, a queen from RuPaul's Drag Race U.S. Joey Jay of season 13 takes to the ice with Calgary's own comedian and drag queen Karla Marx at Prince's Island Lagoon. Joey Jay will also be doing a meet-and-greet with fans before the show! Then Dos Leches , DJ Molly Fi and DJ Cybervvitch take over the outdoor stage with unforgettable dance music. Between the live performances and 14 larger-than-life art installations (open to the public daily Jan. 30–Feb. 16), you'll find glowing, engaging roving performances from Three Left Feet , Le Cirque de la Nuit and Puppet Stuff Canada , and the opportunity to try drytooling, Canada's next Olympic Sport, with the Alpine Club of Canada . Then just next door, Seconds Collective Market (Jan. 30–Feb. 1) takes over the Chinese Cultural Centre (197 1 St SW) with the best vintage finds from local vendors. Plus skate on Prince's Island Lagoon! Don't have your own pair? No problem, the Skate Hut has rentals with Alberta Blue Cross offering the first 50 rentals free on selected days. WEEKEND 2 – High-energy beats meet immersive cultural experiences ● Friday, February 6 - Eau Claire Plaza will be packed with live performances from Prairie Sparks: Local Lights presented by The Werklund Centre as well as local artists Dempsey Bolton and the Cruz Brothers ( DJ Fatrok & DJ C-SIK ). Join the National Music Centre at The Dome (sponsored by Calgary Foundation) for the Canadian Song Circle, an outdoor sing-along featuring songs by iconic Canadian artists, try snow tie-dyeing with Mohar Gupta . DJ Molly Fi is back, this time spinning the beats at the Lagoon for those who want to skate their hearts out. ● Saturday, February 7 - PK Sound & Friends present - MOVE - an open-air electronic music showcase is sure to heat up the season with deep beats (using PK T8 sound system) and standout local and regional talent including, The Librarian , Esette B2B Jon Delerious , Cary Chang , Safi , DJ Hannah and Dan Solo. In collaboration with Le Cirque de la Nuit , Versions , I Love Techno YYC (ILTYYC), and B!G ART , this vibrant night blends music, art and fire spectacle where friends and family can gather and dance! Discover Cirque in the Snow! (SnowGlow Circus) with the Little Red Ball Company . All weekend discover roving performances from Three Left Feet, skate the lagoon or visit the Authentically Indigenous for the Winter Frost: Indigenous Market (Feb. 6–8) at the Chinese Cultural Centre. WEEKEND 3 – Fest finale packed with family fun ● Friday, February 13 - Calgary Opera will present Serious Family Fun: Little Red Riding Hood, the classic tale brought to life through a delightful and charming children's opera at The Dome. Asian Heritage Foundation will be taking over the outdoor stage with the ImaginAsian Showcase, featuring over a dozen artists, who will explore diverse genres of music and performances, including a dragon dance, Korean drumming, and martial arts demonstrations. ● To celebrate Lunar New Year and Chinook Blast, the Chinatown BIA presents a live ice sculpture activation (Feb. 6–13), with live carving taking place at Eau Claire Plaza on February 12 and 13. Master ice sculptors from Harbin, China, the world's largest ice and snow festival, will transform large blocks of ice into striking works of art, with additional sculptures on display throughout Chinatown. This free, family-friendly experience invites visitors to experience the artistry and cultural tradition of ice sculpting as part of Calgary's winter festival season. ● S aturday, February 14 - On Valentine's Day, Blue Jay Sessions: Amped Up! will bring Calgary's favourite singer-songwriters, including Tea Fannie and Alex Hughes , to perform collaborative high-energy sets of love songs and heartbreak anthems. ● Sunday, February 15 - YYC Music Awards , in partnership with JazzYYC , will present a vibrant showcase including Métis/Colombian singer-songwriter Damase Elis , Indigenous techno/electronic artist Sean Beaver , folk-pop phenom Maclayne , and multi-award-winning hip-hop king K-Riz & The Family . Or take a beat and watch live freeform sculpting with wood carving from Michael Penny and ice carving by Marie-Line Gagne . Plus, The GOOD Games will present a high-energy freestyle soccer showcase, led by five-time world champion Andrew Henderson . This dynamic performance blends athleticism, creativity, and modern street-soccer culture as part of the festival's sport programming. ● Monday, February 16 - Festival of Animated Objects takes over the Plaza with winter-themed roving puppets and masked characters. Ethnik Festivals returns with performances from Skinny Blaiz and Ray Val . Then Bollywood Jam with Dhanak , a high-energy fusion music experience, takes to the stage, followed by DJ Jadé , who will wrap up Chinook Blast with her genre-bending dance music. In addition to this back-to-back entertainment, Family Day long weekend at Chinook Blast will also feature engaging all-ages entertainment fit for the whole family including, Bravo Circus (Feb. 13–14) and YYC Princesses (Feb. 15–16). With Lunar New Year around the corner, the Chinese Cultural Centre will be home to a Chinese Market and Celebration (Feb. 14–16) which will include dragon and lion dances, multicultural performances, local food vendors, a marketplace, and other festive activities celebrating culture and community. A New Spot to Sip and Warm Up Chinook Blast is expanding the festival experience with a new beer garden from Eighty-Eight Brewing Co. , who will serve their signature craft beers along with mulled wine, Baileys, and other seasonal favourites to help you warm up and enjoy the winter fun. Chinook Blast brings people downtown during a traditionally quieter season, supporting local artists, performers, makers, businesses, and restaurants while activating Calgary's winter core. As a free, community-driven festival, it encourages winter participation and connection, and in past years has generated up to $15 million in economic impact. Chinook Blast continues to strengthen Calgary's reputation as a vibrant, creative, and welcoming city. “Calgary's creative economy isn't just about art, music or performance—it's about innovation, vibrancy and bright minds seeing the world with a unique lens. Events like Chinook Blast show the world that Calgary is a city where creativity fuels economic growth and builds a strong sense of community. People want to live in an inclusive city where they can work hard, play hard and feel connected, and this winter festival is proof of the creative pulse that makes Calgary that place, all year round.” Brad Parry, President and CEO, Calgary Economic Development (Part of The Chinook Blast Executive Committee) As Calgary's signature winter festival, Chinook Blast continues to anchor and energize the city's cold-season calendar. The festival is proud to see the momentum it has helped build, inspiring other major winter experiences, including The GOOD Games Winter Edition at the BMO Centre, February 13–15, Sport Calgary All Sport One City February 7–16, East End Cold Spell , and other local events, adding even more vibrancy to the season for Calgarians and visitors alike. See the full lineup, explore other winter events in Calgary, and discover food and hospitality specials at ChinookBlast.ca . -30- About Chinook Blast Chinook Blast is Calgary's signature winter celebration that unites partners from arts, nonprofit, neighbourhood, tourism, and sports communities to showcase the best of the city during the winter season. Our vision is to create a uniquely Calgary winter experience that attracts visitors globally. Learn more at www.chinookblast.ca . Chinook Blast Executive Committee is comprised of the following organizations: About The City of Calgary Chinook Blast is The City of Calgary's Winter City Strategy in action, bringing people together to celebrate the season through art, culture and community. By winterizing public spaces, supporting local businesses and creating experiences that celebrate the season, Calgary is a city where winter is something to embrace. Learn more about how to love winter at Calgary.ca/LoveWinter . For media inquiries, contact media.relations@calgary.ca or 403-828-2954. About Calgary Arts Development As the city's designated arts development authority, Calgary Arts Development supports and strengthens the arts to benefit all Calgarians. We invest and allocate municipal funding for the arts provided by the City of Calgary and leverage these funds to provide additional resources to the arts sector. Our programs support hundreds of arts organizations, individual artists, artist collectives, and ad hoc groups in Calgary. For more information, visit: calgaryartsdevelopment.com . About Calgary Economic Development Calgary Economic Development is an opportunity-maker, helping to spark and fuel Calgary's growth. Our job is to connect people with resources that can help them grow their careers or businesses, thrive in new locations or markets and feel at home in our community. We steward the economic strategy, Uplook: An Action Plan for Our Economy with the mandate to position Calgary for long-term economic success by supporting the expansion, retention and acquisition of companies, capital and talent. We offer a wealth of information to help everyone succeed and we tirelessly promote Calgary, in Canada and around the world. For more information, visit www.calgaryeconomicdevelopment.com and follow us on LinkedIn . For media inquiries, contact media@calgaryeconomicdevelopment.com or 403-880-7040. title: Chinook Blast Unveils First Look at 2026 Festival With a New Home at Eau Claire Plaza
summary: Winter in Calgary is about to feel a lot warmer with Chinook Blast blowing in from January 30th to February 16th, 2026. For its sixth edition, the festival will debut at the newly renovated Eau Claire Plaza (101 Barclay Parade SW) with an “art-full” winter wonderland featuring larger than life light installations, live music, performances, sports and an unforgettable experience for all-ages. “Calgarians know how to make the most of winter, and Chinook Blast is proof of it. This festival brings our downtown to life with the energy from our creatives, businesses, and community builders, and it reminds us why Calgary is one of the best places to live, work, and play. From live music and illuminated art to recreation and family fun, Chinook Blast continues to show the world that our city is vibrant, welcoming, and rich in opportunities.” New Year, New Winter Adventures - All Free The new location at Eau Claire Plaza is just the tip of the iceberg. This year, guest curators, Paul Magnuson , Victoria Bucholtz (aka Karla Marx ), and Kayla Bigras (aka Smokey Waters/B.Sassidy) bring their creativity and experience to the festival hub, filling it with new installations, dynamic entertainment, and the kind of winter magic you can only find at Chinook Blast. Art That Shines Bright The Plaza will shine with 14 of the best and brightest installations created by Calgary artists alongside select international works. Local highlights include a 13 metre geodesic light-up dome that anchors the site with an unmistakable glow and two Winter City Design Competition winners, Out from Under the Shadows3 and Luminisona +. International showstoppers include Electric Dandelions, a series of 28-foot-tall firework sculptures from California and The Cloud Swing, an illuminated swing that lights up with colour as you move. See the full lineup of projection mapping, LED displays, and other glowing art at ChinookBlast.ca . Live Entertainment That Turns Up the Heat It's going to be a party at Chinook Blast as the festival turns up the heat with these first big reveals. ● January 31 with Drag on Ice 4, a Chinook Blast favourite, returns bigger and better for a full-on Frozen Disco Extravaganza at the Prince's Island Lagoon. Joey Jay from RuPaul's Drag Race and Calgary's own comedian and drag queen Karla Marx will light up the ice with big wigs, bold looks, and a show that proves drag on skates is the only way to start a festival. ● The energy keeps building on February 7 as PK Sound & Friends present -MOVE- an open-air electronic music showcase sure to heat up the season with deep beats & standout local and regional talent. In collaboration with VERSIONS, ILTYYC, and B!G ART, this vibrant night blends music, art & spectacle where friends and family can gather and dance! ● On February 14, Blue Jay Sessions will bring a Valentine's Day edition packed with Calgary's favourite singer-songwriters such as Tea Fannie and Alex Hughes, performing collaborative high-energy sets of love songs and heartbreak anthems. “What began as a way to brighten the coldest months has become a winter tradition that celebrates the artists, performers, and community builders who make Calgary what it is. This year, we're welcoming a handful of international creators to join our amazing local talent for a festival that is sure to excite, inspire and delight.” - Patti Pon, Chair of Chinook Blast Executive Committee and President and CEO of Calgary Arts Development Festival Partners Bringing Crowd Favourites to the Hub Chinook Blast's Pillar Festival Partners are bringing their talent to the RISE UP Calgary Outdoor Community Stage. High Performance Rodeo kicks off the celebrations on January 30 with Kris Demeanor and Cedric Lighting. A multidisciplinary artist and Calgary's inaugural Poet Laureate (2012–2014), Kris brings his signature blend of sharp wit, storytelling, and music to the audience. Calgary Folk Music Festival's Block Heater keeps the momentum going on January 30 with two back-to-back performances, starting with L'omelette and their colourful, genre-blending art-rock sound, followed by Tribe Artist Society , an Indigenous-led Hip Hop and arts collective dedicated to mentorship, empowerment, and creative expression. Ethnik Festivals brings the vibes on February 16 with Skinny Blaizfaya, an Afropop artist, and Ray Val, a singer and songwriter, creating an energetic Family Day performance. New Market Location The markets are back with a new home and a fresh mix of local artists and businesses. The Calgary Chinese Cultural Centre (197 1 St SW), just steps away from Eau Claire Plaza, will welcome the return of Authentically Indigenous , along with Seconds Collective , Calgary's coolest vintage and secondhand pop-up market. A New Spot to Sip and Warm Up Chinook Blast is expanding the festival experience with a new beer garden from Eighty-Eight Brewing Co. , who will serve their signature craft beers along with mulled wine, Baileys, and other seasonal favourites to help you warm up and enjoy the winter fun. The full line-up for the sixth edition of Chinook Blast will be released in January 2026. As Calgary's signature winter festival, Chinook Blast continues to anchor and energize the city's cold-season calendar. The festival is proud to see the momentum it has helped build, inspiring other major winter happenings, including The GOOD Games Winter Edition at the BMO Centre from February 13 to 15 and East End Cold Spell , adding even more vibrancy to the season for Calgarians and visitors alike. -30-

title: Winter is wonderful in Calgary parks
summary: So many reasons to look forward to winter this year When temperatures dip below zero, Calgary parks come alive with winter-only experiences made possible by ice, snow and earlier sunsets. Resist the urge to hibernate by trying these winter activities available in city parks during the colder months of the year. Twinkly, cheery light displays Skies darken earlier in the winter creating the opportunity for free, fantastic light displays to take centre stage in many of Calgary's parks. Here are a few showstoppers for you to check out. Eau Claire Plaza - Snap your holiday magic here! A giant 40-foot Christmas tree steals the show, joined by a forest of festive trees, a glowing polar bear, wreaths, and more. Eau Claire Plaza is also hosting The City's New Year's Eve celebration on Dec. 31, ending the night with spectacular fireworks. Visit calgary.ca/nye for details. Prairie Winds Park - The outdoor skating rink is glowing brighter than ever—festive lights have tripled, and we've added even more fire pits and seating for the ultimate winter hangout. Confederation Park Golf Course – For 39 years, Lions Festival of Lights has lit up the night along 14 St NW north of 24 Avenue. This family-friendly free light display will be available every evening, ending after January 8, 2026. Bowness Park - The magical atmosphere created by so many trees wrapped in lights that you can see it from kilometers away is a sight not to be missed. This winter wonderland will brighten your evening walk or skate along the ice trail or lagoon. North Glenmore Park - Explore this park bursting with bright lights and fantastic winter fun including an illuminated tunnel over the ice trail, beautiful strings of light along the skating area that includes two Crokicurl rinks, curling and shinny hockey rink. So many places to skate There are so many options for getting your skate on in Calgary. We have eight outdoor, natural skating rinks , over 60 volunteer-run Adopt-a-Rinks and indoor skating . Keep in mind that the building of outdoor natural ice rinks can only start once temperatures are consistently between -7 and -12. As a result, our outdoor rinks are typically available around mid-to-late December. Visit Calgary.ca/rinks to check the status of rinks near you throughout the season. Downtown skating destinations Looking for a place to skate downtown after enjoying the festive lights at Eau Claire Plaza? Prince's Island Park lagoon skating rink is less than a five-minute walk from the plaza. Just cross the brightly lit Jaipur bridge to the lagoon. Skate rentals will be available for the first time this year and more firepits and seating has also been added. Downtown skating enthusiasts can also visit the popular rink at Thomson Family Park . Experience the beauty of enchanting ice trails Calgary's answer to the Rideau Canal is our ice trails. Visit North Glenmore and Bowness parks this winter to enjoy a skate along an illuminated natural ice pathway. At Bowness Park you skate past trees wrapped with hundreds of lights. North Glenmore Park's trails are lit by draped strings of lights and a light tunnel you can skate through. Unique winter experiences Across Calgary, winter transforms our parks, streets and neighbourhoods into spaces for connection, celebration and creativity. It's a season that offers unique experiences that are unavailable during any other season. Here are a few unique activities that you can look forward to trying this winter. Try a bicycle built for…skating?! Does the thought of gliding across ice on two thin blades make you queasy? Try an ice bike instead. Ice bikes can be rented at Bowness Park and offer a safe, stable alternative for all ages and skill levels. If you are not a strong skater, you can still join in and have fun on the ice. The front wheel of an ice bike has been replaced by skates and the back wheel moves on the ice and is surrounded by skates. It has a wide base, so you don't even have to balance, just pedal and steer as if you're riding a normal bike. These boots are made for…playing Crokicurl Try out this fun winter activity suitable for all ages — no prior experience required! All you need to do is travel to Bowness Park , North Glenmore Park , and, new this year, Barb Scott Park and bring your mitts, boots and a friend or two and you are set. Crokicurl is a large-scale version of the Crokinole board game combined with curling. The only equipment needed is the curling stones which are provided at the park during the rink's opening hours. Bowness Park has four full-sized Crokicurl rinks — three with a firepit in the middle — and a junior Crokicurl rink. North Glenmore's two full-sized Crokicurl rinks are located near the scenic ice trails. Barb Scott Park has one Corkicurl rink in the main greenspace. Plan a cozy downtown adventure This season, downtown Calgary is your ultimate winter wonderland! From free events like Chinook Blast to cozy café dates, twinkling lights, and delicious treats, there's something for everyone. Bundle up, bring your friends, and make this winter unforgettable. As Calgarians, we don't just survive winter, we celebrate it! This is your invitation to step into the heart of the city and enjoy a winter packed with festivals, activities and cozy vibes you can't find anywhere else. From November – March, check out new monthly itineraries that provide a mix of fresh, fun and unique ideas to plan your perfect downtown winter outing with friends, family, or just yourself. Plan your downtown adventure today at www.exploredowntownyyc.com. Frosty fun at Chinook Blast Chinook Blast is back for its sixth year, January 30 to February 16, 2026. Chinook Blast is Calgary's signature winter celebration that brings together partners from the arts, nonprofit, tourism and sports communities to create an event that showcases the best of our winter city. New for 2026, Eau Claire Plaza will serve as the central hub for Chinook Blast, offering a fresh, purpose-built space for winter celebration in downtown Calgary. There is so much to experience in our City parks this winter including cross-country skiing and snowshoeing, booking winter fire pits and more. Looking for more ideas on how to fall in love with winter? Visit Calgary.ca/LoveWinter

There are more than 150 volunteer-run associations that provide all kinds of social, sport, arts and cultural opportunities for Calgary's more than 200 neighbourhoods. You can find your local Community Association through the Federation of Calgary Communities here . We hope all Calgarians will find a winter holiday experience to enjoy. title: Calgary is ready for the future of 9-1-1
summary: Calgary 9-1-1 has successfully transitioned to Next Generation 9-1-1 (NG9-1-1), marking a significant milestone in this federally mandated, multi-phase upgrade to Canada's emergency communications system. NG9-1-1 replaces legacy 9-1-1 systems across Canada with a faster, more resilient Internet Protocol (IP)-based network that is capable of transmitting both voice and data. This upgrade paves the way for new 9-1-1 services in the future such as real-time text messaging and other advanced tools that will provide quicker and more accessible communication for Canadians and first responders during emergencies. While the Federal Government advises these enhancements are still several years away, Calgary's successful transition to NG9-1-1 ensures The City is ready to adopt new services as they're rolled out across Canada in the years ahead. The transition to NG9-1-1 does not change how Calgarians connect with 9-1-1. In an emergency, residents should continue to call 9-1-1 for police, fire, or ambulance services, just as they do today. “We are proud to be taking this important step forward in modernizing Calgary's emergency communications system and preparing for the future of 9-1-1 in Canada”, said Dan Heyde, Deputy Chief of Operations, Calgary 9-1-1. “When the new features become available, our technology and our team will be ready.” In addition to laying the foundation for future services, the new system brings several behind-the-scenes improvements, including enhanced cybersecurity, increased network resilience, and expanded backup capabilities. The Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) has directed all Public Safety Answering Points (PSAPs) in Canada to migrate emergency calls to the NG9-1-1 network by March 31, 2027. Calgary 9-1-1 completed the transition on October 30, 2025, well ahead of the national deadline. Once all PSAPs have made the switch to NG9-1-1, further details about the timeline for the rollout of new services and tools are expected. This milestone was made possible thanks to the dedication of The City's NG9-1-1 project team and Calgary 9-1-1 employees, with support from our City and regional partners, and in collaboration with our telecommunications partners - TELUS and Intrado. Calgary 9-1-1 answers more than one million calls each year, making us one of the largest PSAPs in western Canada. Our team of highly trained Emergency Communications Officers serve as the critical link between residents and the emergency support they need, 24 hours a day, seven days a week. For more information about NG9-1-1 in Canada, visit: Next-generation 9-1-1 | CRTC -30-

title: City of Calgary Animal Services Reduces Adoption Fees for November
summary: This November, Calgarians will have the chance to welcome a new furry family member for less. The City of Calgary's Animal Services Centre is reducing adoption fees for both cats and dogs throughout the month to help more animals find loving homes before winter. Cats: $84.52 + GST (regularly $169 + GST) Dogs: $100 + GST (regularly $225 + GST) “Every adoption gives an animal a second chance and opens space in our shelter for others who need help,” says Kathleen Dickson , Coordinator of Animal Care and Clinic Services. “We hope this price reduction encourages more Calgarians to come meet the incredible pets waiting for homes.” All animals adopted from Animal Services are spayed or neutered, vaccinated, microchipped, health-checked , and include a one-year City of Calgary pet license . These comprehensive adoptions ensure pets are healthy, identifiable, and ready to start their new lives safely. With colder weather arriving, Animal Services is also reminding Calgarians to keep pets warm and safe this season. “If it's too cold for you, it's too cold for them,” adds Dickson. “Bring pets indoors, ensure they have warm bedding, and limit outdoor time when temperatures drop.” Adoptions take place at the Animal Services Centre (2201 Portland Street S.E.) , open seven days a week. Visit calgary.ca/adoptapet to view available animals, learn about the adoption process, and schedule a visit. -30-

title: Calgary's Dale Hodges Park honoured with World Urban Park award
summary: The City of Calgary has been recognized for transforming a 40-hectare former gravel pit into Dale Hodges Park — an international-award winning natural environment park showcasing one of the largest public artworks in North America and a stormwater treatment facility. “This award recognizes what a special place Dale Hodges Park is,” said Director of Parks & Open Spaces Kyle Ripley. “I'm proud of the team that transformed this space into a vibrant, functional park that serves both the community and the environment. Their ongoing work to operate and maintain this area has helped it become a cherished gem in Calgary's park system.” World Urban Parks (WUP) recognized Dale Hodges Park as the winner of the Large Urban Park Award in the North America Region category as part of their WUP@10 Awards 2025. The awards celebrate excellence and innovation in parks, public spaces and community initiatives around the world. The award ceremony took place on October 10 during the World Urban Parks Symposium in Istanbul, Türkiye. “We received over 100 nominees from around the globe, and the quality and diversity of the projects was truly inspiring,” said Michael Boland, Chair of the WUP@10 Awards program. “The winners of the WUP@10 Awards represent the best of what our profession can achieve—parks and public spaces that connect communities, restore nature, and improve lives. It has been a privilege to chair this year's awards program and to recognize such outstanding work.” The WUP@10 Awards were established to celebrate World Urban Parks' 10 th anniversary and to recognize organizations that are making an exceptional impact on the parks and public space sector. WUP is the international representative body for urban parks, open space and recreation. Nestled along the bank of the Bow River, adjacent to Bowmont Park in the northwest, Dale Hodges Park demonstrates the value of habitat restoration and sustainable urban development that supports local ecosystems. The park is dedicated to former Calgary Alderman Dale Hodges in recognition of his 30 years of public service at The City of Calgary and dedication to the rehabilitation and preservation of this greenspace for future generations. Dale Hodges Park is one of the largest public landscape artworks in North America developed by artists Sans façon in close collaboration with City of Calgary staff and contractors including water engineers and landscape architects. Park features make the storm water treatment process visible as it travels to the Bow River through stormwater ponds, marshes, a wet meadow, streams and riparian areas. This park is intended to inspire curiosity and a deeper understanding of how our natural and human-made systems interact. Thousands of native trees, shrubs and wildflowers were planted throughout the greenspace recreating the natural prairie and riparian forest environments once found in the area. These plants offer food and shelter for local wildlife, including bees and butterflies. The park includes specially designed pathways and greenspaces that act as wildlife corridors allowing animals to move safely throughout the park. Dale Hodges Park has become a sanctuary for wildlife and a beloved destination for residents and visitors alike. To learn more, visit calgary.ca and watch this video tour through the park led by those who designed the space. -30-

title: Revitalization of Calgary's Erlton Chinese Cemetery Preserves Heritage and Strengthens Community Ties
summary: Established in 1908, Calgary's Chinese Cemetery is one of the city's oldest cultural burial grounds. At a time when Chinese residents were excluded from other cemeteries, this sacred site became a dedicated place of remembrance and community. Today, it remains a vital heritage landmark, honouring the legacy of early Chinese Calgarians and their contributions to the city's growth. The Erlton Chinese Cemetery Revitalization Project , funded through the Parks and Playground Amenities Program , balanced historical preservation, cultural respect, and modern engineering solutions, while deepening the City's relationship with Calgary's Chinese community. In June 2024, City leadership met with members of Calgary's Chinese community to begin shaping the project's scope and priorities. A site visit by a Feng Shui Master ensured that all restoration work respected cultural traditions. Community input played a central role throughout the project, guiding how fragile monuments were handled, restored, and repositioned to honour their cultural and historic meaning. By 2024, many of the cemetery's concrete monuments had deteriorated, with several broken into multiple pieces. To safeguard these fragile structures, Cemeteries staff: Carefully removed and epoxied monuments to stabilize cracks and breaks. Worked with community translators to identify inscriptions and ensure stones were returned to their correct locations. 343 monuments were included in the project, with 177 monuments restored and reset on 'Monugrid Reinforced Soil Foundations' which are a sustainable, low-carbon alternative to concrete. “This project was deeply meaningful for our team,” said Jeff Sieben, Cemeteries Operations Foreman. “Seeing these fragile monuments carefully restored and re-set, while working alongside community volunteers who treated each stone with such respect, was a memorable experience I'm proud to have been a part of.” Volunteers from Calgary's Chinese community were instrumental in revitalizing the grounds. Using eco-friendly solutions, they gently cleaned monuments and restored turf through loaming, seeding, fertilizing, and watering. “The revitalization of the Erlton Chinese Cemetery is an act of remembrance and respect. I was honoured to be part of this work with the community to ensure traditions were respected and voices heard. By honouring Calgary's early Chinese pioneers, we recognize their struggles and contributions while preserving a vital piece of our heritage and strengthening bonds with the Chinese community for generations to come,” said Ward 7 Councillor Terry Wong. All monument and turf restoration was completed by late August 2025. The project officially concluded with a Community Celebration on August 23, 2025, attended by City staff, provincial representatives, community leaders, volunteers, and families. The event recognized the hundreds of volunteer hours contributed, shared stories of cultural heritage, and highlighted the cemetery's enduring importance as a place of remembrance. By protecting 343 historic monuments—many at risk of being lost forever—through careful stabilization, accurate repositioning, and sustainable foundation technology, the project demonstrated how heritage preservation can be both respectful and innovative. “This project truly demonstrates the power of collaboration, strengthening the bond between the City of Calgary and the Chinese community” said Gary Daudlin, Cemeteries Lead. “The success of this project ensures that this cemetery continues to stand as a meaningful cultural landmark for generations to come."

title: City and partner activities for Calgary kids during Alberta teachers' strike
summary: With public school classes cancelled across Alberta due to the teachers' strike, The City of Calgary and its partners are stepping up to support families with a wide range of programs and activities for children. Contemporary Calgary More local options Find even more day activities in Calgary's Child Magazine: ATA Strike Programming and Childcare . Families can also connect with local community associations and sport organizations for drop-in programs and neighbourhood activities: Federation of Calgary Communities: Find your community association. Sport Calgary: Discover local sport organizations, “try-it” programs, and community opportunities to keep kids active and learning. Please visit calgary.ca for more details on activities for children during the strike.

title: City of Calgary Animal Services hosts two upcoming adoption events
summary: The City of Calgary's Animal Services Centre is inviting Calgarians to open their hearts and homes to a new furry friend at two special adoption events this fall. Whether you're a cat cuddler or a dog devotee, there's a perfect match waiting just for you. From September 25–27 , all adoptable cats will be available for $84.52 + GST . The following week, from October 2–4 , it's the dogs' turn to shine — all adoptable dogs will be available for $100 + GST . Every animal adopted from Animal Services Centre comes with more than just a wagging tail or a gentle purr. Each pet is spayed or neutered, vaccinated, microchipped, health-checked and comes with a one-year license . This means families can feel confident knowing their new companion is not only affordable, but also healthy, safe and ready to settle into their forever home. “These events are a wonderful opportunity for Calgarians to meet some of the incredible pets in our care and give them the loving homes they deserve,” says Kathleen Dickson, Coordinator, Animal Care and Clinic Services. “We're proud to provide high-quality, cost-friendly adoptions that not only connect people with new companions but also support responsible pet ownership in our city.” Adoptions will take place at the Animal Services Centre ( 2201 Portland St S.E. ) during regular hours of operation. Stop by, meet some four-legged friends and see if one steals your heart. For more information and to view adoptable animals, visit calgary.ca/pets/adoption

title: Council Chamber and service counters on Municipal Building's third floor receive lifecycle upgrades and modernization work to improve accessibility, functionality
summary: 1985 was a busy, memorable year in Calgary. The Calgary Centre for Performing Arts (formerly Arts Commons and now Werklund Centre) opened its doors. The young Saddledome, two years into its operation, hosted concerts by Tina Turner, Neil Diamond and Dire Straits, among others. And in October 1985, the Municipal Building opened under the proud leadership of Mayor Ralph Klein. Since then, the building's public spaces have stood the test of time and remained largely original. These spaces, including Council Chamber and the Fair Entry, City Payments Services (formerly Corporate Cashiers) and Assessment & Tax (formerly Tax Advisory) service counters are key to how we serve Calgarians. They were due for updates, and this fall, we're excited to share how we've revitalized them and incorporated contemporary design, building code and accessibility standards. Council Chamber gets a modern makeover to better serve everyone Council Chamber has received a renovation and lifecycle upgrade—making it more welcoming, accessible and functional for everyone who uses the space. This August, we completed a two-phase modernization project that refreshed the Chamber from top to bottom, with improvements that support Council, City employees and the public in a more inclusive and inviting environment. What's new? The first phase, completed in August 2024, focused on improving the workspace for Council and Administration. Updates included height-adjustable Council desks for improved ergonomics, and enhanced technology integration to better support connectivity in the Council area. The second phase, finished this August, focused on the public gallery, where Calgarians and employees sit during Council and Committee meetings. Key improvements include: New gallery seating that meets today's accessibility and ergonomic standards. Power access on select seating so guests can charge their devices. Dedicated seating for presenters waiting to address Council. New carpet, paint and acoustic wall panels to improve sound quality and rejuvenate the space. These changes are designed to make it easier and more equitable for Calgarians to participate in local government. The project budget for Council Chamber lifecycle upgrades for both phases was approximately $2 million, funded by a facility asset sustainment budget. Third floor service counters become more user friendly for patrons and frontline staff We have made some exciting changes to the Fair Entry, City Payments Services (formerly Corporate Cashiers) and Assessment & Tax (formerly Tax Advisory) service counters, a main stop for Calgarians accessing vital City services. Since the counters opened in 1985, Calgary has evolved tenfold and the demand for services provided at the counters has risen sharply. To better serve the diverse needs of our fellow Calgarians, we've added service points, modernized the layout, increased accessibility and given spaces a fresh, welcoming look. These upgrades will not only bring the space up to current design, building code and accessibility standards but also make it easier for everyone to access the essential services provided by Fair Entry, Assessment & Tax and City Payments Services. Improvements include: More Fair Entry counters. Enclosed meeting rooms for patrons who prefer to speak with City staff in private. Height-adjustable service counters for better accessibility and ergonomics. Improved layout for easier movement and less congestion. A welcome desk to provide help and answer questions. For many patrons, these service desks are a first step toward accessing vital City programs and services. These upgrades help ensure that their experience is respectful, efficient and welcoming. The overall budget for the Fair Entry, City Payments Services and Assessment & Tax service counter renovations was approximately $5 million, funded by a facility asset sustainment budget. Why it matters “These projects are about more than just replacing old furniture and finishes,” says Susan Robinson, Facilities' manager of Building Infrastructure. “We wanted these spaces to better reflect our values—welcoming, inclusive and accessible for everyone. These changes support Calgarians, Council and staff, and we believe they'll make a positive difference in how City services are accessed and delivered." And let's be honest—1985 was a great year for shoulder pads and cassette tapes, but everything from hairstyles to ergonomics and accessible design has evolved since then. These lifecycle upgrades and modernization improvements bring the Municipal Building's public spaces into the present, ready to serve the city for decades to come. Council Chamber The Council Chamber lifecycle upgrades included height-adjustable Council desks for improved ergonomics, and enhanced technology integration to better support connectivity in the Council area. The original 1985 seating in the Council Chamber's public gallery has been replaced with new seating that meets today's accessibility and ergonomic standards. Power access is available on select seats so guests can charge their devices. Third floor service counters New Fair Entry service counters and two enclosed private customer meeting rooms, designed to promote superior customer service. The Fair Entry waiting area features a kid-friendly interactive art installation called a sparkle wall, which lights up when touched and adds an element of fun to the space. Coming soon: Assisted listening devices will be available at designated counters. This technology broadcasts a signal to hearing devices to amplify sound and reduce background noise, making it easier for people with hearing loss to communicate more effectively. Coming soon: The Fair Entry waiting area will feature a bright mural to welcome patrons to the space. Coming soon: The windows along The City Payments Services area will be updated with City images.

title: Calgary's First Forest Bathing Trail Opens at Inglewood Bird Sanctuary Offering Mental Health and Wellness Benefits
summary: The City of Calgary Parks & Open Spaces are excited to open the Forest Bathing Trail at Inglewood Bird Sanctuary , Calgary's first forest bathing trail. Designed to support the well-being of Calgary's residents and visitors alike, the self-guided trail takes users on a sensory exploration of the sanctuary. The trail is certified by the Association of Nature and Forest Therapy (ANFT) — a global leader in training forest therapy guides and promoting forest therapy. While not literal bathing, forest bathing is a chance to “bathe” and be immersed in the forest surroundings. The idea of forest bathing originated in Japan in the 1980s when there was a rise in anxiety and stress-related illnesses as people in Japan were increasingly living and working in urban centers. To support the health and well-being of people living in Japan, research was conducted to determine whether spending time in forested environments was beneficial and “forest bathing” (or “shinrin-yoku” in Japanese), was created as a result. “Research shows truly being in nature – taking time to slow down and really experience the natural world - can reduce stress, improve mood, boost creativity and immunity and even lower blood pressure,” said Carmen Hindson, Manager of Parks Downtown and Centre City Operations, Calgary Parks and Open Spaces. “The Forest Bathing Trail at Inglewood Bird Sanctuary helps teach us how to be present in nature, how to appreciate our natural surroundings, and how we react when we simply be with nature.” The trail starts at a welcome sign offering trail info and proceeds to five stations along a 1-kilometer loop. Each station has a QR code linking to a recorded “invitation” created by Ken Ouendag, ANFT Certified Forest Therapy Guide and Trail Consultant based in Calgary. “Each invitation is unique, but all encourage people to be present and connect with the place through their senses,” said Ouendag. “You can follow the invitation or adapt it in whatever way feels right. We encourage you to listen to your body and give it what it needs during your time in nature on the trail.” Trail users can use their phones to scan the QR codes and listen to the invitations through headphones or earbuds. Printed invitations are available at the trail's welcome sign for those who prefer not to use a phone while on the trail. There is also a bin located under the welcome sign that includes seat mats and tarps that visitors are welcome to borrow for use while on the trail (and return to the bin when finished). The invitation at station 1 is the longest at several minutes. Subsequent invitations average around 1 minute allowing visitors the space to experience their surroundings however benefits them best. Invitations will change seasonally so visitors can return multiple times and experience nature at the sanctuary throughout the year. For more information, visit calgary.ca/forestbathing -30-

title: Teeing up connection in the Golf with Dementia program
summary: After participating in a City-run pilot project exploring dementia-inclusive golf, Joan and Dave Drader are now enthusiastic regulars in the established Golf with Dementia program. Their joy and laughter light up the course, where cheers echo as they sink putts and support one another. When Dave was diagnosed with dementia, the Draders looked for ways to stay active and socially connected. Golf with Dementia, a recreation program offered by The City of Calgary, provides exactly what they need. It's part of a broader commitment to making Calgary a welcoming and vibrant place to live for everyone, including those living with dementia and their care partners. “My husband doesn't remember that we golfed every Tuesday, but once he's here, he loves it,” Joan shares. “Even four hours after we leave, he's still talking about golf.” While Dave plays alongside a group of participants and City staff, Joan also golfs with a group of friends. Many of the women in her group also have partners navigating life with dementia. The program gives them time and space to connect with others who share similar experiences. That sense of connection is at the heart of the program. Whether it's a participant teaching staff how to dance at the tee box or a wave of laughter rolling across the green, the program is as much about community and joy as it is about golf.
