Bev Hansen, another care partner, says the program helps her partner Craig feel more like himself again. “It's night and day, his attitude,” Bev explains. “He's like a whole new person when we get him out here.” When Craig recently hit the green on his first shot, City staff celebrate the moment by adding his photo to the “I'm Celebrating…” wall at McCall Lake Golf Course. It serves as a reminder of the milestones participants can achieve through the program. Led by staff like Jenna Jepson, a Health & Wellness Facilitator and expert in dementia-friendly recreation, the program builds a community where everyone can thrive. “I can confidently say this program is not just important, it is essential for people living with dementia and in particular men living with dementia,” Jenna highlights . “Traditional programs offered for men living with dementia often do not reflect their interests, identities or needs." She adds, “care partners have an option of golfing too, which creates new relationships and support networks for them.” To keep the program running year-round, The City partners with Screen Golf Inc., a local screen golf simulator business that provides participants with a warm, accessible space to continue through the fall and winter. That consistent connection has been a lifeline for many. “We need that consistency,” Bev says. “It makes a real difference.” Programs like this reflect the commitments outlined in GamePLAN: reducing barriers to recreation, expanding recreation opportunities and making smart investments to meeting growing demand. Through thoughtful public investment, strong community partnerships and prioritizing inclusion, we're building a city that balances opportunity with quality of life — a place where everyone can feel at home. Recreation Program Specialist, Gennie Liu, says that there's a growing need for more recreation opportunities for people living with dementia. “That's why we're excited to introduce new dementia-friendly programs this fall like pickleball, skating and yoga,” Gennie adds. “These activities are all about staying active, having fun and creating meaningful moments for both participants and their caregivers.” Together, we're creating a city that's dynamic, welcoming and ready for generations to come. To learn more about our programs for people living with dementia, visit calgary.ca/dementiaprograms . -30-

title: Inaugural Calgary Municipal Golf Championship a Swinging Success
summary: The first-ever Calgary Municipal Golf Championship made a memorable debut over the August long weekend, uniting nearly 60 golfers of varying skill levels for two days of competition, community and varying weather conditions. The championship unfolded across two of Calgary's most popular municipal courses. Day one, Saturday, August 2, was held at Maple Ridge Golf Course, a mature, tree-lined 18-hole course known for its scenic fairways, strategic bunkering, and challenging layout that rewards shot-making and course management. On Sunday, August 3, players moved to McCall Lake's 18-hole course, a track that blends open fairways with water features and subtle elevation changes, offering both accessibility for newer players and shot challenges for seasoned golfers. The tournament was open to adults 18 and over, attracting a diverse group of competitors—some entering their first tournament, others bringing caddies for added support. Despite a short spell of rain on Saturday, the skies quickly cleared, and players enjoyed sunny weather for most of the weekend. It was evident when the weather cleared up that players were able to maximize their scoring opportunities. Players praised the organization and set up of the tournament. “The Municipal Championship was a great introduction to competitive golf, and I would highly recommend it to anyone who is wanting to get into the competitive scene,” said participant Josh. “The organizers and staff worked above and beyond to put on a great event, and I will definitely be competing again next year.” “The first City of Calgary Golf Championship was more than just a successful tournament—it was a true celebration of our city's passion for the game. From the first tee-off to the final putt, the energy, sportsmanship, and community spirit on display were nothing short of inspiring,” said John Faber City of Calgary Golf Lead. “We saw seasoned players and rising talent come together on the fairways. It was a proud moment for Calgary, and a strong foundation for what I know will become one of the most anticipated events in our golf calendar each year.” Participants received first tee kits at registration and were treated to both flight prizes and draw prizes throughout the event. The spirit of sportsmanship was on full display, and organizers noted the energy and excitement shared by competitors from all walks of life. Looking ahead, the City of Calgary golf team hopes to make the Calgary Municipal Golf Championship an annual event, evolving its format and offerings over time. Early details for next year's tournament are expected to be announced in 2026. Stay tuned and thank you to everyone who helped make this year's championship a hole-in-one experience. -30-

title: Rolling into a more inclusive Calgary
summary: If you roll into Southland Leisure Centre on a Saturday afternoon, chances are you'll hear the echo of a basketball bouncing across the gym floor. Follow that sound and you'll find a diverse group of Calgarians taking part in The City's weekly wheelchair basketball program, a welcoming, high-energy space that shows what it means to level the playing field. Darcy Whitaker, a team lead with Recreation & Social Programs explained the program's approach. “This drop-in adaptive program reflects The City's commitment to making recreation inclusive, accessible and equitable for all,” she said. “It's one way we're putting our equity goals into action, by designing programs where all participants, regardless of ability, can play together, learn from one another and experience the benefits of physical activity and social connection.” Greg, a regular participant, said the program changed his life. “After every session, I left with a smile on my face, feeling like I had a great workout,” he shared. “That optimism carried into my week. I started exercising more, preparing for the next session. It motivated me in ways I didn't expect.” Beyond fitness, Greg found community. A place where he felt seen, capable and connected. For programs like this to succeed, they need broad participation. “I believe it's worth mentioning that wheelchair basketball is available to able-bodied folks,” Greg said. That openness is a key part of removing social barriers, creating shared experiences that challenge assumptions and build understanding. Theresa, one of the able-bodied players, said the program deepened her understanding of what inclusion looks like in practice. “It wasn't just a chance to be active, it was a chance to participate in something that centered accessibility and dignity,” she said. “City staff were outstanding, particularly the instructor. Not just friendly, but intentional about making sure every person felt welcomed and valued.” This intentionality directly supports the principles outlined in GamePLAN , which call for dismantling systemic barriers and creating spaces where everyone feels safe, respected and empowered to participate. It's part of building a Calgary that supports connection, opportunity and well-being for residents. Murdoch, a recreation programmer with Recreation & Social Programs sees that vision come to life every week. “It's been so fun getting people of all different ages, abilities and backgrounds together for a fun yet semi-competitive game. It's more than basketball, it's connection.” And he's excited to see what comes next. “I'm thrilled to see what The City of Calgary can offer in the future for adaptive sports and fitness.” Programs like wheelchair basketball reflect more than just recreation, they're about creating a city that works for everyone. When we design public spaces with inclusion in mind, we remove barriers, foster equity and build a sense of belonging. By intentionally welcoming people of all abilities, we are shaping a city where everyone can thrive, stay connected and feel at home. “Our community cares about showing up for one another. Wheelchair basketball is one of many ways we can build a city that reflects that spirit,” Darcy added. Know someone who'd love this program? Share this story and help build a more connected Calgary. To learn more about our adaptive recreation programs, visit www.calgary.ca/adaptiveprograms .

title: How community, consistency and courage helped build a new beginning
summary: In 2015, Roxy's life took an unexpected and challenging turn. She was diagnosed with Stiff Person Syndrome, a rare condition that left her facing the reality of relying on a walker or cane for mobility. In an instant, Roxy's world shifted. One moment she was self-sufficient and moving freely. The next, she could no longer walk or stand independently. While the news was devastating, it sparked a determination in Roxy to fight for her future. “I'm full of resilience and consistency,” Roxy told herself. “I'm going to walk without a walker. I'm going to walk without a cane. I just made up my mind. Nobody would do it for me so I will do it myself.” In 2022, she started attending drop-in fitness classes at Renfrew Aquatic & Recreation Centre six days a week. These classes included Gentle Fitness which is designed to be low to moderate intensity and can help maintain strength, balance and wellness. They're also spaces where participants can build confidence in their bodies, move at their own pace and connect with others. With consistent effort and by participating in a variety of workouts, she slowly rebuilt both strength and hope. Kandi, a program specialist who led several of Roxy's classes, spoke highly of her dedication. “Roxy is a perfect example of what's possible with commitment and the right support. She started in our gentle fitness classes, and over time, her balance and stability improved so much that she now takes part in many of our higher intensity fitness classes, as well as aqua fitness. It's been amazing to witness her growth. She inspires us all”, said Kandi. “The classes, pool and gym have helped me a lot to build my muscles, to build trust in my legs and to build up my self-esteem.” Roxy explained. After a full year of commitment, Roxy accomplished what once felt impossible and achieved the remarkable feat of walking on her own. “My hard work has paid off and I'm happy,” Roxy declared proudly. “Renfrew has given me the hope that I can do it.” For Roxy, the impact goes far beyond building physical strength. The support and encouragement she received from instructors and fellow participants helped her find a sense of community and belonging. Her newfound friends at Renfrew continue to cheer her on today. “I consider everyone [at Renfrew] as family. I've built a good family here and nothing is going to separate me from this gym because it is making me what I am now and giving me that push.” Stories like Roxy's are a reminder of what's possible when people have access to inclusive spaces, welcoming programs and a supportive community. Renfrew Aquatic & Recreation Centre has recently reopened after undergoing electrical repairs. To celebrate, we're inviting the community back with free public swims and fitness classes on August 13, 2025 from 12 – 7 p.m. Register for classes at calgary.ca/RenfrewPool and click “View drop-in schedule”, then "Book now" on your selected class. T hrough GamePLAN , The City of Calgary is investing in programs, facilities and partnerships that help Calgarians of all ages and abilities stay active, connected and resilient. From renewing aging infrastructure to expanding affordable programming, we're working together to create a city that's livable, inclusive and ready for the future. Roxy's journey is just one example of how these efforts make a difference and how, with the right support, Calgarians can find strength, connection and joy in every step forward. Roxy's resilience, and the community that cheered her on, is what we're building toward: a city that works for everyone. Her story is one of many that shows how investments in recreation make a real difference. -30-

title: Finding Maple: A Story of Second Chances and Unbreakable Bonds
summary: Maple wasn't the dog Kory and his family were looking for—because they weren't looking for a dog at all. But sometimes the right dog finds you anyway. For two weeks, a fluffy German Shepherd–Australian Cattle Dog mix was spotted wandering through the neighbourhood, dodging cars, evading capture, and slowly stealing hearts. Community Safety Peace Officers responded multiple times to try and bring her to safety. Eventually, she was caught in a humane trap after suffering a broken leg—injured but still full of fight. “She'd been on the loose for a while,” Kory recalls. “I decided that if no one stepped forward to take her, I would.” The family contacted Calgary Animal Services and followed Maple's recovery. “We weren't even looking for another dog,” Kory said, “but something about her was special.” When they finally visited the shelter, they brought their resident dog along to meet her. It was a bit overwhelming at first—for everyone—but by the second visit the next day, the two dogs were getting along. On day three, Maple went home. She didn't respond to any name, except one: “Maple” was the first name she listened to. And it stuck. Since then, Maple has quickly become a beloved member of her new family. “She loves people and wants to please. She's got a bubbly personality, but she also likes to work. If you throw a ball, she'll make it her mission to bring it back.” She's smart, routine-driven, and just a little anxious at bedtime. Although, her anxiety seemed to lighten up ever since she started to take her ball to bed. One thing the family needs to be cautious of: Maple can open doors, so they now have to keep doors locked so she can't break through. Maple's new life is full of dog parks, playtime, and unconditional love. “We're outside more, we walk more, we go to the park more. It's changed us a lot.” When asked what they'd say to someone considering adopting from the Animal Services Centre, her family doesn't hesitate: “Definitely go for it. These dogs have so much to offer—they seem to be really appreciative. Maple's a total velcro dog. She's always close by.” They also had high praise for the Animal Services staff. “They were really helpful and made sure Maple was the right fit. It didn't feel rushed. They care about the dogs, and it shows.” Maple may have started her story on the streets, but thanks to the dedication of Animal Services and one family's open heart, she's now right where she belongs—home.

title: Collaborating over 40 years to create more parks in more communities
summary: Terry Hawitt spent most of his leisure time in Calgary's parks - walking through them, talking to neighbours, enjoying the views, biking on pathways and golfing. He was passionate about how these public spaces created opportunities for people to connect and build community. Terry wanted everyone to have a meaningful park experience within walking distance of their home. Helping was what he did, so he turned a discussion around the dinner table into a series of phone calls to people he knew and that was the start of Parks Foundation 40 years ago. Terry and Norm Harburn started the Parks Foundation by bringing likeminded people together to support the development of new parks that preserve Calgary's natural beauty and encourage amateur sport. As a not-for-profit organization, Parks Foundation leverages donations from individuals and organizations and partners with The City of Calgary and other organizations to enhance existing park spaces and create new ones. Terry passed away in 2021 and left behind a legacy that is enjoyed daily by people visiting park spaces throughout Calgary. His daughter Karen Hawitt often visits Terry Hawitt Vista, located along the Britannia off-leash area looking down on the Elbow River, to remember her dad and his passion for the outdoors. “Dad would walk this path to the river every day for 10 to 15 years,” said Karen. “At 91, he still walked this path. Going for a walk with Dad anywhere would take hours. He would stop at every memorial bench and read everyone's name and sometimes sit and tell stories about that individual. “He was a very vibrant, enthusiastic human being. Dad always had dreams, and they always came to fruition, somehow.” Today, Terry's vision continues through the generosity of countless donors who share his passion for creating accessible green spaces. From individuals to corporate partners, philanthropic support has been essential in making Parks Foundation's projects possible. True to Terry's belief that working together brings about beautiful results, The City of Calgary and Parks Foundation have partnered on hundreds of projects since 1985, creating more opportunities for Calgarians to enjoy nature, wildlife, and each other. “Communities often require help turning their dreams into reality,” said Sheila Taylor, CEO, Parks Foundation. “Parks Foundation helps by connecting donors and partners with relevant and innovative park and sport projects.” This partnership resulted in the creation of the bench and picnic table dedication program, amateur sport grants, numerous inclusive playgrounds , several bike pump tracks and unique projects like Alberta's first mental health park and Canada's first dementia-inclusive park (expected to open in 2026). “Parks matter to Calgarians,” said Nico Bernard, Manager, Parks & Open Spaces, Public Spaces Delivery. “They are cherished places where we play, connect with each other and immerse ourselves in nature. Together, The City of Calgary and Parks Foundation have created many more vibrant public spaces that have increased the quality of life for Calgarians.” Parks Foundation will be honouring its 40 th anniversary in several ways throughout 2025. Visit Parks Foundation Calgary for more information. -30-

title: It's a wrap on the Branching Out tree partnership program for 2025!
summary: Our Branching Out residential tree partnership program officially wrapped in June with 5000 trees going to new homes. Registration for the trees took place in April with each quadrant of the city having a designated week to apply. This year, we allocated the same number of trees to each quadrant as in 2024; 1000 each to the northwest and southwest and 1500 each to the northeast and southeast. As the northeast and southeast include areas with the lowest tree canopy in the city, they are allocated more trees as we work toward a more equitable distribution of trees across Calgary. Once registration opened for each quadrant, applications came in faster than any previous year in the Branching Out program's history. The trees allocated for northwest Calgary went the quickest with all trees spoken for in an unbelievable six minutes. Northeast Calgary registration showed the biggest improvement since last year – in 2024, there were still trees left a week after registration opened. This year, all the trees were spoken for in under an hour. Tree pickup events were held over two weekends in June, with City of Calgary Parks & Open Spaces staff onsite to help many hundreds of Calgarians find their new trees each day. Staff also handed out information on planting and watering new trees, and helped the new tree owners load up mulch, which was also provided onsite. At the end of each weekend, any leftover trees that hadn't been picked up were given away on a first come, first served basis – this proved to be a popular option for folks who hadn't been able to secure a tree during the very busy quadrant registrations. We're pleased to report that everyone who lined up at each 'first come, first served' opportunity was able to take home a new tree. Some happy new tree owners shared feedback with staff using an online survey shared via QR code at the pickup events, including: “The staff was so friendly and knowledgeable when we picked up the trees, this program was so amazing. Thank you to all the wonderful city workers who helped with this program.” “Thanks for having such a wonderful program for the citizens of Calgary. A great way to increase the urban canopy and such a varied selection.” “This is a great project! The registration and the emails explaining the process were easy to understand and provided great information. The staff was helpful, and pickup was smooth” “Very well organized, efficient, and fast. I was expecting hours in a lineup but was in and out quickly” The program was even more wildly popular this year than expected and we were blown away by the demand. “We love to see how dedicated Calgarians are to help grow our urban canopy,” said Alan Joiner, Urban Forestry Superintendent for Calgary Parks and Open Spaces. “We understand that registration for some quadrants went so quickly that there were people who hoped to secure a tree but unfortunately were unsuccessful. We want to try to ensure that everyone who wants a tree will receive one. So, we are happy to announce that in 2026 we will be providing even more trees for Calgarians. While the exact number isn't confirmed, we are looking to supply a lot more trees to go to new homes.” We're excited for another successful Branching Out in 2026 and want to say a huge thank you to Calgarians for helping grow our urban canopy! Information for Branching Out 2026 will be shared in late February/early March 2026 at calgary.ca/BranchingOut .

title: Calgarians connect through art, culture and community on Neighbour Day
summary: On Saturday, June 21, 2025, Calgarians came together across the city to celebrate Neighbour Day . It was a chance to connect with one another, build a community and highlight local creativity. This year saw the launch of the Neighbour Day microgrant, which offered up to $2,500 per event. All $70,000 in available funding was distributed, helping support 43 community events that attracted more than 20,000 Calgarians. Despite the rain, Neighbour Day 2025 was a great success, with Calgarians coming together to celebrate community spirit across the city. Among the initiatives funded through the new microgrant were painting petite chairs in Chinatown, providing wellness services downtown and decorating birdhouses in the southeast. Each reflecting the diversity and heart of Calgary's neighbourhoods. Painting community pride in Chinatown At the Chinese Cultural Centre, the Chinatown Business Improvement Area (BIA) welcomed attendees to a lively cultural event that included martial arts performances, lion dances, vendor booths and hands-on art activities. A key highlight was a chair painting station where families, children and seniors painted miniature Adirondack chairs to take home. These pieces of art served as symbols of expression and connection while honoring Chinatown's rich cultural heritage. Event attendees at the Chinese Cultural Centre painting miniature Adirondack chairs. “Neighbour Day is all about bringing the community together, connecting with one another and simply enjoying the day,” said Judy Eng-Hum, event organizer with the Chinatown BIA. “It's a chance to share stories, build relationships and celebrate what makes our community so unique.” Caring for community at Good Neighbour At the Central United Church, the local nonprofit Good Neighbour hosted the Be a Good Neighbour celebration. The organization operates out of the church basement year-round providing food clothing and trauma-informed support to low-income Calgarians including newcomers, seniors and unhoused residents. Dozens of partner agencies contributed their services, making it a true community-wide effort. Volunteers served BBQ meals while guests received free wellness services including massages, haircuts and access to health resources. Games, music and conversation brought a sense of joy and dignity to the day. With Good Neighbour being a volunteer operation, organizers welcome Neighbour Day with open arms to celebrate their community and give back to those in need. “The funding really helps grassroots nonprofits like ours afford more fun things,” said Alice Lam, co-founder of Be a Good Neighbour. “I also love that it's a citywide highlight on all the incredible neighborhoods and all the incredible volunteers that make the city run.” Birdhouses and belonging in Millican Ogden At the Millican Ogden Community Association (MOCA), the focus was on creativity and inclusion. Families gathered to paint wooden birdhouses with colorful designs and unique personal touches. The event also included music and games with a calm friendly atmosphere that encouraged meaningful connection. Zev Klymochko, vice president of MOCA, was appreciative with how Neighbour Day binds the community together with simple activities. “I think it helps people realize that we can promote neighbourhood pride,” said Klymochko. “When people attend events in their community, they don't have to go out of their neighbourhood. It strengthens that community.” Neighbour Day continues to grow Neighbour Day was first introduced in 2014 and continues to grow each year, with communities putting their own spin on what it means to connect. Whether through cultural celebration, public art or social support, the day is a reminder that great neighbourhoods are built on one conversation, one shared experience and one moment of kindness at a time.

title: Look no further than Calgary parks for free summer staycation ideas
summary: Extended hours of sunshine and school wrapping up creates more opportunities to enjoy City of Calgary parks. There is so much to explore in our City that is free, fun and family-friendly. Try something new or rediscover a park you haven't visited for a while. Checking out some, or all, of the following park activities is sure to ward off boredom and keep you — and the children in your life — busy with new adventures all summer. You're invited to the opening celebration at Eau Claire Plaza! Join us on Wednesday, July 2 at 12 p.m. for a community celebration as we officially open the newly reimagined Eau Claire Plaza. This event is a chance for Calgarians to explore the revitalized Plaza. The celebration will begin with a 30-minute formal ceremony, followed by a lively community gathering that highlights the plaza's versatile design and thoughtful integration of historic elements. Come enjoy delicious bites from local food trucks, fun giveaways, remarks from City Council and live entertainment. Everyone's welcome and we can't wait to see you! For more information, visit calgary.ca/eauclaire Free youth basketball clinics with Calgary Surge at Century Gardens This summer, The City's Downtown Strategy team and the Calgary Surge are teaming up to bring FREE youth basketball clinics and a high-energy 3-on-3 tournament to the heart of our city. The community program kicks off at the end of June, offering youth ages nine-17 the chance to sharpen their basketball skills with professional-level coaching at the Century Gardens Basketball Courts (826 8 Avenue SW). The 3-on-3 basketball tournament is happening later this summer with details coming soon. To sign-up for the priority waitlist, visit calgarysurge.ca/downtown-summer-youth-basketball-clinics . Free recreation classes downtown at Lot 6 This summer, The City's Downtown Strategy team in partnership with Recreation are proud to offer free recreation classes at Lot 6. Get ready to stretch and flex those muscles! More information will be available shortly at calgary.ca/exploredowntown. Cool off with a trip to a spray park or wading pool that you haven't visited before Check out calgary.ca/sprayparks for a list of all City spray parks and wading pools. Did you know that select parks also have aquatic wheelchairs that you can borrow for free? Tour the City's playgrounds using online map Looking for a new playground to visit? Check out the playground finder map that has all City playgrounds, including inclusive playgrounds (square icons) with something for everyone. The map includes information about the play surface for each playground (e.g., gravel or inclusive playgrounds that have accessible rubber surfaces). These are just some Calgary playgrounds; the map only shows City of Calgary playgrounds and not community or school playgrounds. To learn more about inclusive playgrounds, visit Calgary.ca/inclusiveplay . Golf, disc golf, bike pump tracks, tennis, beach volleyball and more Get active this summer! Never tried golf or haven't been golfing for years? We have a course and program for everyone. Check out Calgary.ca/golf for information about the seven City of Calgary courses, family golf nights and several youth programs and golf lessons. Our parks also have four permanent and some temporary disc golf courses for you to enjoy during a nice summer day. Take a break during your bike ride along the City's regional pathway to try a bike pump track . The City also owns and operates over 60 outdoor tennis courts . Find out where you can play beach volleyball this summer and much more at Calgary.ca. Outdoor programs and fun for the whole family and it's free Looking for outdoor activities this summer? The City offers FREE, supervised fun for the whole family. Starting in July, free summer programs are back. Whether you're a child, a youth, an adult or a family looking for quality time together, there's something good for everyone. These supervised outdoor programs are carefully crafted to foster new friendships and exciting learning opportunities. From dynamic drop-in programs like Stay n' Play, to engaging registered youth leadership initiatives, there's an activity fit for every interest and age group. Find some fun at Calgary.ca/free . Book a picnic site or greenspace, discounts in some downtown parks Grab some friends and family and have a picnic in a park this summer. You can take a chance finding a spot or pay to reserve a picnic site for a small or large group or book an entire greenspace or park . Also, this summer your event could qualify for a discounted booking fee at select downtown park spaces including Harmony Park, Sien Lok Park and Thomson Family Park. This offer applies for all of 2025 but please note that 30 days' advance notice is required to process these requests. For more information about booking your summer activity in a park, please visit Park bookings . Public washrooms in parks Parks' seasonal public washrooms will remain open typically until Thanksgiving weekend in October. Find washroom locations and operating hours at Calgary.ca . By removing cost barriers, The City ensures that everyone can participate in activities that enhance well-being and foster community connections. This approach supports the City's commitment to equity and the belief that all Calgarians deserve access to quality recreational experiences. -30-

title: City completes residential street sweeping program; thanks Calgarians for their support
summary: As Calgarians prepare to head into summer, they can do so knowing their streets are clear of debris. City crews marked the end of community sweeping on Wednesday, June 18, on time and on budget. Since mid-April, City crews of about 200 staff have been diligently working Monday through Friday to clear neighbourhoods of debris and have now completed the residential program 100 per cent on schedule. “We would like to thank Calgarians for their cooperation while our crews worked to keep our streets safe and clean for everyone,” says Chris Hewitt, Manager of Maintenance. “This is an important program that requires cooperation between Calgarians and The City.” June 18 marked the final day of community sweeping, and the entire project – 386 community sweeping days completed by our sweepers – was finished within the budget of approximately $7.5 million. Through the course of the program, the team picked up a whopping 19 million kilograms of gravel and other debris from Calgary's streets – the equivalent weight of approximately 11,875 four-door sedans. “The Spring Clean-up program plays an important role in keeping our waterways clear. Thanks to your help, we've significantly reduced the amount of debris from entering our waterways through our stormwater systems.” The success of the program is a collaboration between The City and Calgarians. Residents can recognize sweeping is coming through signs posted within their communities, but we also offer other ways to find your date, including an easy-to-use e-mail/text notification signup. “Signing up for sweeping notices is an easy way to keep yourself informed every year,” Hewitt explains. “The nice thing about notifications is you can sign up anytime at Calgary.ca/sweep and your address is saved to your account. You'll get the notifications every year without having to sign up again.” Calgary Parking also plays a key role supporting Spring-Cleanup to ensure the program is a success. Parking officers validate community sweeping bans by verifying community signage is accurate and visible to residents ahead of time. Camera-equipped cars helped to enforce temporary sweeping bans on sweeping days. “We'd like to thank Calgarians for helping us make a clean sweep,” says Todd Sullivan, Leader of Patrol and Investigations at Calgary Parking. “Our program runs more efficiently when cars are removed from the street, helping our sweepers complete their work. We thank Calgarians for their cooperation during the 2025 program.” While the residential sweeping program comes to an end, some of our sweepers will next be seen as part of the Calgary Stampede parade, keeping the route clean of debris. Additional information: The budget for the Spring Clean-up Program is approximately $7.5 million. 31 sweepers work out of nine maintenance districts across Calgary. During the program we have about 200 staff working daily to clean our streets! We sweep more than 17,000 lane kilometres of roadway. Residential roads are swept Monday through Friday. Major roads are swept overnight. On average City Crews remove between 20 and 30,000 tonnes of winter sanding materials and debris remaining from the prior winter season. The street sweeping program is a collaboration between Calgarians, Mobility Maintenance and Calgary Parking. As of June 18, 2025, over 34,175 tags have been issued by Calgary Parking.

title: Calgary Local Immigration Partnership launches campaign to highlight the importance of immigration
summary: The Calgary Local Immigration Partnership (CLIP) has launched a new campaign aimed at emphasizing the critical role immigration plays in the city's growth and development. Immigration Matters YYC seeks to foster a more inclusive community by showcasing the contributions of immigrants to Calgary's economy, culture, and social fabric. Jaya Dharan, CLIP Council's co-chair, underscores the significance of this initiative. "Immigration is vital for Calgary's economy. Immigrants bring diverse skills and perspectives that drive innovation and entrepreneurship, which are essential for our city's growth," says Dharan. The educational campaign will highlight how immigrants contribute to various sectors, including technology, healthcare, and education. "Immigrants complement the local workforce by filling critical gaps in jobs, which increases our productivity," Dharan adds. CLIP's coordinator Arevik Tokmajyan emphasizes the importance of community engagement in the campaign. "We want to create a welcoming environment where newcomers feel valued and supported. This campaign is about celebrating the diverse talents and contributions of immigrants who call Calgary home," says Tokmajyan. The campaign also aims to address common misconceptions about immigration. Tokmajyan notes, "Immigrants help expand the economy by creating new businesses and job opportunities. About 250,000 immigrants in Canada are job creators and more than 60% are middle income or above, which contributing to our tax base." As Calgary continues to grow, the contributions of immigrants will be crucial in maintaining the city's vibrancy and competitiveness. "Immigration is not just about numbers; it's about the people who bring their dreams, skills, and cultures to enrich our community," says Tokmajyan. For more information about how immigration matters to YYC, visit Calgary Local Immigration Partnership .

title: Six steps to keeping our rivers healthy
summary: Calgary is a growing city on two small rivers. When it rains, water runs off our streets, driveways and yards, and ultimately ends up in our rivers, creeks and wetlands. This runoff is called stormwater. Stormwater picks up garbage, chemicals, pet waste, salt, fertilizers, dirt and other debris, washing it into our storm drains and carrying it to our rivers. Calgary is seeing higher volumes of stormwater, which is resulting in urban flooding and more pollution flowing into our rivers. The City of Calgary and Calgarians need to work together to manage our stormwater. The City's Stormwater Management Strategy reduces the impact of flooding, ensures public safety, reduces damage to property and helps keep our rivers healthy by way of storm drains, outfalls and storm ponds. Storm drains reduce stormwater off sidewalks, streets and roads, bringing it into an underground pipe system and carrying it all the way to the nearest outfall. Outfalls are the exit points by which stormwater leaves the pipe system and enters our rivers or creeks. Storm ponds naturally treat stormwater by slowing the flow, allowing sediment and pollution to settle before entering our rivers. While storm ponds are found in newer communities, stormwater is not cleaned by a treatment plant, which is why keeping it free of pollution is critical. Clean stormwater ensures our rivers, creeks and surrounding lands, as well as local wildlife and fish, remain healthy for future generations. You can help keep stormwater clean and our rivers healthy by doing these simple actions: Point downspouts toward lawns and gardens or use a rain barrel. Limit the use of fertilizers and pesticides. Sweep up debris from your garage and driveway instead of washing it away. Wash your vehicle at a car wash instead of your driveway. Never pour anything down the storm drain. Pick up pet waste and litter and put them in the proper waste containers. What ends up on our streets, ends up in our rivers. To learn more about keeping our rivers, creeks and wetlands healthy, visit calgary.ca/stormwater .

title: Your Tax Dollars at Work: Investing in what matters most to Calgary
summary: Every day, your property taxes help run the essential services and infrastructure that make Calgary a great place to live. With 63 cents of every property tax dollar staying right here, we're able to invest in the things that matter most to Calgarians like public safety, transit, infrastructure, housing, and more. “Calgarian's receive great value for their tax dollars,” says David Duckworth, Chief Administrative Officer. “Property tax supports service like 24/7 police, fire and emergency response, and 40,000 registered and drop-in recreation opportunities.” Building a Great Place to Live From where you live to how you get around, your tax dollars are helping shape a more livable city. Since the start of 2025, close to 8,000 new homes have been added to Calgary's housing supply, giving families, newcomers, and long-time residents more choice than ever before. This growth supports a city that's evolving to meet the needs of a rising population and changing housing preferences. New additions to Calgary's housing stock include: 3,700 high-rise apartments 760 rowhouses and townhomes 480 semi-detached homes 1,700 secondary suites 1,300 single detached homes These investments are part of The City's broader efforts to expand housing options, increase supply, and improve affordability—creating vibrant, inclusive communities across Calgary. Wherever you're headed, we're making it easier to get there Whether you're heading to work, dropping your kids off at school, or meeting friends across the city, getting around Calgary should be safe and reliable. That's why The City is continuing to invest in transportation infrastructure and programs that make every day travel easier for all Calgarians. “We know that the way people move around Calgary impacts their quality of life,” says CAO Duckworth. “These investments are about more than just infrastructure, they support public safety, housing, and transit, which has helped make Calgary one of the most livable cities in North America and the world. This year's key investments include: $30 million to improve pavement quality across the city $26 million for upgrades to existing roadways $19 million to support the Calgary Transit Low Income Monthly Pass program Together, these improvements are helping to maintain essential infrastructure, expand access to transit, and keep Calgary moving as our population grows. When it's time to unwind—you've got options In addition to a vibrant local economy with restaurants, pubs, and entertainment options, Calgary offers access to more than 200 City-owned recreation facilities and over 50 operated sites, plus more than 9,000 hectares of parks and open spaces across the city. From splash parks and recreation centres to arenas and arts spaces, these are the places where Calgarians connect, stay active, and build community. And it's all made possible through continued public investment. Investing in a Safer Calgary Whether you're walking through your neighbourhood, commuting downtown, or enjoying a local event, feeling safe is essential, and it's something Calgarians consistently say matters most. That's why The City is continuing to invest in initiatives that strengthen public safety, enhance emergency response, and support community well-being. Recent public safety investments include: $31 million to increase Calgary Police Service $6 million to improve downtown safety initiatives $4 million to improve emergency response capacity These initiatives are part of a broader commitment to build a resilient city where people feel secure in their homes, communities, and shared public spaces. We're investing in what matters most, building a Calgary that works for everyone. To explore how your tax dollars are being invested this year, visit calgary.ca .

title: The City creates more homes for Calgary's wildlife in Rotary Park
summary: Adding native plants to Calgary parks creates homes for birds, bees and other wildlife and keeps these greenspaces healthy and thriving. This spring, more native plants are being added to Rotary Park in Calgary's northeast. The City of Calgary has partnered with EcoLogic Horticulture to reinvigorate the greenspace surrounding the Centre Street Bridge lion sculpture. EcoLogic Horticulture donated the native shrubs, grasses and flowers and additional plants and materials were donated by Golden Acre Home & Garden and Eagle Lake Turf Farm & Landscape Supply. This section of the park has been temporarily fenced off to allow for the site to be prepared for planting. The fencing will be removed later this summer once the plants are established. Parks & Open Spaces and the Public Art team are collaborating to beautify this section of Rotary Park while protecting the integrity of the Centre Street Bridge lion sculpture. After being subject to repeated vandalism in recent years, the sculpture has undergone careful conservation treatments. To protect the lion while maintaining public access, the Public Art team recently installed new lighting to deter vandalism and highlight the statue's historical and artistic significance—especially at night. The native planting project supports the overall conservation goals by subtly guiding respectful engagement with the artwork and integrating the sculpture more harmoniously into its park setting. Many benefits to adding native plants to your own yard and garden “A native plant is a plant species that existed in a particular area prior to European settlement of that area, or without ever having been introduced by humans,” said Caylee. She says there are several benefits of adding native plants to your yard and garden. “Native plants are well adapted to Calgary's climate and soil conditions and often require little maintenance, water and fertilizer once established,” said Caylee. “Plants suited to Calgary's climate also provide homes, food and nesting materials for pollinators and other wildlife.” There are a few ways that these water wise, native plants differ from non-native plants. “Native plants are more in tune with our seasons here in Calgary,” said Caylee. “So that means that they can be a bit slower to germinate initially and they tend to wake up a little later in the season, compared to non-native plants – they know better! In many cases, native plants establish faster and more successfully than non-natives with less help from us. This is because they evolved alongside local climate, soil and other factors giving them a competitive advantage.” Once native plants are established (meaning their roots are strong and the plant remains resilient no matter the weather) they only need rainfall or water after two to three weeks of consistent, hot weather with little rain, said Caylee. Below are some examples of native plants that grow successfully here in Calgary that we are also planting at Rotary Park. Smooth Blue Aster A drought tolerant plant that blooms in the fall, asters are known to attract bees and butterflies. They produce many flowers with bright yellow discs in the centre surrounded by striking purple petals. Smooth aster can reach up to four feet. Photo courtesy James L. Reveal, Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Canada goldenrod Low goldenrod will be planted at Rotary Park, which is very similar to Canada goldenrod. Canada goldenrod is a showy late-season bloomer that is an especially important source of pollen for native bees. Growing from three to six feet in height with large, pyramid-shaped clusters of yellow flowers, Canada goldenrod is a favourite of both gardeners and pollinators. Yarrow With feathery foliage and tight clusters of white flowers, this easy-to-grow plant is a must have for any backyard garden. Growing up to three feet in height, yarrow tolerates dry conditions and is attractive to pollinators. Yarrow blooms throughout the summer. Where to find native plants There are an increasing number of garden centres selling local native plants. Call ahead to ask which native plants they offer. Centres will often label if a plant is native or not. The Alberta Native Plant Council has great resources to help you discover plants native to Alberta. For more information on how to create a beautiful, water wise yard and garden by adding native plants, visit calgary.ca/yardsmart

title: Learn about the importance of our feathered friends during a free, family-friendly event this weekend
summary: During the 22 years Trina Vickery has worked for Parks & Open Spaces, she has seen many birds fly through Calgary's green spaces. Her favourite? The Western Meadowlark. “Growing up, it was the bird call that my grandparents would pick out when we were on the farm,” said Trina, Supervisor, Parks Programs. “It was the first bird call that I learned.” We recognize incredible feathered travellers like the Western Meadowlark and their contribution to our ecosystem on the second Saturday in May during World Migratory Bird Day (WMBD). This year, WMBD falls on Saturday, May 10 and will be celebrated at Calgary's Inglewood Bird Sanctuary from 1 pm to 4 pm. This rain or shine, free, family-friendly event requires no registration. Come learn more about migratory birds and nature, view birds using spotting scopes, take a guided walking tour and enjoy a children-focused performance. Visit calgary.ca/wmbd for more information. “Migratory birds are such an important part of our larger ecosystem,” said Trina. “They are pollinators, important in transporting seeds from one place to another and worthy of our recognition for how they help keep our natural spaces healthy.” There are many green spaces in Calgary where you can often spot migratory birds visiting city parks between mid-April to mid-September, especially Inglewood Bird Sanctuary and Ralph Klein Park. “Calgary is one of the few places that has a federal migratory bird sanctuary within city limits – and so close to downtown,” said Trina. “Most other sanctuaries are outside urban areas.” Bird enthusiasts can also expect to see different migratory birds at Ralph Klein Park than Ingelwood Bird Sanctuary. “At Inglewood, you tend to see more songbirds and waterfowl and more wading birds and raptors at Ralph Klein,” said Trina. Gulls are the true indicator that the spring migratory season has started, said Trina. “A lot of people think when they see robins that this means our migratory birds are back but it's actually the first time you see a gull that you know that the spring migration has started,” said Trina. If you are on the hunt to see migratory birds this spring, Trina suggests you go for a quiet walk at dawn or dusk and bring binoculars with you. “It has usually been when I'm by myself that I see something really interesting or cool,” Trina said. “The quieter you are, the more you are likely to see. And binoculars are a good idea because you are likely to hear them before you see them since their calls carry a long distance.” What can you do to help make our city more bird friendly? Help make our city more bird friendly by: Planting native – Plants that are native to your community provide the food and shelter birds need. You can also remove invasive plants that can take over. Making windows visible – Birds don't recognize plane glass and may collide with windows. Placing decals on the outside of windows can reduce bird strikes that can stun or kill birds. If you find a stunned bird, place it in an open box outside (with a small amount of water) to protect it from predators while it recovers. If it hasn't flown away after a day, it is worth reaching out to a local wildlife rehabilitation centre. Protecting insects – 95% of birds depend on insects at some time during their lifecycle. Ask your local garden centre how you can address pests in your yard in a bird-friendly way and avoid using pesticides and other chemicals in your yard where possible. Restraining your pets – Follow the Responsible Pet Bylaw which includes keeping dogs on leash except within the 160 designated off-leash areas in Calgary. It is especially important to keep dogs on leash while visiting natural areas to protect birds and their nesting habitats. For example, dogs aren't allowed (except assistance dogs) at Inglewood Bird Sanctuary to protect the birds that visit the park. Taking your trash with you – When you are in a park space, either put your trash in a garbage can or take it with you when you leave. For more information about migratory birds, visit calgary.ca

title: Whitehorn Community Association pop-up pantry supports families struggling with food security
summary: In the early days of 2020, when the world was reeling from the impact of a global pandemic, a simple yet powerful idea took root in the heart of Whitehorn. The community of Whitehorn witnessed the cost of groceries soaring and the need for assistance grew – that is when volunteers of the Whitehorn Community Association seized an opportunity to provide free bread to seniors struggling to make ends meet. What began as a modest offering—one item, one need—has since blossomed into a community lifeline, helping over 200 families on a weekly basis. Jenn Curley, a Neighbourhood Partnership Coordinator with The City of Calgary, supports the Whitehorn Community Association, providing support and connection to resources within The City. Jenn directly supports the community association in strengthening our neighbourhoods, making them amazing places to live, work and play. "The food security program at Whitehorn is amazing. The volunteers have tirelessly worked to ensure everyone has access to this essential need. While they make it look effortless, I know it requires immense effort and dedication,” shares Jenn. “These volunteers donate countless hours each week, driving to pick up donations, organizing the food, preparing hampers, facilitating pick-up days, and even delivering to those who need support but cannot come to the hall. The Whitehorn food security program exemplifies how community association volunteers are making Calgary a better place to live.” This initiative, now known as the Whitehorn Community Association Pop-up Pantry, owes much of its success to the incredible support from partners like Second Harvest and Guru Nanak Free Kitchen. But at its core, this program is powered by a dedicated group of volunteers, each bringing their unique skills and heart to the operation. Some gather donations, others sort and pack food, and many contribute their time to serve the families who rely on this resource. "The greatest wealth is the ability to share with those in need and in a world where food is wasted, no one should go hungry,” says one Whitehorn Community Association pantry volunteer. “The pantry does this amazingly well, impacting every facet of our lives with smiles and comfort of a better community." The pantry offers more than just food. In a time when hope and connection were in short supply, it has become a symbol of community and resilience. The success of the pantry was no accident—it is the result of the unwavering commitment and selflessness of the volunteers. "The work to help people with food insecurity that is done at Whitehorn community truly brings hope back into the world. The countless hours that volunteers spend is truly inspirational. To see people have a bit of relieve from the concern of how they are going to feed their families is awe inspiring." -Pantry Volunteer People of all ages have worked tirelessly, ensuring that there is always something available for those in need. Through their collective efforts, the pantry has transformed from a simple food distribution point into a symbol of solidarity, compassion, and shared strength. As the months and years have passed, the pantry's impact has only deepened. Families who once struggled with hunger now sit at their tables with dignity, enjoying the meals they receive. The pantry has given them more than just nourishment—it has given them a sense of belonging, a reminder that they are not alone in their struggles. A family, who has directly benefited from the pantry, shares the difference it has made to them and gives thanks to all the volunteers who made this a possibility. "You guys are the best. Everyone is nice and more patience than I would have imagined. You have helped my family so much. I'm a one income house with a lot of bills and just getting that bag or two of food every week helps so much. Thanks again for everything you guys do." It has shown them that when a community comes together, no challenge is too great to overcome. Today, as the Whitehorn pop-up pantry continues to thrive, the simple vision that started it all has become an essential lifeline for many. It serves as a powerful reminder that, in the face of hardship, compassion, resilience, and unity can transform lives.

title: Donation provides more places to play in countries with few playgrounds and keeps equipment out of landfills
summary: Well-designed, free public spaces make a community vibrant and improve the quality of life for residents. Playgrounds are one of these places. They let kids engage and interact with peers, make friends, develop language, motor and social skills and encourage physical activity. While Calgary has over 1,000 City of Calgary playgrounds – not including community and school playgrounds – there are many places throughout the world that have very few playgrounds. For this reason, when City of Calgary playground equipment no longer meets Canadian standards, we donate the pieces that would otherwise end up in a landfill to charitable organizations that repurpose the equipment. “While the equipment may no longer meet City of Calgary standards and Canadian Standards Association (CSA) guidelines, it can still be of great value and provide safe play opportunities for children in other countries after being refurbished and professionally and properly installed,” said Artur Kochanczyk, Infrastructure Lead, Parks & Open Spaces, City of Calgary. The City's Parks Infrastructure Team has repurposed playground equipment for years, donating it to various charitable organizations. In 2024, The City donated over 40 pieces of equipment to Alberta-based not-for-profit organization, Hope Mission. They collect, refurbish, transport and professionally install playgrounds in countries where children have less access to free play amenities. “(By partnering with The City), we have been able to give the gift of 'play' to orphanages, schools and communities that would otherwise never have access to developmental play,” said Deryk Kirchner, International Director for Hope Mission. “Each playground has had volunteer teams from the sponsoring groups go with a professional certified builder from Alberta to install the equipment together with local community members and hosts. Many of our builders have come from Calgary and they ensure the playgrounds are installed properly and safely.” One such playground was built at an orphanage and school in Belize where the power of having more opportunities to play was very evident shortly after the equipment was installed. “When the children come into the classroom they are chatting and already socially engaged and the teachers felt they had gained one to two hours of effective education because of the playground,” said Kirchner. In addition to providing opportunities for play, donating this equipment reduces waste by repurposing equipment that would otherwise end up in a landfill. “Our Parks & Open Spaces staff are always looking for ways to reduce waste and find a new use for materials, where possible,” said Kochanczyk. “This program to donate playground equipment that we can no longer use here in Calgary is a great example of this.” Photos courtesy of Hope Mission: Children enjoying refurbished playground equipment at an orphanage and school in Haiti. Photo courtesy of Hope Mission: A playground in Mozambique built using donated playground equipment. Photo courtesy of Hope Mission: A child enjoying a new playground built in Bullet Tree Falls, Belize. Examples of the types of playground equipment donated by The City of Calgary to Hope Mission in 2024 to be refurbished and professionally installed in communities outside Canada.

title: Charlie's Journey: From Stray to Forever Home
summary: When Charlie, a one-year-old Shepherd-Great Pyrenees mix, was found as a stray, little did he know that his life was about to change forever. His path led him to the Calgary Animal Services Centre, where he would eventually find a place filled with love. In the fall, Terry and his family were ready to expand their hearts and home by adopting a dog. They were looking for a calm companion, and when they saw Charlie's picture on the shelter's website, something clicked. They decided to meet him. "When we saw Charlie, we knew we had to meet him. He just looked like the dog we were looking for," said Eileen, Terry's wife. "But when we met him in person and gently put his head on our laps, that was it. He chose us." At first, Charlie was shy, unsure, and hesitant to come inside the house. He wouldn't even go through the front door. But as he settled in, his loving nature began to shine through. The family quickly discovered that, despite his initial shyness, he was a bundle of energy with a heart full of love. "He's a real runner," Eileen said with a smile. "He loves going to obedience school and the dog park. He adores running around at the park—he's so fast, it's amazing to watch." Winter brings joy to Charlie, as he loves the snow and can often be found running around the yard or curling up in his favourite cool spots in the house. He's quite the gardener, digging in the backyard and hiding his bones in the ground. "We were surprised at how feisty he was at first," Eileen recalled. "But we love that about him. He's got so much energy and personality. He's always finding new ways to make us laugh." Charlie enjoys his own space in the living room, watching the world through the window. He's a social dog, never growling or barking, always eager to meet people and other dogs. His temperament is lovely, and he has become a great addition to the family. "He's so gentle," said Terry. "He loves meeting new people and other dogs. He's always calm and friendly, which is exactly what we were hoping for." While he can be a bit of a toy destroyer, they've found durable toys that can stand up to his playful energy, including his beloved Kongs. "Charlie can rip through a toy in about 15 minutes," Eileen laughed. "But we've learned to keep plenty of durable toys on hand." Charlie's journey wasn't always easy. He's still a little hesitant about certain things, like the garage and the Swiffer. But each day, he grows more confident, even venturing upstairs and enjoying the comforts of the family's home. "He was so hesitant when we first brought him home," Eileen explained. "He wouldn't even go inside the front door, and he avoided the garage like the plague. But little by little, he's come out of his shell.” Charlie's new family feels lucky to have him. "We always wonder what his life was like before we adopted him," Eileen shared. "But he's so happy now, it doesn't really matter where he came from.” "As much as we were looking for a dog, we had no idea just how much happiness Charlie would bring into our lives," Eileen reflected. “He's brought so much joy and laughter, and we're so glad he's with us.” As spring and summer approach, they can't wait for more outdoor adventures with their energetic, happy boy. Charlie has found his place, and his family feels complete with him by their side. Charlie's story is a testament to the power of adoption and the unconditional love a rescue dog can bring to a family. Thanks to the Calgary Animal Services Centre, he found his forever home, and his family couldn't be happier. To view adoptable animals at the Animal Services Centre, visit our website: calgary.ca/pets/adoption.html .

title: Splash science: How we keep pool water quality top notch and how you can dive in for free this Family Day!
summary: We are inviting you to take the plunge this Family Day with free public swimming at select City of Calgary operated pools. Every splash is supported by a dedicated team working hard behind the scenes to ensure our pools are safe, clean and ready for you to enjoy. That's exactly what Madison, a Calgary student, discovered when she embarked on a mission to uncover the science of pool water safety for her grade 7 science fair. Fascinated by how bacteria thrive in different conditions, she wanted to understand how pool water is treated to prevent bacteria growth. Her journey led her to Village Square Leisure Centre, uncovering the science and the incredible efforts that keep our pools pristine. Every time you plunge into a pool, a complex dance of science and dedication is at play to ensure every swim is as safe as it is refreshing. “Our team is committed, highly invested and take great pride in the daily maintenance of our facilities,” says Bruce Ottway, recreation team lead. “With countless swimmers diving in and out every day, keeping them safe is a full-time job and one that we take very seriously. Pools must meet Alberta regulations, standards and requirements for safe operation at all times, no matter how busy we are. And with a capacity of 650 guests, we can get really busy.” “I reached out to The City because I knew they had the resources to help me with my project,” says Madison. “I was very happy when I was greeted by kind people and provided the information I needed for my project.” Bruce invited to take Madison behind the scenes to show her how we ensure pool water remains safe despite the constant activity. “When I first saw that Madison had submitted a request to discuss her science fair project, I jumped at the opportunity to showcase Village Square Leisure Centre.” Up first was a tour of the basement that houses the high-efficiency boiler system, designed to maximize energy efficiency by capturing and reusing heat and maintain the water temperature around 29-30 degrees. Although this range is ideal for swimmer comfort, preventing bacteria growth in pool water relies on more than just temperature control alone. A liquid chlorine system is used to disinfect the water park that spans approximately 225,000 square feet. This system uses sodium hypochlorite to sanitize the water by killing bacteria and other harmful microorganisms. Additionally, a sophisticated filtration system that removes physical debris and microorganisms from the water is designed to clean the entire volume of water nine times every eight hours, handling around eight million litres in 24 hours. To put this into perspective, it's like emptying and refilling about 50,480 bathtubs daily. Next, Bruce introduced Madison to the team who continuously test and monitor the water quality parameters that help maintain a safe environment every four hours. Maintaining pH levels is essential to balance chlorine effectiveness and swimmer comfort. “Bruce answered all of my questions about the filtration system and how it works,” Madison shares. “I feel very comfortable in City pools. The staff clearly care about the quality of water as it is tested multiple times a day and corrected at even the slightest change in cleanliness.” “Our standards for each City of Calgary swimming pool surpass even the highest monitoring requirements, ensuring unparalleled safety and cleanliness. We are dedicated to providing an environment where our guests can confidently enjoy our facilities every day, knowing their well-being is our top priority,” says Bruce. This Family Day, make a splash - on us! We're offering free public swimming on Feb. 17 from 1-2:30 p.m. and 3-4:30 p.m. at these locations: · Acadia Aquatic & Fitness Centre ( 9009 Fairmount Dr. S.E. ) · Bob Bahan Aquatic & Fitness Centre ( 4812 14 Ave. S.E. ) · Thornhill Aquatic & Recreation Centre ( 6715 Centre St. N.W. ) Good times with friends and family are good for everyone.

title: From Stray to Family: Titus, the Cane Corso, Finds His Forever Home
summary: For one Calgary family, their search for the perfect dog led them to a life-changing bond with a three-year-old Dogo Argentina named Titus. "I've always loved big dogs," Geoffrey shared. "Our last dog was a black Cane Corso. He was with us for eight wonderful years until we lost him. My son, who was the same age as that dog when we first brought him home, is now 16—and it was him who wanted another dog this time." Initially, the family looked through private sellers, but his wife suggested they check out the City of Calgary Animal Services instead. That suggestion led to their first appointment, where they met Titus. Titus had been waiting at the shelter for several months to find a family, so the staff were thrilled when Geoffrey showed up to meet him. “We fell in love with him right away,” he said. "The staff at the Animal Services Centre told us that Titus could be nervous around men, but we were surprised because he warmed up to us immediately.” Settling into Family Life Titus has brought a lot of joy to his new home, even as the family works on some challenges. "He still acts like a puppy sometimes," the father explained. "We're working on his leash walking because he's scared of cars, which can be tricky. But he's settling in. We've even created a way to ease his anxiety around cars—we leave treats on our car's bumper so he can enjoy them when we get back from walks, and that's helped." The family – familiar with big breeds, knew that Titus would require lots of exercise, but that wasn't a problem. “We're very active. We take Titus on three walks a day, and he loves every minute of it.” At home, Titus has become an emotional anchor as well, especially for the mother, who works from home most days. "He can sense when she's stressed and will comfort her—he's so in tune with us." Even the youngest son, who wasn't initially an animal lover, has fallen for Titus. "It's amazing to see how much Titus has brought us all together." A New Start for a Stray As a former stray, Titus' story is one of transformation. Now, he has a family who adores him and a home filled with love and activity. For the family, adopting Titus was the "greatest Christmas gift" they could imagine. “Titus has completed our family,” the father said with a smile. "He's a big dog with an even bigger heart. We can't imagine life without him." This story is a testament to the life-changing impact of adoption—and a reminder that sometimes, the perfect addition to your family is waiting for you at a shelter. To view adoptable animals at the Animal Services Centre, visit our website: calgary.ca/pets/adoption.html .

title: Downtown washroom attendants continue to enhance cleanliness and safety
summary: To further improve accessibility, cleanliness, and safety for downtown park visitors, the Downtown Washroom Attendant Program is active seven days a week at Century Gardens, Central Memorial Park and Devonian Gardens throughout 2025. Other downtown locations are also being considered and will be added throughout the year. This year's program, operated by Hiregood , launched at the end of 2024 as a key initiative through the Downtown Safety Leadership Table and positions trained attendants at select high-traffic washrooms in parks that provide a welcoming and reassuring presence for users. Supporting clean and safe public spaces Public washrooms in parks provide a vital amenity for those working and shopping nearby, allowing those spending time or attending an event in a park space to do so comfortably. "The washroom attendant program shows our ongoing commitment to creating a downtown that is accessible, safe, and clean for everyone," said Joy Norstrom with Parks & Open Spaces. Hiregood's expertise in providing an attendant program follows successes in Edmonton where emergency calls were reduced by over 90 per cent at key locations leading to expansion of the program to additional locations. Calgary is addressing downtown challenges with focused solutions. The Downtown Washroom Attendant Program is one of 28 recommendations from the Downtown Safety Leadership Table to improve safety and support those experiencing vulnerabilities. Other strategies include increasing police and security presence, expanding festivals and events as well as connecting people with essential services and supporting the housing sector by delivering additional non-market housing. Learn more about the downtown washroom attendant program at Calgary.ca/washroomattendants . -30-

title: Chinook Blast 2025 Ignites Calgary's Winter Spirit with Winterrrrific Lineup of Events
summary: Chinook Blast 2025 is back for its fifth year, running from January 31 to February 17, 2025 . This annual celebration has firmly established itself as a must-attend winter tradition, drawing Calgarians and visitors to experience Calgary and its downtown in a whole new way. This year's festival promises to dazzle with a lineup of events that highlight the best of Calgary's creativity and community spirit. Featuring a dynamic mix of live music, outdoor sports, captivating art installations, and unique cultural experiences, Chinook Blast 2025 offers something for everyone. “Winter is a season that begs participation and we answer the call with gusto. Now in its fifth year, Chinook Blast is gaining national and international recognition as a must-attend winter festival. Starting January 31st, bundle up and take part in this year's incredible lineup of outdoor sports, performances, and art installations.“ - Mayor Jyoti Gondek “Chinook Blast has become a cornerstone of Calgary's winter identity, celebrating the vibrant talent and creativity that define our city. As we mark the festival's fifth year, we're excited to share an incredible lineup that highlights the power of community collaboration. We invite Calgarians and visitors to embrace the magic of winter and create lifelong memories together!” – Patti Pon, Chair of Chinook Blast, and President and CEO of Calgary Arts Development Chinook Blast Core Programming in 2025: Discover Chinook Blast's New Festival Footprint – Stephen Avenue With feedback from past years' attendees expressing a desire for a more concentrated and cohesive experience and Olympic Plaza being under construction, we've reimagined the Chinook Blast footprint for 2025. In partnership with Calgary Downtown Association, Chinook Blast will transform four blocks of the iconic Stephen Avenue into a vibrant and immersive winter wonderland (1st Street SE to 3rd Street SW). This partnership adds another layer of excitement for families and anyone looking to embrace the winter magic of vivid lights, mesmerizing art, live performance, and family friendly excitement on the weekends. Three Weekends of Markets – This year, Chinook Blast welcomes two new market partners: Art Spot Inc. with their Under $200 Art Show and Authentically Indigenous . Alongside the Asian Heritage Foundation , these markets will offer festival-goers an extraordinary blend of shopping, culture, and community spirit. Held at a new location, The Pioneer , these markets promise a truly unique and unforgettable experience for all. Seven New Art Installations! – Stephen Avenue will be transformed into an art lover's paradise with seven never-before-seen installations debuting exclusively at Chinook Blast. From Brian Faubert's shadow mural artwork to Tonya Hart's piece INFRA, composed of adult-sized wolf sculptures, these works highlight the incredible talent of our local artists. Each piece will have you snapping photos and striking poses for unmissable Instagram moments. Live experiences and performances on Stephen Avenue – The footprint may look a little different, but the diverse lineup of artists and performances continues! Along the street, take in live music and roving performers. You might even come face-to-face with a life-size puppet! These vibrant showcases will ignite excitement and are sure to create a warm, electric atmosphere, promising an unforgettable experience for everyone! All-New Winter Sport Hub – The Confluence will be the new hub for daytime and sports programs. Whether it's skating, cross-country skiing, outdoor activities , or sports programs , this is the ultimate destination for thrills, joy, and memorable family moments . The Confluence celebrates the wonder of winter with ice skating and cross-country skiing on the site, complete with food and beverage options! Once you've had your fill outside, come inside to warm up with winter-themed movies, craft sessions, a poetry reading or a haiku writing workshop. Sport Calgary is bringing back their Sport Calgary Day at The Confluence. For this 4th iteration, visitors will get to learn, watch and dive into the excitement of unique winter activities on and off ice with try-out opportunities for free! Drag on Ice 3! – The Cabaret Company is back, back, back again for 2025! Hosted by Karla Marx and starring Kaos (Canada's Drag Race Season 4), Addi Pose, Dogii Chow and more, Drag on Ice will feature stunning drag performances at The Confluence. Stay, Dine, and Celebrate! – Turn your festival adventure into a full weekend escape! Calgary's hotels and restaurants are rolling out exclusive deals and packages to keep the fun going. Whether you're visiting from out of town or planning a staycation, the winter vibe doesn't stop at the festival. Chinook Blast Festival Partners Return! High Performance Rodeo kicks off the new year with an extraordinary showcase of theatre, music, dance, and multidisciplinary art. Experience three exhilarating weeks featuring over 190 talented artists and a spectacular lineup with 28 productions and 10 free events, from heart-wrenching marionette masterclasses to riotous clowning and unconventional book club meetings. January 14–February 2 Block Heater , powered by ATB. Calgary's dynamic winter music festival is back, celebrating a decade of ice-melting programming, with an eclectic mix of independent artists from the local scene, Canada and the globe. Experience magical performances at downtown venues, with a spectacular lineup featuring Kathleen Edwards, Basia Bulat, Black Mountain, TEKE::TEKE and more! February 14–15 Ethnik Festival returns to celebrate the rich traditions of Calgary's Afro-Canadian and Caribbean communities. This vibrant cultural gathering will showcase an impressive array of talent from Calgary, across Canada, and around the world, spotlighting creativity and connection. February 21 - Calgary Food War @ Carya Village Commons East Village. February 22 - Main Festival Celebration @ The Genesis Centre Northeast Calgary. Additional Must Visit Events This winter, East Village invites you to embrace the season with unforgettable experiences that celebrate the beauty, coziness, and adventure of the colder months. Every day after sunset until February 17, delight in a wintertime short story exhibit that moves you through four locations in the heart of East Village with Journey Through the Stars . After which, strap on your cross-country skis and hit the East Village Nordic Loop , and then warm your toes by the fire pit at the Hygge Hut . National Music Centre On February 8, in celebration of Black History Month, the National Music Centre will present a special event spotlighting the evolution of Black Canadian music, stay tuned for lineup. Visit Studio Bell on Family Day, February 17, for a jam-packed day of musical fun for all ages! Admission is free. Explore five floors of interactive activities, National Music Centre's latest exhibitions, and enjoy live performances, including a headlining set from a local favourite – soon to be revealed! Murmuration at WinSport Event Centre is an adrenaline rush for the whole family! Fascinating in their precision, enthusiasm and virtuosity, the artists of Le Patin Libre are faster on their skates than ever! Their new work – inspired by the mysterious phenomenon of flocking birds – is choreographed from simple algorithms that are made more and more complex: gliding, darting, and moving in unison, Murmuration is a high-speed performance on ice! Friends and Family discount - 15% off for groups of four or more! Discount applied automatically at checkout. Presented by Arts Commons Presents. February 12 Exposure Photography Festival The annual Exposure Photography Festival celebrates the art of photography by featuring exhibitions from internationally acclaimed artists as well as emerging and established talent from Alberta. This vibrant event serves as a dynamic hub for photographers, art enthusiasts, curators, and photography professionals worldwide to connect and engage. Sport Fans: Your Favourites Return ISU Speed Skating World Cup Top skaters return to the fastest ice in the world! Long track speed skaters from over 3 countries return to Calgary's Olympic Oval for the third ISU World Cup Speed Skating event of the season.
